title: audit-properties can report clean while sync is incomplete — the pre-flip check that can lie
description:
Found by Codex on PR #583; the code is PR #500's, already merged.

src/plugins/agent-runtime/propertyRegistrationAudit.ts builds its histogram by scanning the currently materialized `blocks` rows. If it runs during an initial download, or while the sync observer still has a staged backlog in `blocks_synced_changes`, rows that have not landed yet are simply not scanned.

## Why this one matters more than a normal stale read

`audit-properties` is advertised — in AGENTS.md — as THE workspace-wide pre-flip check: 'Use it when a property isn't migrating or before any properties-as-blocks flip.' Its whole job is to enumerate the keys a flip cannot carry.

So the failure is: operator runs it on a device mid-download, gets a clean report, concludes the graph has no unregistered keys, and flips. The keys that were in the un-arrived rows stay cell-only forever — property migration skips unregistered keys silently (propertyChildrenProcessor: no schema -> continue), and after a later cell-off cutover a fresh device has no synced representation of those values at all.

A report that says 'nothing to fix' is acted on. An empty result and an incomplete scan are indistinguishable to the reader.

## Fix direction

Refuse rather than report while either queue is outstanding: connected-and-not-downloading AND `blocks_synced_changes` empty (the runner already has both checks — see Repo.assertBackfillMayWrite, which gates writes on exactly this pair). A refusal the operator retries is cheap; a clean-looking report that is wrong is not.

Worth stating the coverage in the output either way, so a future reader can tell a complete scan from a partial one.

title: Implement BackfillCompletionClaim (synced, once-per-graph)
description:
HANDOFF from PR #508 to slice C. The WorkspaceBackfill seam is complete and safe EXCEPT for this: no production BackfillCompletionClaim exists, so Repo refuses every registration. Slice C's cell->children pass cannot run until this lands.

## What to build

`BackfillCompletionClaim` (src/data/facets.ts):
  isDone(workspaceId, backfillId): Promise<boolean>
  markDone(workspaceId, backfillId): Promise<void>

Inject via `RepoOptions.backfillCompletionClaim` at the composition root (src/context/repo.tsx, where the Repo is constructed).

The record MUST live in synced data, not `client_schema_state`. That is the whole point: every pass on this seam uploads, so N devices each running it independently is N chances to write from a stale local row and overwrite concurrent edits (apply_block_patches assigns properties_json wholesale). A local marker cannot express 'already done for everyone'. Design docs call this 'operator-run-once per workspace' (properties-as-blocks-migration.html §11).

Shape is yours to choose — a workspace-scoped record block, a column, a synced table. Watch out: whatever you pick, the claim itself is a synced write, so two devices can race to claim. Decide whether that needs to be atomic or whether a duplicate run is tolerable.

## What is already done, so don't rebuild it

The runner enforces, each pinned by its own test in src/data/internals/workspaceBackfillRunner.test.ts:
- sync gating (onSyncSettled: connected, not downloading, no downloadError) armed BEFORE the idle deferral, so an offline session schedules nothing rather than parking a promise
- preconditions asserted in THREE positions: before the scan, inside every transaction, and before recording completion. A chunked pass writes over minutes, so a single check only ever covers the first batch; and a run that finds NO candidates never calls tx, which is exactly what a partially materialized graph looks like
- staged-sync-queue drain check (blocks_synced_changes empty) — 'downloaded' is not 'materialized'
- workspace generation token, so an A->B->A revisit doesn't let an earlier visit's job write
- skipUndo, so the pass is not on the user's undo stack
- scope pinned to BlockDefault so assertNoSeedDefinitionWrites keeps applying — do NOT move it to a maintenance scope, that would hand the pass the ability to rewrite code-owned seed rows

## Still owed, tracked separately

- clearing the workspace undo stack when a migration writes (see the sibling bead). skipUndo cannot reach entries already on the stack.
- progress checkpointing INSIDE a chunked run: a mid-run abort currently re-scans from scratch on the next open. Fine for a small repair, expensive for ~650k creates.

## Testing

createTestRepo injects a local stand-in claim so the machinery stays exercised; it deliberately does NOT model cross-device visibility. Pass `backfillCompletionClaim: undefined` to exercise the refusal path.
close_reason:
Implemented on the slice C branch (PR #583), commit 8dea5ca20.

Shape: one claim BLOCK per (workspace, backfill), deterministic id under a workspace-scoped Migrations page (getOrCreateKernelPage, same as Properties/Types; tagged into SYSTEM_BLOCK_TYPES so Recents skips it). Injected at the composition root in src/context/repo.tsx via a lazily-bound repo reference.

Workspace-scoped rather than per-user is load-bearing: a shared workspace with a user-anchored claim is invisible to the other user's devices, which reintroduces the duplicate upload-carrying pass. I built the per-user version first and it was wrong for exactly that reason.

The seam's three questions, answered with measurements from a new two-DATABASE harness (real upload loop -> fake server -> deliver -> materialize), which the single-DB suites could not reach:
1. Atomicity: convergence is by STAMP. Ordered clocks -> both DBs agree on one owner and the loser backs off. Indistinguishable stamps -> neither adopts the other's row and each keeps its own claim. Duplicate runs are reachable, not theoretical. Both cases pinned in graphBackfillClaimRace.test.ts.
2. Crashed device: the claim stays held, no lease, deliberately — a lease expiring under a slow-but-alive run would re-arm the duplicate pass. Recovery is deleting the visible block. releaseClaim covers every abort the runner can see.
3. Duplicate tolerable: it has to be, given 1. Every pass on this seam must stay idempotent per row.

Also fixed while wiring: the claim's own fields are declared as kernel property seeds, not raw keys — an unregistered key is precisely what property migration skips silently, so a migration's bookkeeping must not be the one thing a migration cannot carry.

Still owed, unchanged and tracked elsewhere: undo-stack clearing (sibling bead) and in-run progress checkpointing.

title: Fuzz pack: props-as-blocks bounded suites (codec, MATERIALIZE/PROJECT, rejection sweep, convert-guard, metadata parity)
description:
Part of #430. Branch `claude/fuzz-props-children` exists (empty, at origin/master). The bounded slice of the props-as-blocks explorer findings (the stateful dual-write oracle and N-way rename permutations are tracked as heavyweights in #430). Main example corpus / harness reference: src/data/propertyChildren.test.ts.

1. **Codec round-trip across the property type zoo** — `propertyValueToChildContent` / `propertyChildContentToEncodedValue` (+ `needsEscape`, null-sentinel escaping) in src/data/propertyChildren.ts, all schema codec types (string/url/date/number/boolean/ref/json-enum).
2. **MATERIALIZE/PROJECT are a convergent idempotent pair** (src/data/internals/propertyChildrenProcessor.ts): cell→children→cell reproduces the cell; re-running either is a no-op.
3. **Un-decodable raw cell write rejection completeness** (5377a74c1): any codec type's undecodable raw value aborts the whole tx — never a silent skip or partial materialization (propertyChildren.test.ts:163 pins one example/one type only).
4. **`convertEmptyChildBlockToProperty` lattice sweep** (src/utils/propertyCreation.ts) — TWO independent holes already fixed in this one small guard (6956dfc63 cell-only check, b0392a7c9 structural-children check): sweep cell-keys × structural-child-rows × flipped/unflipped × artificially-diverged states; delete iff truly empty in BOTH representations.
5. **Child-row metadata parity** (7a34b5120): field/value child rows written under a parent write with `skipMetadata:true` must carry real metadata — differential vs the no-skipMetadata scenario.
6. **Merge-retarget scope-independence arb extension** (cedcb65c2): extend the existing referencesRecompute.fuzz generator so property-field ChangeScope varies; assertions generalized only as needed.

title: Fuzz: uploadTransactionsWithFallback retry state machine (model-based)
Fuzzing roadmap 3: history-mined + props-as-blocks targets (supersedes #372)
description:
Fresh state of the fuzzing roadmap, superseding #372 (every target listed there landed via #371/#384 — see closing comment there). This issue tracks what a **history-mining pass** (2026-07-23) surfaced: 9 miners over git fix/revert history since Jan 2026 (4 subsystem shards), all GitHub bug issues, incident-memory postmortems, and newly-landed master code, plus 3 explorers over the just-merged props-as-blocks slices A/B range (`6254cfbe1..b51975798`) — **75 patterns total**, triaged below.

## Landed from this pass
- #388 fixed → PR #427 (override keybindings install normalised, dispatch-dead spellings can't strip live defaults)
- PR #429 — SQL write-target recognizer differential fuzz (`syncedTableWriteGuard`), the guard behind the 19-day silent-sync-loss incident class

## Ready-to-implement packs (sub-issues)
Each sub-issue carries targets, oracles, and evidence; they are independent and sized for one PR each.

## Product bugs surfaced by mining (fix + pin, not just fuzz)
- #378 — three `tx.restore` call sites (`kernelPage.ts:89`, `dailyNotes.ts:133`, `dailyNotes.ts:228`) still resurrect a tombstone's stale alias claim; mirror the `stripAliasesOnRestore` fix from `dailyNotes.ts:329` + add an invariant sweep. (Implementation was scoped and started; punted with the rest.)
- `formatRelative` divergence — see the editor/shortcut-utils sub-issue: `src/plugins/recents/RecentsPageBlockRenderer.tsx`'s local formatter disagrees with `src/utils/relativeTime.ts` at `ts=0` (verified: `'56y ago'`-style output vs `''`). Unify + differential pin.

## Heavyweights (high value, high effort — pick deliberately)
- **typedBlockQuery differential interpreter** (`src/data/internals/typedBlockQuery.ts`): compiled SQL vs a pure-JS reference interpreter over generated trees/properties/query specs. The SQL three-valued-logic (NULL≠FALSE) class broke SRS due-cards to zero once already (fc2c2c4a8, 77a97bb2f, 113c64308). Flagship target of the whole mining pass.
- **Stateful bag↔child eager dual-write oracle** (props-as-blocks): extend `fuzzKernelHarness` with setProperty/unsetProperty/setProperties/raw-update ops; oracle = project-from-children == decode(cell) after every op + reconciler idempotence. Evidence: 26c92a687, b26fdd94b, 7a34b5120 each fixed one instance of this class.
- **N-way same-tx definition renames incl. swaps/cycles** (`propertyRenameProcessor.ts`): existing tests stop at n=2; the swap-safe re-key helper (f4c73b4a2) exists precisely because permutations are tricky.
- **JS §9 recognition walk vs recursive-CTE SQL twin** (`childrenOf({hidePropertyChildren})` vs `CHILDREN_S*` SQL): two independently-coded classifiers of the same relation; differential over generated trees (analogous to the existing SUBTREE_SQL-vs-JS differential in repoMutators.fuzz).
- **undo/redo TOCTOU** — #227 (concurrent tx during replay await resurrects stale redo entry); needs interleaving harness.
- **`reconcileMarkdownSubtree`** (`agent-runtime/commands.ts`): streamed-reply tree reconcile under concurrent user edits — content conservation, no orphans/reorders.
- **`runArrivalProcessors` per-row quarantine model** (`syncObserver/arrivalProcessors.ts`, landed 94b16def0): N processors × M rows × random failures — quarantined rows isolated, healthy rows always processed, no wedge.
- **`stampReferenceTarget` never-triggers-upload invariant** (66382e2be): local-only write mode; oracle = ps_crud stays empty across generated stamp sequences.
- **panelLayoutProjection close-reconciliation** (`src/utils/panelLayoutProjection.ts`): next-active-panel selection after close never picks a removed panel; layout tree stays valid.
- **eslint `no-raw-synced-table-writes` vs recognizer differential** (c3a9c9dad, 50d75bdae): generated template-literal AST shapes vs the runtime recognizer PR #429 now covers — the rule's static-fold path is the untested half.

## Smaller deferred (from the 75-pattern pool)
`uploadTransactionsWithFallback` leftovers beyond the model pack; roam-import tombstone restore-vs-preserve predicate; attachment downLane budget accounting; grouped-backlinks sticky-group stability; useDebouncedSearch staleness races; `blockedWikilinks` NFC-substring guard (agent-dispatch); readwise template-line classifier (needs extraction first); dynamicExtensionSeeds bind idempotence/WeakMap identity; type-registry two-winner-folds agreement; `harvestNestedPropertySeeds` determinism; `parseTypeDefinitionMetadata` total-parser; `injectThemeBootDefaults` codegen round-trip; scope-policy-mismatch guard sweep across write seams; export/import property round-trip (#401); schema-rename orphan cascade (#72 — partially superseded by the landed rename processor, re-check); property-derived reference retained-vs-stripped remainder; roam-import protected-range rewrite pipelines; `replaceAsync` offset tracking (social-media-publisher); TOCTOU races in `atomicFile`/`pidfile`/`channelSecret`; SRS/daily-notes calendar math (`addDaysIso`); one-shot backfill marker set-on-write-nothing.

title: Pre-flip correctness: property-machinery containment gaps (movement, ref-deletion, unguarded raw writes)
description:
Found by a 5-agent special-casing audit run during PR #386 (properties-as-blocks slices A/B).

These are **pre-flip correctness** items, filed separately from #389 on purpose: #389 tracks post-flip *healing* seams that land **with** the flip tooling, whereas these should be fixed **now, or before slice C starts**. Different phase, different urgency.

## Severity framing

Two items are **live today in every workspace** (not flip-gated). The rest are dormant until a workspace is child-backed — but they are **flip blockers rather than deferrals**: several are silent data loss, and the flip is precisely what arms them.

---

## Live today

### 1. The raw-write bug class is unguarded — `guardSyncedTableWrites` covers only the bootstrap handle

`guardSyncedTableWrites` is wired only to the bootstrap `LocalSchemaBackfill` db handle (`src/data/repoProvider.ts:405-417`). The general `repo.db.execute` surface — including the agent bridge's raw `sql execute` verb (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts:173`) — has **no guard at all**: no chunking/CAS discipline, no audit row, no processor pipeline.

This is live in **every** workspace, not only flipped ones: `typeify` (properties → `block_types`) and `NORMALIZE` (references) are not flip-gated, so a raw `UPDATE blocks SET properties_json = …` desyncs derived state today.

**Why this is the highest-leverage item in the issue:** every other entry here is a fixable instance; this is the only one that stops the *class* from regrowing. Three independent reviews have now each found a *different* missing cell in the hand-audited #402 matrix — hand-auditing is demonstrably not converging. This is the same move as the `callback-set` lint that made `CallbackSet` reinvention impossible instead of sweeping instances.

Worth noting the bridge is documented in AGENTS.md as the sanctioned way for agents to inspect and edit a live client, with nothing warning that a raw write silently desyncs all four kernel derivations.

### 2. NORMALIZE never runs on sync arrival

The Phase-2 upsert in `src/data/internals/syncObserver/materialize.ts` trusts arrived `references_json` as already-canonical and never re-verifies it locally. Currently benign *only* because every writer normalizes before upload — i.e. a latent cross-device invariant dependency with no local enforcement. Not flip-gated.

---

## Flip blockers (dormant now; silent data loss once armed)

### 3. ~~Movement mutators can relocate a property onto an unrelated block~~ — WITHDRAWN, replaced by a much smaller item

**This was filed wrongly and is corrected here.** The original claim was that `outdent` on a field row makes the owner lose a property and the grandparent gain it, framed as data loss. Two problems with that:

1. **That transfer is intended behaviour**, not a defect. Moving a field row moves the property — the coherent everything-is-a-block semantics. The PR #285 spike documents it as consistency case 7 and pins it with a test named *"reprojects both parents when a property child is moved."*
2. **The destructive mechanism I described is not reachable in the current code.** `indent` (`src/data/mutators.ts:521`) reads `visibleChildrenOf`, so a hidden field row yields `ix === -1` and it no-ops. `moveVertical` (`:647-649`) has a `findIndex(...) === -1 → return false` guard covering both branches. `outdent` (`:570`) uses the raw `childrenOf` for grandsiblings, so `parentIx` is found and the stale-read `-1` fallback — the thing that makes the spike's version genuinely destructive — is never hit.

**What actually remains is an asymmetry, not data loss.** `indent` and `moveVertical` no-op on property machinery, while `outdent` acts on it. That is harmless while field rows are hidden, but once the two-tier display makes them visible, a user will be able to outdent a property row and not indent it. Resolve it as part of designing movement semantics for visible property rows (see the #288 divergence note), not as a correctness fix.

Separately, and still worth doing: **movement semantics for property rows are undesigned in both implementations.** In the spike, `outdent`/`moveVertical` on a *value* row hits a `-1` fallback that silently deletes the property, untested. The current branch avoids it by accident of using a raw sibling read rather than by an explicit rule. Whatever the two-tier display lands on should state the intended rule and test it, rather than inheriting either implementation's accident.

### 4. Deleting a ref-target silently deletes the property

`inlineDeletedBlockReferences` rewrites every live `((id))` referrer into inlined prose when the target is deleted, with no property-child exclusion. A ref-typed value child **is** `((targetId))`, so it becomes prose and its `reference_target_id` clears. PROJECT has already run by then (kernel processors precede plugin ones, single pass, no fixpoint), so the owning cell stays stale until some later unrelated edit re-triggers PROJECT — at which point the property vanishes with no visible cause.

**This is a behavioural regression versus the cell era**, where deleting a ref target left a dangling reference with the property *retained*. It is the same failure shape as the `next-review-date` incident, where a derived-data pass silently removed ~10.5k cards' projected backlinks.

**Proposal: skip property value children in `inlineDeletedBlockReferences`, leaving `((deletedId))` intact as a dangling ref.** That restores cell-era semantics exactly — deleting a referenced block leaves the property pointing at a tombstone rather than deleting the property. Recognition is the ancestry-aware interior check; flip-gated.

**Why dangling beats inlining, decisively: inlining is irreversible, a dangling ref is not.** Soft-delete leaves the target as a tombstone, so `((deletedId))` can be fully restored — restore the block and the property snaps back. Inlined prose has thrown the id away; there is no recovering which block it pointed at. This repo has direct precedent: the dangling-refs remediation re-pointed and restored refs, which was only possible *because the ids were still there*.

Framed properly, this is not an exception to `inlineDeletedBlockReferences`'s principle but the same principle applied to a different content type. Inlining preserves *readable text*, which is right for prose; for a typed value the thing worth preserving is *identity*, and inlining destroys exactly that.

(Correction to an earlier draft of this issue: it cited `mergeRetargetProcessor`'s "rewrite the id in place" as the pattern to copy. That does **not** transfer — merge has a surviving id to point at, deletion does not. It is only useful as the contrast showing that inlining prose over a typed value is the wrong instinct.)

**Durability note.** Verified: `deriveReferenceTargetId` resolves a `((id))` block-ref purely textually with no existence or `deleted` check (`src/data/internals/referenceTargetProcessor.ts:60`), so the stamp survives the target's deletion, the value child stays parseable, and the property survives a full re-materialization from children. Worth naming the real asymmetry versus the cell era though: there, a dangling id was *inert data* nothing re-derived; here the cell is a projection, so the id's survival is a live derivation chain — only as durable as the set of passes that might rewrite or delete a value child. That is an argument for items 5 and 1, not against this fix.

### 5. Find-and-replace writes content with no codec validation

`applyContentReplaceMutator` (`src/plugins/find-replace/dataExtension.ts:138-196`) writes straight to `content` via `tx.update`. Replacing text inside a `number` / `date` / `boolean` value child can make it fail its codec; PROJECT's `firstProjectedFieldValue` then silently skips the unparseable child and drops the property key, with no error surfaced to the user who ran the replace. A programmatic-scale version of the "users type arbitrary text into typed properties" case.

### 6. ~~Sync-driven hard-delete never reprojects the old parent~~ — DOCUMENTED ASSUMPTION, won't-fix (Vlad, 2026-07-20)

`DELETE_BLOCK_SQL` (`syncObserver/materialize.ts`) removes a hard-deleted row without reprojecting its owner. If the removed row was a property field/value child in a flipped workspace, the owner's projected cell keeps the now-orphaned key.

**Decision: don't fix on the arrival path.** Reprojecting on arrival means writing `properties_json` — a SYNCED column — from the sync path, which is a categorically different move than the local-only derivations that path is allowed to make (deriving it locally would never reach the server and every peer would recompute its own; see the `arrivalProcessors.ts` invariant). Not worth taking that on for a case that isn't reachable in normal operation.

**Why it's not reachable normally.** A user delete is a SOFT delete (`deleted = 1`, an UPDATE) — it arrives as an upsert, not a `removed`, and the deleting device already ran PROJECT and uploaded the corrected cell, so peers converge. A `removed` is a physical row disappearance: either a **stream-exit** (scope-granular — it takes the parent too, so nothing local is left to reproject) or an **out-of-band individual-block hard delete** (manual server SQL / admin op / a hypothetical block-level GC — none exist as a normal path today). Only that last case strands a cell.

**Recovery if it ever happens:** the parent's next content edit re-triggers PROJECT locally, or a manual reproject. **Revisit if** a routine server-side individual-block hard-delete is ever introduced. Recorded as a code comment at the `DELETE_BLOCK_SQL` site.

### 7. ~~Recognition divergence: SQL and JS disagree on unmaterialized seed definitions~~ — MOVED to #389 item 7

**Not a pre-flip item.** Re-triaged 2026-07-19: this is dormant until a workspace is child-backed, and what it actually breaks is the **invisibility half** that *gates* the slice-C flip (§11) — the blanket hide that keeps C's backfill from dumping raw `((fieldId))` rows into production outlines before slice D's tree UI exists. That is flip-gated containment, which is #389's bucket (it sits directly alongside #389 item 4, whose proposed fix — a deterministic seed-id check instead of the registry resolver — is the same mechanism).

Two refinements found while auditing, both carried over:

- **There is a second window.** Besides boot-before-materialization (closed operationally by the slice-C runbook), a field row can arrive over sync *ahead of its definition block* on an already-warm device — which no boot-time ordering rule covers. That window is what makes this worth fixing rather than documenting.
- **Only the SEED half is a divergence.** For user-authored definitions neither side knows the definition until the block arrives, so both answer "not a definition" — consistent and self-healing, not a divergence.

Also recorded there: converging the *other* direction (making the tx layer forget seeds) is not an option, because that same checker is the write-side positional gate (`txEngine.isInsidePropertySubtree` / `isProspectiveFieldRow`), where under-recognizing lets the `setProperty` dual-write nest machinery that recognition can never reclaim.

### 8. Smaller items

- **Copy drops user content nested under a property value.** `serializeBlock` (`src/utils/copy.ts:17`) builds the clipboard from `subtree({hidePropertyChildren: true})`; because the filter excludes the field row, nothing in its subtree is visited — including ordinary user content under a value child.
- **`src/data/repo.ts` (~2830)** hand-rolls `sibling.referenceTargetId !== change.fieldId` instead of calling `isPropertyFieldInstance`.
- **SQL ancestor walks lack a visited-guard.** The "up" walks in `treeQueries.ts` and `backlinks/query.ts` lack the cycle guard their descendant-CTE siblings have (see #183) — classification still converges, but it spins to the depth cap on a cyclic DB.

---

## Suggested order

1. **Item 1 (the guard)** first — the only item that prevents regrowth, and live today.
2. **Item 4** before slice C — silent, irreversible data loss.
3. Items 2, 5, 6 alongside.
4. Items 7, 8 opportunistically. Item 3 is withdrawn as a correctness item; its residue belongs to the two-tier display design.

## Related

- **#389** — post-flip *healing* seams (recognition invalidation, background-workspace recognition, backfills). Lands with the flip tooling; different phase from this issue.
- **#402** — same-tx derivation liveness. Item 1 here is its structural sibling: #402 stops a derivation going stale *inside* the pipeline; item 1 stops writes bypassing the pipeline entirely.
- **PR #386** — where the audit was run.

---

## Verified correct

Recorded so the audit reads as complete rather than partial. No gap found in: undo/redo and `repo._replay` (atomic and consistent across property writes); direct delete of a field row or value child (reprojects correctly); outline keyboard navigation (machinery structurally unreachable); block merge (explicitly property-aware); export (`export_document` uses the visible view); and the in-pipeline write paths — `txEngine` primitives, `WorkspaceBackfill` and all its users, the post-commit processors (each opens its own fresh `repo.tx`), `typeTagger`, the local-schema backfills, and the schema migrations.

title: Sync: merged echo can share the author's local stamp — equal-stamp skip hides the other device's concurrent edit
description:
Found by the new two-repo convergence fuzzer (issue #372 Batch 3) on its first deep run. Minimized repro is deterministic; see the suite (`src/data/test/twoRepoConvergence.fuzz.test.ts`) with `FUZZ_SEED=2019987000 FUZZ_PATH="9:4:4:4:6:8:8:2:3:3:3:4:4:4:5:6:6:6:6:7:7:7"`.

## Observed fingerprint

Device A and device B both edit the same row before syncing. After full quiescence (all uploads drained, all deliveries materialized):

- server row = B's content + A's properties, `updated_at = S`
- device B row = same as server ✅
- **device A row = A's stale base + A's properties, `updated_at = S`** — A never materializes the merged row and permanently misses B's edit (until some future write to that row bumps past `S`).

## Mechanism (verified against the real trigger SQL and reproduced through the real upload pipeline)

`blocks_clamp_updated_at` (migration `20260612000000`, UPDATE path) computes, for a content-changing patch:

```
NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at)      -- floor
NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at + 1)  -- content bump
```

The `+1` guarantees the merged stamp strictly exceeds the **old server stamp** — the trigger comment says its goal is that "a peer sitting at OLD.updated_at sees a strictly-greater stamp", and that works (B applies A's merge). But when the client-proposed stamp wins the `greatest` (i.e. the patch author's wall clock is ahead of `OLD.updated_at + 1` — the *common* case for a genuinely-later concurrent edit), the merged row's stamp **equals the author's local stamp**. The author's echo then hits `decideStagingRow`'s equal-nonzero-stamp skip (`reconcile.ts` invariant I1), which assumes equal nonzero stamps ⟺ identical content. That assumption is sound between successive *server* states but false between a device's local row and a server row that merged someone else's change beneath that device's own patch.

Timeline of the minimized case (deterministic clocks; all stamps abbreviated):

1. B patches `content` → server floors+bumps to `002`.
2. A (not yet delivered B's edit) patches `properties` with local stamp `003` → server merges: B's content + A's properties, `updated_at = greatest(003, 002+1) = 003`.
3. Echo to A: staging `003` == local `003`, no pending upload → skip-stale. A's disk keeps the pre-merge content forever; the cache LWW never sees it either.

Note this is a *strict generalization* of the documented I1 blind spot (`reconcile.ts:108-121`, same-deterministic-id/same-ms mints): it needs no id or millisecond coincidence — just two devices editing one row concurrently with the later editor's clock ahead of the earlier server stamp + 1 ms.

## Candidate fixes (each has a real cost — needs a design call)

1. **Server: bump strictly past the proposed stamp on content change** — `NEW.updated_at := greatest(NEW.updated_at, OLD.updated_at) + 1` (or `greatest(NEW+1, OLD+1)`). Restores "newer stamp ⟺ changed content" globally, so the author's echo always applies. Cost: *every* edit's echo now re-materializes on its author's device (today the clean-edit echo equal-stamp-skips) — disk rewrite + FTS/alias trigger churn per edit, fleet-wide. This is the same echo-amplification concern that made the create-touch path deliberately NOT bump (see reconcile.ts's I2 discussion), though here it's once per real edit, not per retry.
2. **Client gate: equal-stamp skip only when content columns are byte-identical.** Directly conflicts with the 429fd4b2 protection this skip exists for (a stale in-flight server read carrying different content under the same ms stamp must NOT clobber the local row) — same fingerprint, opposite correct actions, indistinguishable without provenance. Probably a dead end.
3. **Protocol: send the client's base row-version in the PATCH** (expected `OLD.updated_at`). Server bumps past the proposed stamp *only* when applying onto a drifted base (`OLD.updated_at != base`). Precise — the author echo re-apply cost is paid only on genuine merges — but it's an upload-envelope + RPC + trigger change.

The two-repo fuzzer's convergence property is left strict, so nightly deep runs will stay red on this seed until a fix lands (per the red-nightly-is-a-real-bug posture in docs/fuzzing.md).

title: iPad OPFS SQLite corruption (recurring) — add out-of-band forensic instrumentation
description:
## Summary

The same iPad PWA has now hit **two local OPFS SQLite corruptions within ~24h** (2026-06-30 and 2026-07-01), same 1.4 GB database. Both times **no data was permanently lost** (the server copy + intact local `blocks_synced`/`ps_oplog` had everything; `ps_crud=0`), but the app was left unusable until recovery.

We can diagnose the *end state* well (live remote-inspector forensics), but not the *sequence* that produced it — so we can't yet distinguish the candidate mechanisms. **This issue tracks the incident and adds out-of-band instrumentation so the next occurrence is self-diagnosing.**

Recovery UI for the open-time case shipped in #281 (merged). This is the observability + follow-up tracker.

## Incident #2 forensics (2026-07-01, read-only, on-device)

- Surfaced as a **runtime** error inside the running app: `powersync_control: internal SQLite call returned CORRUPT` (latched in PowerSync `downloadError`; sync-apply crash-loop, `connected:false/connecting:true`). **Not** a DB-open failure — the DB opens fine.
- Full-file OPFS byte scan (347,405 pages × 4096, ~3s) found **exactly ONE fully-zeroed live page** (confirmed not on the freelist), its neighbors pristine. That page begins at byte offset **exactly 1 GiB (2³⁰)**.
- Damaged: the `blocks` table tail (last ~460 of ~341K rows — index-only counts still work, full table scan fails) + FTS5 shadow tables (`blocks_fts_data`/`content`/`rowids`). Everything else intact.
- **Zero data loss:** `ps_oplog` full scan clean (~342K rows, ~211 MB), `blocks_synced` full content scan clean (~342K rows), `ps_crud=0`.
- Ruled out: quota (7% of 41 GB used), a pending hot journal (`-journal`/`-wal` both 0 bytes), random bit-rot (damage is page-aligned + cleanly zeroed at a power-of-two offset), auto_vacuum (off).
- Consequence metrics: the crash-loop saturates the single wa-sqlite thread → app queries run 9–23s.

## Root cause — hypotheses only (not settled)

The mechanism is **not proven**. Candidates:
1. Non-durable OPFS `flush()` on iOS process suspend/kill.
2. A **WebKit-OPFS write/durability bug at the file-size/extent boundary** (the exact-1 GiB alignment leans here — a random killed-mid-write would lose an arbitrary in-flight page, not specifically the 2³⁰ one; a lone zeroed page at exactly 2³⁰ is a 1-in-347K coincidence otherwise).
3. A wa-sqlite `OPFSCoopSyncVFS` coop-lock / handle-close-on-background issue.
4. Coincidence.

The end-state alone can't discriminate these — hence instrumentation.

### External corroboration (known class)
- PowerSync reports ~40 corruption reports / ~40K users ("database disk image is malformed", OPFS VFS, disproportionately Safari/iOS).
- PowerSync documents that `OPFSCoopSyncVFS` access handles get closed when the app is backgrounded.
- A ~400 MB FTS5 WASM DB was corrupted "semi-reliably" by killing the process mid-write (SQLite forum).
- `PRAGMA fullfsync=ON` helped **native** iOS SQLite (survived 10 hard-reset loops) but is a **no-op for wa-sqlite/OPFS** (JS VFS over `SyncAccessHandle.flush()` — durability is whatever WebKit does, un-tunable via PRAGMA).

## Proposed instrumentation (this issue)

All forensic state lives **outside** the OPFS SQLite file (IndexedDB, via the existing `IdbKeyedStore`), stays small (ring-buffered), and is sampled — because the thing we're debugging is the SQLite file being corrupt.

1. **Auto forensic snapshot on `SQLITE_CORRUPT` detection** (open *or* runtime): before any recovery, capture the bundle we gather by hand — OPFS zero-page scan + offsets, which tables fail, `ps_buckets`/`downloadError`, OPFS inventory + sizes, quota, freelist, DB size — and persist it (+ offer download). Turns every future incident into a rich report with no live-inspector session.
2. **Unclean-shutdown flag + lifecycle log:** set `cleanShutdown=false` at startup, `true` on `pagehide`; a still-`false` value on next boot ⇒ the process was killed. Log `visibilitychange`/`freeze`/`resume` timestamps. This is what **discriminates the process-kill hypothesis** (correlate unclean shutdown ↔ later corruption).
3. **Periodic cheap zero-page scan + DB-size log** (startup/idle; ~3s over 1.4 GB, not full `integrity_check`): catches corruption *near when it happens* and records **DB size at corruption** across incidents to directly test the 1 GiB-boundary hypothesis.

Follow-up (not in the first cut): a write-transaction breadcrumb ring buffer (last N tx boundaries: kind, op count, DB size at commit, checkpoint opid).

## Related / out of scope

- **#281 detection gap (separate follow-up):** recovery detection is DB-*open*-scoped only (`toLocalDbOpenError` at `ensurePowerSyncReady`) and `CORRUPTION_SUBSTRINGS` omits `"internal SQLite call returned CORRUPT"` — so this runtime class opens fine and the recovery UI never fires. Widen detection to runtime sync errors + add the phrasing.
- **Bigger durability levers (need a spike, not a blind swap):** `AccessHandlePoolVFS` + WAL (more torn-write-resilient, single-tab) or `IDBBatchAtomicVFS` (atomic commits, but degrades >100 MB / Safari call-stack errors — not viable at 1.4 GB); shrinking the DB (history/tombstone pruning, VACUUM) buys maybe ~30%.
- Consider filing an upstream PowerSync/WebKit report — the "single zeroed page at exactly 1 GiB" fingerprint is more specific than the public reports.

title: Matrix messages diverge on different clients
description:
So what I observe is that I have two different clients that both independently synchronize the matrix messages.
 And then sometimes when it happens and then I edit one of the messages on one client and then another one brings it from matrix independently before
