title: Field-level merge: concurrent edits silently lost (whole-row LWW)
description:
Surfaced by the extension-seam audit — `docs/extension-seam-gaps.md`, gap **D2**. This is a standalone data-loss issue, independent of the extensibility work.

## Problem
Incoming synced rows are accepted/rejected **whole-row** by `updated_at` in `applyIfNewer` (`src/data/blockCache.ts:~173-177`: `snapshot.updatedAt <= existing.updatedAt` gate). There is no per-field / per-property merge.

Impact: when two devices concurrently edit the **same block** — even different properties, or both appending to a `refList` like `tags` — the row with the higher `updated_at` wins wholesale and **silently drops** the other side's change. Most painful for list/counter-style properties where a union/additive merge is the intuitively-correct outcome.

`docs/field-level-sync-merge.md` designs a per-key shallow merge but is **on hold**, and even as designed it's a fixed shallow merge, not pluggable per property.

## Suggested direction
A `fieldMergePoliciesFacet` (keyed by property name / codec type) consulted **before** the default LWW gate, returning `{value, accepted}`; default stays LWW so behavior is unchanged unless a property opts in. Pairs with the conflict-resolution/reconcile policy (audit gap D9).

## Severity
Silent data loss on concurrent edits. The small device fleet limits how often this fires, but doesn't eliminate it — and the fix is additive (default-LWW preserved).

title: [meta] Codify & enforce "derived data is add-only / retain-on-source" across all derive paths
description:
**Type:** invariant / architecture · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread #2: derived data replace-written, lost on error/absence)

## Problem
Derived data (backlinks, references_json, SRS intervals) is recomputed and **replace-written**; any error or absence during recompute loses it instead of retaining. You already learned this once and fixed the **reprojection** path (add-only, retain-on-absence) — but the principle didn't propagate to siblings:
- #189 — one bad `refList` element throws → projection contributes nothing → the whole field's backlinks are replaced with `[]`.
- #194 — SRS interval isn't recomputed when its sibling date field shifts → stored interval diverges from reality.
- #187 — undo replay re-derives and clobbers the restored value.
- the historical ~10k `next-review-date` backlink wipe.

## Recommendation
Codify **"derived data is add-only / retain-on-source"** as a named, documented contract, and enforce it everywhere it's derived — not just reprojection. Provide a shared assertion helper ("recompute never reduces the derived set when the source value is present/unchanged") and apply it to the projection processor, the importer reference rebuild, and the refList decode path. Decoding/recompute that partially fails must retain prior derived data, never strip to empty.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A short principle doc (or section) stating the contract + why (link the incident history).
- [ ] A shared test helper asserting the add-only property, applied across all derive paths.
- [ ] Audit the derive sites against it (relates to #189, #187, and the importer).

title: SRS scrub-shift diverges stored interval from realized due date → corrupts interval + snapshot-history
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** plugin (SRS rescheduling) · **Status:** confirmed (traced + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (C1)

## Summary
Scrub-shifting a staged SRS reschedule date diverges the stored interval from the realized due date, permanently corrupting the interval property + snapshot-history and drifting the SM-2.5 curve off the real schedule.

## Where
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:366-377` (`shiftPlanDate`)
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:198-206` (`basisFromPlan`)
- `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:284-310` (`applySrsReschedulePlan` write)

## Scenario (traced)
Card `interval=10, factor=2`, today 2026-05-05. Stage GOOD → `newInterval=20`, iso=2026-05-25. User scrubs date −10d: `shiftPlanDate` updates the date to 2026-05-15 but leaves `newInterval=20` → commit writes `interval=20` + next-review-date=05-15 (a 10-day gap) + `snapshot{interval:20}`. Worse, regrading the shifted draft: `basisFromPlan` seeds `interval=plan.newInterval(20, UNSHIFTED)` but `scheduleFrom=dateFromIso(nextReviewIso)(05-15, SHIFTED)` → `schedule(40)` → stored `interval=40` against a realized 50-day gap.

## Proposed fix
Recompute the interval from the shifted date on `shiftPlanDate` (or deliberately decouple them and pin which is intended). The committed interval + snapshot must be consistent with the gap between the reviewed date and the next-review date.

## Acceptance criteria (C1 + C1b test)
- [ ] Test: stage GOOD on `interval=10/factor=2`, `draft.shiftDate(-10).commit()`, assert the stored interval + snapshot.interval are consistent with the realized gap.
- [ ] Test: regrade off a shifted draft computes interval from a basis consistent with the shifted `scheduleFrom`.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: PostgREST errors carry no status field → dead 4xx classification → upload queue jams forever
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** sync (PowerSync upload edge) · **Status:** confirmed (vs SDK source + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (B2)

## Summary
PostgREST error objects carry no `status` field, so the upload-error classifier's "permanent on 4xx" branch is dead. An unrecognized permanent 4xx is classified `transient`, PowerSync retries the same batch forever, and the **upload queue jams permanently**.

## Where
- `src/services/powersync.ts:318,333,353` (upload sinks `throw error`, dropping HTTP status)
- `src/services/uploadErrorClassifier.ts:52-54` (`err.status` 4xx branch — never present)

## Why (verified against postgrest-js)
`PostgrestError` exposes only `{message,details,hint,code}`; HTTP `status` is a sibling of the response tuple, not on `error`. For a non-JSON 4xx body, postgrest-js sets `error = {message: body}` with no `code` at all. All three upload sinks destructure `{error}` and re-throw it, so `status` is lost → the classifier's status branch is dead → an unrecognized permanent 4xx (401/403 expired JWT, 413, generic 400, non-JSON body) falls through to `transient` → infinite retry → queue jam. (Code-based classification at `uploadErrorClassifier.ts:38` still catches known codes like `23xxx`, so only codeless/status-only errors jam.) The existing classifier test builds synthetic errors *with* `.status` — a shape production never produces (false confidence).

## Proposed fix
Thread the HTTP status through the throw (e.g. `throw Object.assign(error ?? {}, {status})`) and classify on it; add a test that feeds a codeless permanent-4xx-shaped error and asserts record-then-complete (not retry).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a PostgrestError-shaped error `{message, code:undefined}` with NO `status` for a permanent 4xx is classified permanent (recorded+completed), not transient.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: refList with one malformed element silently strips ALL of a field's backlinks (cross-device data loss)
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** sync/codecs + reference projection · **Status:** confirmed (probe + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (B1)

## Summary
One malformed element in a `refList` property silently deletes **all** of that field's backlinks. `refList.decode` maps every element through `stringCodec.decode`, which throws on a non-string; the throw aborts the whole `map`, the projection catch contributes nothing, and the references processor then *replaces* the references column with the empty set. Same structural class as the historical ~10k `next-review-date` backlink wipe, and it propagates cross-device.

## Where
- `src/data/api/codecs.ts:170-173` (`refList.decode` = `j.map(stringCodec.decode)`)
- `src/plugins/references/referenceProjection.ts:34-52` (try/catch → `[]` on any throw)
- `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts:188-189,234` (replace-write of `references_json`)

## Scenario (probe-proven)
`['valid-1','valid-2',42]` → `refList.decode` throws on `42` → projection yields `[]` → processor replaces references → both valid backlinks lost, triggered by the next unrelated content edit (the processor watches content+properties). `setProperty` does not validate on write (`stringCodec.encode` is identity), and the `copy` sync path copies `properties_json` verbatim — so a wrong-shape value written by a buggy plugin / schema skew on device A syncs to device B and strips backlinks there. `retainedAbsentRefs` does not help: it only retains refs whose schema is *absent*, and here the schema is present.

## Proposed fix
Decode `refList` element-wise and drop only the bad element (or reject the write), so a recoverable list never strips the whole field's derived refs to `[]`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a `refList` value with one bad element keeps the good elements' backlinks (no whole-field strip).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Latent cross-client alias dup wedges all property edits and restore of the affected block
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (alias schema/triggers) · **Status:** confirmed (sqlite repro + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A4)

## Summary
Two blocks that arrived via sync can both hold the same alias in one workspace (the uniqueness trigger is source-gated OFF for sync — documented intended-until-V2). Any later **local** edit touching the affected block's `properties_json` re-inserts its aliases, trips the uniqueness trigger, and `RAISE(ABORT)`s the **entire user transaction** — making the block uneditable and un-restorable through no fault of the user.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:762-772` (`blocks_alias_update`: DELETE + re-INSERT aliases)
- `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:821-840` (uniqueness trigger, `WHEN source IS NOT NULL` at :824)
- surfaced at `src/data/repo.ts:1039-1051` (whole tx rolls back → `ProcessorRejection('alias.collision')`)

## Scenario (sqlite repro)
Sync seeds live blocks `X` and `Y` in one workspace, both with alias `foo` (source=NULL bypasses the uniqueness gate). A later local `setProperty` on `X` that merely adds a type (keeps `foo`) runs `blocks_alias_update` → `DELETE block_aliases WHERE block_id=X` then re-INSERT → the re-insert of `foo` (local ⇒ source set) sees `Y` still claims `foo` → `RAISE(ABORT)` → whole tx rolls back. Every property/type/alias edit on `X` fails; **restore of `X`** (deleted 1→0 re-inserts `foo`) also aborts → `X` is un-restorable while `Y` lives. Content-only text edits survive (they don't fire `alias_update`).

## Proposed fix
Make the local alias re-insert tolerant of a pre-existing cross-client claim (the self-reclaim mitigation currently only covers the block's *own* prior alias, not another block's), or reconcile duplicate aliases on materialization so the latent dup is resolved before a local edit hits it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: two live blocks sharing an alias with `source=NULL` (sync), then a local `setProperty`/type edit on one does NOT throw `alias.collision`.
- [ ] Test: restore of the affected block succeeds.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Self-merge (core.merge intoId===fromId) silently tombstones + doubles content + orphans children
description:
**Severity:** High (latent — unguarded public mutator) · **Area:** data kernel (merge) · **Status:** confirmed mechanism, reachability-gated (2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A3)

## Summary
`core.merge({intoId: x, fromId: x})` (block merged into itself) silently soft-deletes the block AND doubles its content AND orphans its children under the tombstone. No data corruption today *only* because every current UI caller happens to exclude self — but `core.merge` is a **public mutator** (agent bridge / macros / plugins) with no guard.

## Where
- `src/data/blockMerge.ts:49-65` (`mergeBlocksInTx`)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:723` (`core.merge`)

## Mechanism (probe-proven)
`tx.delete(x)` writes an `after=tombstone` snapshot; `tx.update(x,…)` then reads that tombstone via `requireExisting` (no `deleted` filter → no throw) and writes `content = x.content + x.content` while the row stays `deleted=1`; `from`'s children re-home under the tombstone. Probe output: `deleted=TRUE, content="foofoo"`, child orphaned under a tombstone parent.

## Why it's currently unreachable via UI (verifier note)
`MergePicker` excludes the source (`excludeBlockIds:[sourceBlockId]`); the alias path self-excludes (`claimant.id===plan.id→continue`); backspace `previousVisibleBlock` never returns current. So this is defense-in-depth for the public mutator, not a live UI bug.

## Proposed fix
One line in `mergeBlocksInTx`: `if (intoId === fromId) return` (no-op self-merge). Add a test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: `core.merge` / `mergeBlocksInTx` with `intoId === fromId` on a block with children + content leaves the block intact (not deleted, content not doubled, children not orphaned).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: move() cycle guard bypassed by a soft-deleted intermediate → durable structural cycle
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (tx engine / tree CTE) · **Status:** confirmed (probe + 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A2)

## Summary
`move()`'s cycle guard filters `deleted=0` in its ancestor walk, so a soft-deleted node on the ancestor chain makes the guard miss a real cycle. A move can create a **durable structural cycle** that is invisible to reads, uploads to the server, and propagates fleet-wide — surfacing as a live cycle when the deleted node is restored.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:406-418` (move cycle preflight via `IS_DESCENDANT_OF_SQL`)
- `src/data/internals/treeQueries.ts:119-137` (`deleted=0` at base case :125 and every hop :132)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:828-841` (`requireParentInWorkspace` — no deleted filter)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:328-359` (`restore()` — no cycle recheck)

## Scenario (reproduced byte-for-byte)
Tree `root→A→B→C`. Soft-delete `B`. `move(A, {parentId: C})`. The ancestor walk from `C` hits `B(deleted)` and stops, never reaching `A` → `hit=null` → move proceeds. Result: `A.parent=C, B.parent=A(deleted=1), C.parent=B` — closed cycle `A→C→B→A`. All tree reads filter `deleted=0` so it's invisible until `B` is restored (which runs no cycle check → live 3-cycle). The `cycleScanSql` telemetry shares the same `deleted=0` blind spot, so nothing detects or repairs it. The corrupt `parent_id` routes to `ps_crud` and uploads.

## Dominant real-world trigger
Concurrent sync: one device soft-deletes `B` while another moves/outdents `A` under `C` through a still-visible surface. `move()` is a public primitive (indent/outdent/move/setOrderKey, blockMerge, dailyNotes, roam-import).

## Proposed fix
Make the descendant walk traverse `parent_id` **regardless of `deleted`** — cycle-freedom is a structural invariant independent of soft-delete. (Consider the same for `cycleScanSql` so the detector stops sharing the blind spot.)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: `move(A under C)` with the intermediate link `B` soft-deleted MUST throw `CycleError` and roll back (currently does not).
- [ ] Test: restoring a node never exposes a live cycle.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Tied order_key siblings make Enter-split / reorder / outdent throw and silently drop the edit
description:
**Severity:** High · **Area:** data kernel (mutators / order-keys) · **Status:** confirmed (adversarial verify + probe) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A1)

## Summary
Two adjacent siblings sharing an `order_key` is an explicitly *supported* on-disk state, but the mutators that insert between neighbors call `keyBetween(equal, equal)`, which throws `"X >= Y"` and rolls back the whole transaction — **silently dropping the user's edit**. This hits the core editing surface (Enter-to-split, reorder, outdent, insert).

## Where
- `src/data/mutators.ts:95,99` (`orderKeyForInsert` after/before)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:396` (`insertChildren` → `keysBetween`)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:531` (outdent)
- `src/data/mutators.ts:685` (split)
- `src/data/orderKey.ts` (`keyBetween`/`keysBetween` wrap `fractional-indexing-jittered`, which throws on equal bounds)

## Why this state is reachable (not contrived)
- The sibling index `(parent_id, order_key, id)` is **non-unique** (`src/data/blockSchema.ts:97-99`).
- `orderKey.ts:5-8` documents that concurrent same-slot inserts collide and are resolved by the `(order_key,id)` secondary sort — i.e. ties are a designed, supported state.
- `treeQueries.test.ts:89-97` seeds two siblings at `'a0'` on the **read** side and asserts the tiebreak. The **write/mutator** side has zero coverage.
- Ties arrive via import, `setOrderKey` (no collision check), and concurrent sync.

## Impact (proven by probe)
With two siblings both at a valid library key, `createSiblingBelow`/`createSiblingAbove`/`split`/`insertChildren(before|after)` all throw `"<key> >= <key>"` and roll back (5 of 6 structural ops; only `moveVertical`'s adjacent-swap dodges it). The Enter handler (`src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts:630-701`) has **no try/catch**, and it dispatches the after-cursor suffix into the editor *before* calling `split` — so on rollback the editor shows the split text while SQL keeps the original: **editor/SQL divergence + a silently lost edit**.

## Proposed fix
Add an equal-bounds re-key fallback in `orderKeyForInsert` / `split` / `outdent` / `insertChildren`: when the computed neighbor bounds are equal (or `lower >= upper`), generate a key against the next *distinct* neighbor, or re-key the tied run, instead of calling `keyBetween` with equal endpoints.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A mutator-level test that raw-inserts siblings with identical valid `order_key`s, then drives `createSiblingBelow`/`moveVertical`/`split`/`outdent`/`insertChildren` across the collision and asserts each **succeeds** (currently throws) — written red-first.
- [ ] Enter-to-split across a tied block preserves the typed text (no editor/SQL divergence).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Move agent-runtime tokens from localStorage to user-page blocks
description:
## Problem

Agent tokens live in `localStorage` keyed by `(userId, workspaceId)`, managed by `AgentTokenStore` (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/tokens.ts`, storage key `agent-runtime:tokens:{userId}:{workspaceId}`). localStorage isn't actually more secure than a block on the user page — same-origin is the boundary either way — and a block fits the "everything is a block" model better (undoable, exportable, manageable inline on the user page).

## Current state (verified)

- Tokens are still in `localStorage` via `AgentTokenStore`.
- Only scopes today are `BlockDefault` (synced), `UiState` (ephemeral `local-ui`), `UserPrefs`, `References` (`src/data/api/changeScope.ts`). **No** persistent device-local (OPFS, non-syncing) scope.
- **No** `kind: agent-token` renderer.

## Blockers to land first

1. **A persistent device-local block scope.** Existing `local-ui` is per-session-ephemeral; tokens need persisted-but-non-syncing. New scope must (a) write to OPFS, (b) never enqueue into `ps_crud`, (c) avoid `row_events` if that audit is also gated to local. Add an engine guard so `kind=agent-token` blocks can't have their scope upgraded by an `update_block` tx (defends against an edit flipping a token into a synced row).
2. **Renderer for `kind: agent-token`.** Read-only display of label + createdAt + a Revoke button. Hide from QuickFind / autocomplete / outline rendering.
3. **Multi-device sanity check.** Confirm a synced user page on Device B doesn't crash when its child set is partially device-local on A.

Once #1 lands, the migration is small: swap `AgentTokenStore` for a thin wrapper around `repo.tx({scope: DeviceLocal})` + `repo.query.children({parentId: userPage.id, kind: 'agent-token'})`. Bridge handshake and CLI stay identical.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: Tx-bound read guards for reference processors (close TOCTOU windows)
description:
## Problem

`parseReferences` and `cleanupOrphanAliases` do their expensive reads **before** opening a write transaction, to avoid the PowerSync queue deadlock documented in `tasks/processor-tx-deadlock.md`. That leaves two narrow TOCTOU windows:

1. Alias ownership can change between "alias missing" and deterministic target creation.
2. A newly inserted alias target can gain a reference between the orphan precheck and the cleanup delete.

## Current state (verified)

- `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts` builds its plan via pre-tx reads (`ctx.repo.query.aliasLookup`, `resolveAliasSeatId(aliasSeatReaderFromDb(ctx.db))`), then applies it inside a single `ctx.repo.tx(...)`.
- A **tx-bound** `aliasLookup(alias, workspaceId)` helper already exists on the Tx path (`src/data/api/tx.ts`).
- **Missing:** a tx-bound "does any block reference this id?" helper. The cleanup processor's reference check runs the `block_references` `SELECT` against `ctx.db` (pre-tx), so the orphan window stays open.

## Fix shape

Add narrow tx-bound read helpers for the final guards on the `Tx`/`TxImpl` path (using the active write-transaction lock context): re-check alias ownership and "does any block reference this id?" **inside** the tx, immediately before creating the fallback alias target or deleting a cleanup candidate. Keep the broad prefilter reads outside the tx. Do **not** call bare `ctx.db` from inside `repo.tx` — that reintroduces the queue deadlock.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: React identity contract for extensions (host-provided peer deps + jsx-runtime transform)
description:
## Problem

Extensions that render into the app's React tree must share the host app's React module identity. Today that's partly enforced (react / react-dom externalized through the page import map) and partly accidental: the in-browser Babel transform uses the `react` preset, which emits `React.createElement(...)`, so extension blocks rely on `window.React` unless they import React explicitly.

## Current state (verified)

- `src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts` runs `Babel.transform()` with presets `['react', 'typescript']` → emits `React.createElement(...)`, **not** `jsx()` from `react/jsx-runtime`.
- `index.html` import map externalizes `react`, `react-dom`, and includes `react/jsx-runtime` + `react/jsx-dev-runtime` entries — but the compiler doesn't target them.
- No docs for extension authors describe React/ReactDOM as host-provided peer dependencies.

## Fix shape

- Document React and ReactDOM as host-provided peer dependencies for extension authors and bundled extensions. Bundled extensions must externalize `react`, `react-dom`, `react/jsx-runtime`, `react/jsx-dev-runtime` and resolve them from the host environment.
- Tighten the in-browser compiler so JSX uses an explicit host import (`react/jsx-runtime`, or an injected `import React from 'react'`) instead of the global `window.React`.
- Keep import-map entries exact where possible, and integrity-pin any CDN-hosted host React modules.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: Harden synced extension-block trust: content-hash re-approval on source change
description:
## Context

A `type = extension` block is **application code, not inert content** — it is compiled and its top-level module code runs on the client. Before this is relied on in shared/collaborative workspaces, extension execution must be safely gated per user.

## What already exists (verified)

The acute "executes by default" risk is **already mitigated**:
- User extensions default to `defaultEnabled: false` (`src/extensions/togglable.ts`).
- `dynamicExtensionsExtension` checks `isEnabled(...)` **before** compiling — disabled extensions never run their module code (`src/extensions/dynamicExtensions.ts`).
- Enablement is stored device-local in `localStorage` keyed `extensions.overrides.{workspaceId}` (`src/extensions/overridesCache.ts`).

So the baseline "available but disabled until enabled" behavior is in place. This issue is the remaining **hardening**, not a greenfield build.

## Remaining gaps (the P0 part)

1. **No re-approval on source change.** Enablement is not bound to the extension's source. Once a user enables extension block `X`, a workspace writer can later **edit `X`'s source** and the new code executes on every member who previously enabled it — with no re-approval. This is a collaborator → collaborator code-execution vector.
2. **`system:disabled` is not a security control.** It is a synced, writer-editable property, so it can't be the trust boundary.
3. **Enablement granularity.** Today's key is `(workspaceId)` device-local; it is not bound to `(blockId, contentHash)`.

## Fix shape

Keep the trust decision outside synced block properties so a collaborator cannot force-enable (or silently re-enable) code for other members. Store an allowlist keyed by `(workspaceId, blockId, contentHash)` in device-local or user-owned settings, and **require re-approval when the extension block's source changes** (content hash differs from the approved one). `system:disabled` can remain an authoring/convenience switch, but is explicitly not the security boundary.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P0 — Security). Reframed: baseline default-disabled opt-in already shipped; this tracks content-hash pinning + re-approval-on-change._

title: Reschedule (and similar multi-helper actions) emit 2–4 txs — one undo entry doesn't cover the whole action
description:
## Problem

`rescheduleBlock` → `applySrsReschedulePlan` (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:319`) calls `getOrCreateDailyNote` **twice** (today + next-review date) before its own `tx.update`, and each of those opens its own `BlockDefault` tx — plus a third for `getOrCreateJournalBlock` if the workspace's journal block doesn't exist yet (`src/plugins/daily-notes/dailyNotes.ts:172`).

On a fresh workspace day a single user-perceived "Good" tap is therefore **2–4 entries on the undo stack**, and cmd-Z (or the toast's Undo button — same `repo.undo()` target) only reverts the property write, leaving the newly created daily notes / journal page behind.

The same shape applies to any action that opens N tx-emitting helpers before its own write — originally flagged on PR #31, but the daily-note coupling means it surfaces in **most SRS first-touches**.

## Current state (verified)

- `applySrsReschedulePlan` calls `getOrCreateDailyNote` twice, then opens its own `repo.tx` afterward (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts`).
- `getOrCreateDailyNote` opens its own `repo.tx` (scope `BlockDefault`) and may call `getOrCreateJournalBlock`, which opens another (`src/plugins/daily-notes/dailyNotes.ts`).
- No `getOrCreateDailyNoteInTx` variant exists; the Tx is not threaded through.

## Fix shape

Thread an optional `Tx` parameter through `getOrCreateDailyNote` / `getOrCreateJournalBlock` so callers already inside a tx can co-opt it. `rescheduleBlock` opens one outer `repo.tx`, calls a `getOrCreateDailyNoteInTx(tx, …)` helper for both daily notes, then performs its own update — collapsing to a single undo entry. Keep the standalone `repo`-only signature as a thin wrapper for existing call sites so this isn't a forced migration.

Wrinkle: `getOrCreateDailyNote` reads outside the tx, then opens a new one to write; the in-tx variant must do its existence check via `tx.get`, which matches the pattern already in `srsBlockDateAdapter.setIso`.

Worth doing before any future surface that needs single-entry undo (e.g. "duplicate card with new schedule", calendar drag-to-reschedule).

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P1)._

title: Clear the workspace undo stack when a data migration writes
description:
Deferred from PR #508 — the shape is agreed, it just has no consumer yet.

`RepoTxOptions.skipUndo` keeps a WorkspaceBackfill's own writes off the undo stack, but cannot reach entries already on it. Undo replay restores an entry's whole `before` row snapshot rather than a field delta, so a user edit made BEFORE the pass, to a row the pass later rewrote, reverts the migration when they hit cmd-Z for their own edit — and permanently, since the completion marker is already recorded.

Agreed shape (with the repo owner): when a migration actually writes, call `UndoManager.clear()` for that workspace and surface it to the user. The entries at risk are exactly the ones unsafe to replay, so dropping them costs recent undo and buys not silently reverting a migration. Rejected alternatives: reloading the page (heavy, doesn't explain itself) and a toast alone (visible, but the loss still happens).

Not built in #508 because deleting `dailyNoteDateBackfill` left zero registered backfills, so it would have shipped as dead code. It should land with slice C of the properties-as-blocks migration — the first real consumer, and the one where it matters most (~650k creates).

The rule itself is in AGENTS.md under 'one-shot catch-up passes'; this issue carries the state (not built, who builds it).

title: Flaky: clientSchema 'samples rather than fully scanning'
description:
Failed once in CI on an unrelated PR (#508), passed on a bare re-run of the same commit, and passes locally (94/94 in that file).

Evidence:
- run 32117309587, src/data/internals/clientSchema.test.ts
- the file took 23290ms under CI load; the failing test 12624ms; siblings 'repairs degenerate "0 0" stats' 4661ms and 'does not repair them without the probes' 5607ms
- re-run of the same commit: pass

What makes it worth a look rather than a timeout bump: the test's own comment says it deliberately asserts on STAT VALUES rather than timing ('which is why this asserts on the stat values rather than on timing'). Its assertions are rowCount === 500 and avgPerWorkspace < 500. So a load-induced failure is not the ordinary slow-under-contention shape, and bumping a timeout would not be the fix.

Two hypotheses worth checking:
1. sqlite's ANALYZE sampling under analysis_limit is less deterministic than the test assumes, so avgPerWorkspace can land at 500 (the unbounded value) under some conditions.
2. cross-test interaction through the shared db handle in that describe block — the preceding test corrupts sqlite_stat1 to '0 0' and reopens.

Not caused by PR #508: that branch touches the backfill runner, facets, firstSync and daily-notes, none of which this file exercises (it drives a raw better-sqlite3 handle with no Repo).

title: Merge into a cell-only target deletes the source field row instead of adopting it
description:
Observed while pinning #389 item 9 (test committed in src/data/propertyChildren.test.ts, 'pre-backfill window (flip day)'). Recording the observation; the root cause is NOT yet established.

## What was traced

Flipped workspace, 'into' holds a cell for a property with NO field rows behind it (the pre-backfill / sync-arrival shape), 'from' is child-backed with a field row for the same property. After mergeBlocksInTx:

- from's field row: deleted = 1, parent unchanged (NOT moved to into)
- into: one field row, with a NEW id
- values under it: ['target-value', 'source-value'] — correct content, target first

So the user-visible outcome is right, and #389 item 9's predicted data loss does NOT occur.

## Why it still looks wrong

blockMerge.ts's adopt branch documents the opposite — 'the whole from field row moves over intact (value + comments), becoming into's field row for it' — and the existing test 'adopts a source field row for a property into lacks (moved, not recreated)' asserts exactly that, citing #23: 'property children always transfer to into, never delete-and-rebuild'. That test passes, so adoption clearly DOES happen when into is itself child-backed. The divergence appears only when into is cell-only.

Both cannot be the intended contract. Either the adopt branch is not reached in the cell-only case (and the comment should say so), or something downstream tombstones the adopted row and rebuilds it.

## Why it may matter

Delete-and-recreate loses anything authored on the FIELD ROW itself (comments nested under the field row rather than under its value). The value-level case is already covered by 'preserves user-authored descendants of the source value child'; the field-row-level case has no coverage either way.

## Next step

Root-cause which branch runs. Then either fix it or correct the comment + the #23 claim. Do not assume it is a defect before that — the outcome is currently correct.
close_reason:
Not a bug — I was reading the fix as a defect.

The delete-and-recreate I traced IS the intended mechanism of e70ebda15 ('fix(merge): a cell-only target keeps its own value when the source is child-backed'), which was already on the branch when I looked: it materializes the target's own field row first for keys held in the cell with no row behind them, so the ordinary collapseDuplicateFieldRow path runs. That path deletes the source row and folds its value onto the target's — which is exactly what I observed, and why the outcome was correct.

Adoption still happens when the target is itself child-backed, which is what the 'moved, not recreated' test pins. The two are different branches, not a contradiction, so the #23 claim stands.

Root cause of the bad filing: I traced a mechanism I did not recognize and reached for 'defect' instead of first checking whether recent branch history explained it. git log on the touched file would have answered it in one command.

title: Grain audit: replace the hardcoded system-property prefix list with a declaration
description:
grainAudit.isSystemProperty (src/plugins/agent-runtime/grainAudit.ts) hardcodes an exemption list — types, alias, system:*, agent:* — that skips ALL grain checks for those names. Split out of #502, which is otherwise resolved.

Two problems with the hardcode:

1. It hid the #502 blind spot for weeks: any future agent:* key the daemon adds without a seed is silently exempt from unknown-property, which is exactly the failure mode #502 existed to report.
2. It is redundant with registration for its stated purpose. unknown-property is the only check that fires without a schema, and every name on the list IS registered (types/alias/system:* are kernel seeds; the 13 agent:* keys have been seeds since 2026-07-21).

Owner direction (Vlad): do not hardcode — a registered property should declare its own exemption.

## The trap: 'just delete the predicate' is wrong, measured

For a USER-created type, typeId = row.id (typeDefinitionMetadata.ts) — a uuid. So 'types' holds uuids that resolve to live blocks, under a string-list (non-ref) schema. Deleting the exemption makes block-id-not-a-ref fire on **1339 blocks** on the prod graph (measured 2026-08-18). That is a flood of false positives: 'types' is the kernel's own type-membership mechanism with its own trigger-maintained block_types index, not a user pointer that wants backlinks.

## The design question

'hidden' is the wrong carrier. It is a DISPLAY concern, and reusing it inverts the answer for the case that matters: all 13 agent:* seeds are declared hidden, and those are precisely the ones the audit SHOULD cover.

So this wants a distinct declaration on the seed — something like 'kernel-structural' / 'exempt-from-grain-audit' — where types and alias and system:* opt in, and agent:* deliberately does not. Open: whether it needs to round-trip to property-schema:* blocks or can live in the code declaration only.

Scope note: isSystemProperty also gates writeWarnings (the live pre-write bridge check) and audit-extension. PR #500's audit-properties carries no exemption list at all and is unaffected either way.

title: Strip legacy YAML frontmatter from migrated bd memories
description:
Session start injects a 150-char preview of every memory (`bd prime --hook-json --mcp`). About 100 memories migrated from the old file-based system still open with YAML frontmatter, so their preview budget is spent on `--- name: ... description: \"` boilerplate and the identifying text is cut off — they are effectively invisible unless recalled by key.

Fix: rewrite those memories to the current convention (first line = one-line description, blank line, then body). Note `bd remember` parses a leading `---` as a flag, so content must come after a `--` separator.

Not urgent, but do it opportunistically for any memory being edited anyway. Context: AGENTS.md memory section.

title: panelScrollAnchor.test.ts flakes under load on a 4-CPU box
description:
Observed 2026-08-15 in an Anthropic cloud container (4 CPUs) running the full gate:

FAIL src/utils/test/panelScrollAnchor.test.ts > alignScrollportToRow — whose scrollport it is > keeps waiting for the exact row after aligning to a scope-drift fallback

`pnpm run check` exited 1 at 223s with that single failure. Re-running the file alone passed 3/3. So it is a timing-budget flake, not a real defect — exactly the class AGENTS.md calls the #1 source of 'a disjoint set of files failed each run' flakes: the gate runs one vitest worker per core, so wall-clock stretches ~3x at p99 and ~6x at p99.9 versus running the file alone, and a 4-core box makes that worse than the dev machines it was tuned on.

Fix per AGENTS.md: measure the test's solo cost, then give it an explicit budget with headroom for the 6x (an `it(…, 20_000)` or `describe(name, {timeout: 30_000}, …)`) plus a comment stating the measured cost. Check every INNER budget (vi.waitFor etc.) is strictly below the enclosing test timeout — otherwise the test timeout wins and you get 'Test timed out in Nms' with no clue which assertion never settled. Do NOT raise the global testTimeout.

Why it matters now: the nightly fuzz-triage cloud routine (trig_01QKM2wXWpkKGuMDWDNGeJou) runs the gate in that same 4-CPU environment, so this flake will intermittently show as a red gate on unrelated fuzz-fix PRs. The routine's prompt tells it to re-run in isolation and treat a pass as a flake rather than 'fixing' it, but that is a workaround, not the fix.

Unconfirmed aside seen in the same log, worth a look but not part of this: 'Error: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND proj.supabase.co' appeared during the run — may be an expected offline-path test, unverified.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #572 (merged 49dbfca2a). Budget ladder in src/utils/test/panelScrollAnchor.test.ts: aligner deadlines 60s > test budget 20s > vi.waitFor 10s > ~300ms of actual work. Root cause was an absolute multi-second worker freeze, not the 3-6x stretch — the test costs 173ms against the 5000ms default. Follow-up km-huno tracks REALIGN_WINDOW_MS having no behavioural coverage.

title: Extension source in block.content is treated as prose by rewrite/derive/show paths
description:
An installed extension's JS source is stored in `blocks.content`, the same column that holds prose. Everything that reads content as text-with-meaning therefore treats a bundle as prose.

Four distinct operation families, all reachable today:
- REWRITE the bytes: find-replace, rename, add-tag, insert-image, ask-agent, reschedule/date-scrub, merge, property materialization (both the eager `tx.setProperty` dual-write and the deferred processor).
- DERIVE from the bytes: reference parsing, `reference_target_id`, `is_field_form`, alias content<->name mirroring, typeify.
- SHOW the bytes: content search, link-target autocomplete, QuickFind recents, reference-property pickers, audit samples.
- SPLICE the bytes into ANOTHER block: deleting a referenced extension makes `inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor` replace `((id))` in every prose referrer with the deleted block's content — i.e. the whole bundle lands in a note. Leaks transitively too, via a deleted prose block that referenced it.

Master today has exactly ONE protection: `referencesProcessor` skips EXTENSION_TYPE blocks, so source is not indexed for backlinks. Nothing else is guarded.

WHAT WAS TRIED AND REJECTED (PR #544, closed): an `opaqueContentTypesFacet` declaring which type ids hold non-prose content, propagated to ~42 call sites. It did not converge — six review rounds produced 3, 4, 3, 6, 8, 1 findings, and most later findings were fallout from the previous round's own guards. Each guard carries cross-cutting obligations that are easy to miss individually: a filter downstream of a bounded query needs over-fetch AND an invalidation dep; a gesture with an editor branch needs a pre-dispatch twin; a rewriter must skip bytes but still drop the derived edge; a refusal must precede the expensive step; symmetric operations need both sides.

DIAGNOSIS: this is a type problem being solved with runtime checks. One column carries two meanings and every consumer must remember which.

RECOMMENDED FIX IF THIS EVER MATTERS: move the payload out of `content` — extension source in its own column/property, `content` holding the extension's name. Then every rewriter, deriver, display path and splice is correct by construction and all the guards can be deleted. Cost is a schema + PowerSync sync-rule change, a data migration, and updating the few readers of extension source (loader, install-extension). Cheapest while there are only a handful of extension blocks.

WHY NOT DONE NOW (Vlad's call, 2026-08-15): the exposure is marginal — a couple of users, a handful of extensions, and extensions are recoverable by reinstalling from the repo. Not worth the design cost yet.

Independently-useful fixes found alongside it were extracted to PR #567.
notes:
Worked example for the "when review rounds stop converging" rule in AGENTS.md.

Shape of the treadmill, measured: findings per review round went 3, 4, 3, 6, 8.
By round 4 most findings named the PREVIOUS round's own guards rather than new
consumers — the work had started reviewing itself. Each round was individually
correct (real bugs, green gate, mutation-verified fixes) which is precisely why
it was hard to see from inside.

The design that caused it: `content` is one column with two meanings (prose vs
machine payload), so correctness lived as ~42 runtime checks across ~30 files
instead of in the data model. Each check dragged cross-cutting obligations —
a filter downstream of a bounded query needs over-fetch AND an invalidation dep;
a gesture with an editor branch needs a pre-dispatch twin; a rewriter must skip
bytes but still drop the derived edge; symmetric operations need both sides.

Verdict: discarded (PR #544). Independently useful pieces extracted to #567.

title: Wikilink completion: hasClosingBrackets scans the whole line for ]]
description:
In `backlinkCompletionSource` (src/utils/backlinkAutocomplete.ts), `hasClosingBrackets` is `afterCursor.indexOf(']]') !== -1` where `afterCursor` is the rest of the LINE. So a `]]` belonging to a LATER wikilink counts as this one's closer.

Repro: line `[[foo and [[bar]]`, caret after `foo`. The query anchors on the first `[[` (searchTerm `foo`), and `afterCursor` = ` and [[bar]]` contains `]]`, so accepting a completion inserts without appending `]]` — result `[[Foo and [[bar]]`, an unterminated link.

The blockref source next door uses `afterCursor.startsWith('))')`, which is right for the common case but would regress `[[foo ]]` (a space before the closer) — so a naive swap is not the fix. Probably: treat the `]]` as ours only if no `[[` occurs before it in `afterCursor`, the way `isInsideBacklinkBrackets` already reasons.

Spotted while fixing the wrapped-selection completion bug (PR #564); deliberately left out of that change's scope.

title: "Close video notes view" button is mostly covered by the notes editor
description:
Found during live browser QA of [PR #549](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/549). **Pre-existing** — reproduced both maximized and un-maximized, so it is the notes-view chrome, not the maximize work.

The button is a 36×36 target, but most of it is behind the notes editor: probing `document.elementFromPoint` across its rect, only **~36%** of sample points actually hit the button (un-maximized; ~22% maximized). Every miss lands on `DIV.cm-line` — the notes editor's first line. Only a strip along the bottom edge is clickable.

Reproduced by clicking the button's visual centre: nothing happens. Clicking a point near its bottom edge closes the view correctly.

The container is `pointer-events-none sticky top-2 z-10 -mb-9 flex justify-end`. The `-mb-9` deliberately pulls following content up under the row, and the editor's line boxes then paint over the button — the button itself is `position: static` / `z-index: auto`, so the parent's `z-10` does not lift it above content that comes later in paint order. (That is the mechanism suggested by the computed styles; I did not bisect the CSS to confirm it is the only cause.)

**Likely fix:** give the button its own stacking context (e.g. `relative z-10` on the button, or make the sticky row a positioned layer above the editor) so the whole 36px target is hittable.

title: Handle revival can mint a sibling at a superseded registry epoch, making stale-resolver staleness unbounded
description:
Split out of #543 at the maintainer's request — flagged there but deliberately not fixed on that branch, since only `Repo` (the epoch owner) can close it.

## Mechanism

Query handles are keyed with the registry epoch:

```ts
const key = handleKey(`query:${fullName}@${this.queryEpoch}`, validated)
```

`src/data/repo.ts:3727` (in `dispatchQuery`). The loader created alongside that key closes over `const registry = this.queries` captured a few lines above, so a handle is pinned to the query-registry snapshot it was created against — deliberately, and documented on `queryEpoch` (`repo.ts:524-556`).

`swapQueries` bumps the epoch only when an existing query is REPLACED or REMOVED — never for a purely additive swap (`repo.ts:3496-3501` for the rationale, the bump itself at `repo.ts:3555`). A bump re-keys everything at once, and the two halves of that are both intentional: fresh lookups compute the new-epoch key and bind to the new registry, while handles already in hand stay at their old key and keep serving their captured snapshot until their subscribers detach and they GC.

That last clause is what #543 changes. Under #543 a disposed handle is a permanent one-hop forwarder: `resolveLive()` adopts the store's live entry at its key, and when the key is vacant it mints a **sibling** from the state the corpse still holds —

```ts
if (this.store.peekHandle(this.key) === this) this.store.remove(this.key)
return this.store.getOrCreate(this.key, () => new LoaderHandle({
  store: this.store,
  key: this.key,
  loader: this.loader,      // ← the corpse's captured registry snapshot
  equality: this.equality,
}))
```

`this.key` is the corpse's key, so the sibling registers at the OLD epoch, and `this.loader` is the corpse's loader, so it resolves against the OLD registry.

## Trace

1. A component renders query `foo`; the handle registers at `query:foo@3`.
2. Its subtree is hidden with `<Activity mode="hidden">`. Effects unmount, the subscription is released, the handle GCs, the `@3` slot is freed.
3. A plugin reload REPLACES `foo`. `swapQueries` sets `mutated`, the epoch goes to 4. Every fresh lookup now keys at `@4` and gets the new resolver.
4. The subtree is revealed. React Compiler has memoized the caller's factory on deps that never change (this is the whole premise of #543 — `block.id` / `block.repo.query`), so the caller still holds the `@3` corpse.
5. The corpse's first `subscribe` / `load` / `read` mints a sibling **at `@3`, running the pre-swap resolver**. It will re-mint the same way on every later GC cycle.

Before #543 step 5 was a dead end: the corpse stayed dead, the caller stayed blank (the bug #543 exists to fix), and the staleness was bounded by the handle's lifetime. Now it isn't — a memoized holder can keep a superseded resolver alive indefinitely, and no new lookup anywhere in the app will dislodge it, because new lookups key at `@4` and never touch the `@3` slot.

Nothing about fresh lookups is affected. This is only about a holder that survives a GC boundary across an epoch bump.

## Reachability

Narrow. It needs a runtime query replace/remove (plugin reload / disable) AND a consumer hidden across it long enough to GC. Nothing in core uses `<Activity>` yet — the only mention in `src/` is the comment in `src/hooks/block.ts` describing the case — so today the exposure is the fork's perspective host. It is a correctness trade to close before `<Activity>` sees wider use, not a live incident.

## Options

**(a) Cheap — retire old-epoch keys on a bump.** On an epoch bump, have `Repo` mark the handles at superseded keys `retired`, a flag distinct from `disposed`, and check it where a corpse would mint. A retired corpse declines to mint and reports itself unusable, so a memoized holder gets a blank-and-remount on plugin reload instead of a stale resolver. This restores exactly the pre-#543 bound (bounded staleness, and the blank is the pre-existing behaviour on a genuine registry swap) without adding any per-resolution work. It does not make the memoized holder recover — it just stops it recovering into the wrong registry.

**(b) Proper — re-derive the key at resolution time.** Let a handle recompute its key from name + validated args when it resolves, rather than capturing a loader at creation. A corpse would then mint at the CURRENT epoch, against the current registry — which is both correct and the behaviour a reveal should have. That means the query dispatch layer owns key derivation as a reusable step (name + args → key + loader) instead of it living inline in the `dispatchQuery` closure, so it is a real refactor of the `Repo`/`HandleStore` seam rather than a flag.

(a) restores the pre-#543 bound. (b) is the actual fix.

Full write-up of the trade in context: `docs/handle-lifecycle-hidden-subtrees.html` (added by #543).

title: Wikilink faithfulness guard doesn't validate through markdown, so renames can silently unlink backlinks
description:
## What

`faithfulWikilinkReplacement` decides whether a `[[alias]]` span can carry a reference by rendering it and re-parsing with the **plain scanner**. The renderer runs the span through **markdown first**. Where the two disagree, the reference index stores an edge that the UI never draws as a link.

Real output, each alias put through `[[…]]` and then the actual `remarkWikilinks` + `remarkBlockrefs` pipeline:

```
"*Part*x"        indexes as ["*Part*x"]       faithful: yes   renders: text("[[") text("Part") text("x]]")
"a`b`c"          indexes as ["a`b`c"]         faithful: yes   renders: text("[[a") text("c]]")
"Book of [x]"    indexes as ["Book of [x]"]   faithful: yes   renders: LINK("Book of [x]")
"Ordinary Page"  indexes as ["Ordinary Page"] faithful: yes   renders: LINK("Ordinary Page")
```

For `*Part*x`, remark consumes `*Part*` into an emphasis node before the wikilink pass sees the text — note the output says `Part` with the asterisks gone and there is **no link node at all**. Backticks do the same.

## Why it matters

Two symptoms, the second worse than the first.

1. **Authored by hand.** A page named `*Part*x` (or anything with `*`, `_`, backticks): the backlink appears on the page, but the `[[…]]` in the source block renders as broken literal text nobody can click.

2. **Produced by a rename.** `references.renameBacklinks` asks this guard before rewriting. Rename a page *to* a markdown-flavoured name and the guard says yes, so every backlink is rewritten to `[[*Part*x]]` — silently converting working links into unclickable text across the graph. The pinned fallback the guard is supposed to escalate to renders correctly:

```
PINNED fallback renders as: BLOCKREF text("Old Name")
```

## Fix direction

Validate through the real markdown pipeline (`parseReferencesMarkdownAware` already exists and returns `[]` for every leaking case above), not only the plain scanner. Two things to weigh:

- The guard gets **stricter**, so renames to a markdown-flavoured name pin their backlinks (`[label](((uuid)))`) instead of keeping late-binding wikilinks. Right block, right display text, but the link stops following future renames. That is the safe direction, and it is what the ladder's pinned rung exists for — but it is a behaviour change for existing renames.
- The two readers measure different strings anyway (the index parses raw `blocks.content`, the renderer parses post-escape-resolution text) — the same divergence #542 tracks for the alias cap. Worth deciding whether these are one fix or two.

## Provenance

Pre-existing, not from PR #548 — `[[*Part*x]]` has no bracket in it and already leaks today. Raised by Codex during that PR's review; the specific example given there (`*Part*[x]`) was blocked only incidentally, by the trailing `]` that #548 stopped padding. Not a regression from that change: `Book of [x]`, the shape #548 added, is markdown-clean.

title: A typed block should be able to say what continuing it looks like
description:
## The gap

Press Enter at the end of a typed block and you get an untyped one. `createSiblingBelow` ([mutators.ts:356](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/mutators.ts#L356)) accepts `content` and `properties`, but the Enter shortcut passes only `{siblingId}` ([defaultShortcuts.ts:718](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts#L718)), so the new block starts bare.

For `todo` that means Enter after a todo gives you a non-todo. For the strength tracker it's worse than cosmetic: the new line *looks* like a set position but isn't a `strength-set`, so `setsOf` skips it, `buildHistory` never sees it, there's no checkbox, and Finish counts it only as "a block you added" in the Discard warning. You'd log a set that doesn't exist.

## Why not a processor

A same-tx processor ([sameTxProcessor.ts](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/api/sameTxProcessor.ts)) is a genuinely good substrate — live staged state, amends the user's tx, one undo step. But it sees *rows*, not gestures. Given an empty block whose previous sibling is a `strength-set`, "set or note?" has no answer in the data: the plan outline uses child bullets as descriptions, and a note about how the third set felt belongs in exactly that position. The distinguishing fact — what the user was doing when they pressed Enter — exists at the keystroke and is thrown away before the processor runs.

## Shape

A facet, not a field on `seedType`: that declaration materializes into a `block-type` block (label, description, property list all round-trip), and a function can't. It would be the one declaration-only field in a declaration whose job is to become data.

```ts
interface StructuralTemplate {
  forType: string
  relation: 'continue' | 'split' | 'descend'
  apply: (source: {content: string; properties: BlockProperties})
    => {types?: string[]; content?: string; properties?: BlockProperties} | null
}
```

**Composition.** `forType` is what makes the model enforceable rather than ordered. Core runs only contributions whose type the source block carries, and rejects one that writes a property its own type doesn't declare — the property list is already in the type registry. A set block is `strength-set` + `todo`; the strength contribution physically cannot write `status`, the todo one cannot write `weight`. Disjoint namespaces mean **the merge is order-independent** and registration order never decides anything. `types` accumulate as a union; at most one contribution may return `content` (two is a dev error).

**Relations**, because the answer differs per type per gesture:
- `continue` — Enter at end, vim `o`/`O`. The main case.
- `split` — Enter mid-text. Content comes from the split, so a contribution supplies only types/properties. `todo` accepts (two todos); `strength-set` declines, since its content is a generated `135lb × 10` label.
- `descend` — Enter when the block shows children. A child of a set is a note (decline); a child of a todo is plausibly a subtask (accept). Exactly the judgement that belongs to the plugin.

One facet with `relation` in the context rather than three facets: the answers share their derivation, so three contributions would compute the same thing and drift. Splitting later is mechanical.

**Where it's read.** At the gesture, not in the mutator — `apply: (tx, args)` ([mutator.ts:9](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/api/mutator.ts#L9)) has no facet runtime. One core helper called from the handful of sites that are genuinely user gestures, passing the result into `createSiblingBelow`, which already takes both fields. Programmatic callers keep today's behaviour.

**Untouched:** the empty-block outdent path. It's the escape hatch that keeps an auto-typing Enter from trapping you in a list of sets, and it becomes load-bearing rather than incidental.

## Honest limits

This doesn't make the ambiguity disappear — press Enter after the last set wanting a note and you still get a set. What changes is where the decision lives: a declaration saying "continuing a set means another set", written by the plugin that owns the type, instead of a heuristic reconstructing intent from committed rows. The override is a gesture that already exists.

It also ships inert: blast radius is zero until a type declares a continuation, and each plugin opts in deliberately — the right shape for a change to the hottest path in the editor.

## Why icebox

The instance that motivated this (an "add set" affordance in the strength tracker) was reconsidered — see #550 — and the remaining value is `todo` plus whatever typed row comes next. Worth building when a second real instance shows up, not before.

title: Legacy extension blocks still carry their whole source as an alias
description:
Split out of #540 (which fixes a *different* path to the same symptom — the wikilink parser minting pages from code).

### Observed

Three installed extension blocks in a live workspace — `readwise`, `matrix-chat-client`, `readwise-sync` — are typed `["extension","page"]` and carry an `alias` array of exactly two entries:

```
alias: ["readwise", "import {\n  actionsFacet, appEffectsFacet, ... <91 KB of bundled JS>"]
```

Entry 0 is the extension slug; entry 1 is the block's entire content. 91 KB, 49 KB and 18 KB respectively, all live in `block_aliases` and syncing.

### Mechanism (verified, not inferred)

`alias.sync` Rule 2 "drift-heal" in [`src/plugins/alias/syncProcessor.ts:133-143`](../blob/master/src/plugins/alias/syncProcessor.ts#L133-L143): when content changes on a block that is *already aliased*, and the old content wasn't itself an alias anchor, it appends the new content as a fresh alias entry:

```ts
// Rule 2 (A3): old content wasn't an alias anchor — heal
// additively by appending new content.
if (afterAliases.includes(after.content)) return null
return { ..., aliasesNext: [...afterAliases, after.content], ... }
```

Correct for an ordinary title-bearing page. Catastrophic for a block whose content *is* 91 KB of source. The rule is type-agnostic and has no upper bound — its only content guard is `after.content === ''`.

### Why these blocks are aliased at all

`61337dbad` ("refactor(extensions): identify extension blocks by extension:name, not alias/page") already removed the `PAGE_TYPE` + alias tagging from the install path for exactly this reason, and diagnosed the mechanism in its own commit message. But it closes with:

> Existing installs keep their alias/PAGE until cleaned up by hand.

No cleanup shipped, and none of these three have been hand-cleaned. Each still re-triggers the parity processor on every `install-extension` that rewrites its content.

### Two things to decide

1. **Clean up the legacy blocks** — drop `PAGE_TYPE` and the source-blob alias entry from extension blocks that predate `61337dbad`. A one-shot repair, or a `WorkspaceBackfill`.
2. **Should `alias.sync`'s drift-heal be length-bounded?** The install path no longer aliases extension blocks, so this specific route is closed — but the rule itself will still mirror an arbitrarily large content blob into the alias index for *any* aliased block. #540 adds `MAX_ALIAS_LENGTH = 1024` to the wikilink parser on the same reasoning (longest human-authored alias in a ~31k-alias workspace: 322 chars); the same bound arguably belongs here. Separate call — it changes behaviour in a different plugin, so it isn't in #540.

title: Sync: a client whose clock runs past the trusted-skew cap keeps a stale in-memory row after a drifted merge (cache LWW never converges)
description:
Residual found while reviewing #525 (the #381 base-version fix). #525 fixes the **disk** convergence for every client; this is the same user-facing symptom surviving in the **in-memory cache**, for the narrow class of clients whose clock runs more than `max_trusted_skew_ms` (1h) ahead of the server.

Not a regression from #525 — the same shape exists today via the pre-existing future-clamp, which knocks a skewed client's stamps down the same way. #525 makes it reachable through one more path (the drift bump is bounded by the same cap) and is what made it visible.

## Symptom

Device A's clock is 1.5h ahead of the server. A and B edit one row concurrently; the server merges and, because A's proposal is past the cap, stamps the merged row at `server_now + 1h` — **below** A's local stamp.

Reproduced through the real pipeline (`concurrentEditConvergence.test.ts` wiring: real compactor → real RPC shapes → `blocks_synced` → `drainStagingWindowOnce` → `applySyncInvalidation`):

```
disk   : content "B-content"  @ 1700003600005    ← converged, correct
cached : content "original"   @ 1700005400004    ← A's pre-merge row, permanently
metrics: applyIfNewerSyncRejected: 3             ← every delivery to A rejected
```

A's UI shows `original` for the rest of the session while disk and every other device hold `B-content`. It heals on reload (the cache rehydrates from the already-correct disk). No divergence on disk, no data loss.

## Mechanism

`applySyncInvalidation` (`syncObserver/invalidate.ts`) writes each materialized row through `cache.applyIfNewer(after, 'sync')`, which rejects when `incoming.updatedAt <= cached.updatedAt` (`blockCache.ts:183`). A skewed client's local stamp is above anything the server will ever issue for that row, so **no future delivery can ever out-stamp it** — and a rejected row also contributes no invalidation, so handles don't re-read either.

## Why the cheap fixes don't work

The reject is load-bearing (invariant from cd8f87a9): it masks a *transient* disk revert during a rescan's ack→echo window, which self-heals when the echo lands. Two candidates, both refuted:

1. **Force the snapshot when the cached stamp is more than the cap above the incoming one.** Unsound: in the ack→echo transient the incoming row is the row's *previous* server version, which can be arbitrarily old (last edited months ago) while the cache holds a fresh local edit. The gap exceeds the cap, so this fires precisely on the case the invariant protects — and force-applies a months-old row over a fresh edit.
2. **Force when `snap.before` equals the cached value** (i.e. the cache was in sync with disk before this write). Unsound for the same reason: that predicate is *also* true in the transient case (the local edit is on disk and in the cache), so it can't separate them.

The two cases are structurally identical at the cache seam. What distinguishes them is whether a later delivery will out-stamp the cached value — which depends on **whether our clock is ahead of the server's**, information no layer currently has.

## What a real fix needs

Either of:

- **A client-side server-clock offset estimate.** Every arriving row carries a server-authored stamp, so the client can bound server-now from below and detect "my clock is past the cap" — the precise predicate this needs. Then the cache can force on reject only in that regime.
- **Clamp local stamps to observed server time.** Change invariant I3 (`local stamp = max(now, before+1)`) to also bound by the freshest observed server stamp plus the cap, so a skewed client never mints a stamp the server can't reach. Fixes the cause rather than the symptom, but touches the most central stamping invariant in the data layer.

Both are their own change with their own review — deliberately not bundled into #525, which is scoped to server-side drift detection.

## Pinned

`src/data/test/concurrentEditConvergence.test.ts` — `'the far-ahead author's cache keeps the pre-merge row even though disk converged'`. It asserts the current (wrong) cache state on purpose and cites this issue; a fix should flip it to assert convergence.

title: Spatial nav's model-agreement guard breaks j/k on surfaces that render blocks outside their model order
description:
## Summary

Since the #494/#513/#519 model-agreement stack, `moveVertical` validates the rendered `j`/`k` neighbour against a model walk. On a surface whose rows are **query results** — blocks rendered in an order the model doesn't define, under a panel whose root is not their model ancestor — every `j`/`k` press now declines to the model handler, which walks the block's *real* ancestry and focuses a block the surface doesn't render. Keyboard navigation on such surfaces is effectively destroyed (hit this on the hosted deploy today, 2026-08-01).

Concrete case: my agenda extension (org-mode-style agenda viewport). Rows are `todo` blocks that live under project pages / a `[[Tasks]]` page; the agenda block's renderer shows them flat, grouped into sections, each section a distinct `renderScopeId`. The panel's `topLevelBlockId` — and therefore `deps.scopeRootId`, inherited through block context (`useShortcutSurfaceActivations`) — is the agenda viewport block, never a model ancestor of any row.

## Trace (master `25c246606`)

1. `moveVertical` (`src/plugins/spatial-navigation/actions.ts`) computes `modelNext = nextVisibleBlock(block, deps.scopeRootId, …)`.
2. `nextVisibleBlock` (`src/utils/selection.ts`) climbs `parentId` links looking for a next sibling, terminating only when the walker *reaches* `scopeRootId`. A row that isn't a model descendant of the scope root never satisfies that guard, so the climb runs up the row's real ancestry — `modelNext` becomes the task's first body child, or the next task under its project page, bounded only by the workspace root.
3. The DOM neighbour is the next agenda row: same `renderScopeId` but a different block, so it fails `takesTheModelRow`; same scope, so it fails `stepsIntoANestedSurface` → `canTakeTheNeighbour` is false → decline (`return false`).
4. The base `move_down` (`src/plugins/vim-normal-mode/actions.ts`) then runs the *same* unbounded model walk and `focusBlock`s the result: either a block the surface doesn't render (focus highlight vanishes; `PanelFocusRecovery` later warps focus somewhere else) or one rendered in a different section (focus teleports). `k` on a first-sibling row lands on its model parent — the project page block.

Before the stack, `moveVertical` took `verticalNeighbor(current, direction)` unconditionally — precisely correct for these surfaces, since the rendered order is the only order they have.

## What seems to be missing

The guard's premise — "the DOM order is a SUPERSET of this scope's model order" — assumes every render scope is model-backed. A query-driven surface's ordering is what #519's own header calls "the list that owns that ordering": no model walk expresses it. What's missing is a **sanctioned way for a surface to say so**.

Mechanically, a row context with **no `scopeRootId`** already yields the right behavior end-to-end today: `modelNext` is gated on `deps.scopeRootId`, the scope-edge/reserved-row branch is gated the same way, and the base `move_down`/`move_up` return early without it — so spatial nav takes the rendered neighbour and model navigation stands down. But that's an accident of factoring, not a documented contract, and nothing pins it.

Design doc PR incoming (options: sanction-and-pin the absent scope root; an explicit `listOwnedOrder` context flag; walker self-detection as hardening). I've worked around it in the extension for now by clearing `scopeRootId` in the rows' context.

title: Tx has no workspace-scoped query, so every extension decision must be made outside the transaction that commits it
description:
Split out of PR #441, where this one gap produced **seven** separate review findings on a single code path.

## The gap

`Tx` can reach a block by id or by structure — `get`, `peek`, `childrenOf`, `parentOf`, `adjacentSibling`, `isDescendantOf`, `aliasLookup`, `aliasClaimants` — but it has no equivalent of `repo.query.typedBlocks({workspaceId, types})`.

So any decision that depends on a workspace-wide question ("is a session already under way anywhere?", "what does history look like?", "does a record already cover this gap?") **must** be computed from a query that ran before the transaction opened, and then committed inside it. The decision and its inputs are separated by an unbounded window: several awaits at minimum, an open dialog at worst, and a sync-applied row needs no race at all.

## What that costs, concretely

In `agent-extensions/strength-tracker`, `closeSession` reads the program, decides whether the session being closed ends a training break, and commits. Every input to that decision needed a hand-rolled fence carried into the transaction and re-checked there. Each one was found by review, one round at a time:

1. the target workout's `strength:date`
2. its session kind (mini vs full — decides whether a layoff is recorded at all)
3. the discard counts (a sibling case, in `discardSession`)
4. the last full session day the gap is measured from
5. that day's *date* — existence was fenced, but the workout could be re-dated
6. the existing layoff record the decision leaned on
7. that record's *tier* — the fence compared a denormalised percentage that nothing reads

Six and seven are fixes to fixes. The pattern is not that the code was careless; it is that the structure generates exactly one finding per unfenced input, and there is no way to enumerate the inputs at the type level.

The same gap forced a per-client serialization of `startSession`, because "is a session under way anywhere in this workspace" cannot be asked inside the transaction that would stamp one.

## What would help

A workspace-scoped read inside `Tx` — even a narrow one (typed-blocks by type, scoped to the transaction's workspace, no subscription semantics) — collapses all of the above: the decision moves inside the transaction that commits it, and there is nothing left to fence.

Open questions for whoever picks this up:

- Is it safe on the write connection, or does it need the same statement/lock discipline as `childrenOf`?
- Does it encourage transactions long enough to hurt contention? A bounded result or an explicit type filter may be the right shape.
- Should it read the pre-transaction snapshot or see the transaction's own uncommitted writes? For the decide-then-commit use case, seeing own writes matters.

## If it is not feasible

The fallback worth having is a shared fence primitive rather than a hand-rolled argument per fact — a declared set of `(block id, fields)` captured at read time and re-verified in the transaction, so "did you fence this input?" becomes a question about one list instead of a question about each parameter. `FinishExpectation` in the strength extension is a hand-built version of that shape and is worth reading before designing one.
