title: Focused-location anchors that can't be re-resolved after a remount
description:
Split out of PR #513 (cursor-anchored scroll restore), where four review rounds each surfaced another instance of the same class.

## The class

A `focusedBlockLocation` is `(blockId, renderScopeId)`. Several surfaces render rows whose location **cannot be re-resolved from that pair after a remount**, so anything that navigates by stored location — keyboard nav into the row, and now scroll restore — cannot reach them:

1. **Block-embed targets.** `BlockEmbed` renders the target only inside the embed's source row, so no wrapper for the target exists until that source mounts. `FocusedRowLazyMount`'s ancestor walk follows the target's DATA parents, which belong to a different tree, so it never requests the source's placeholder.
2. **The video-notes layout root.** `VideoNotesLayout` discards `Shell`'s props (`VideoNotesRenderer.tsx:269`), so its top-level video renders none of `data-block-nav-item` / block id / scope / ref. Focus can land there when entering notes view with existing notes (`ensureEditableVideoNoteChild` returns early), and nothing can find that row afterwards.
3. **Promoted backlink anchors.** `BacklinkItem` can render a promoted ancestor from local `shownId` state; `LazyBacklinkItem` registers only the original source. After a remount the promoted location no longer exists.

Two more of the same class were fixed in #513 because the restore depended on them: backlink entries and recents rows, both of which minted their own lazy cache key and so were unreachable by block id. That was closed by registering under `lazyBlockCacheKey` as well and making `LazyViewportMount.blockId` required.

## Why it isn't urgent

These all **predate** #513 — keyboard navigation to those rows has always been dead — and #513 no longer makes them worse: an anchor that can't be found now falls back to the stored pixel offset rather than stranding the pane at the top.

## What a fix looks like

Either a location-aware lazy registration (a surface declares how to materialize a location, not just a block id), or per-surface: request the embed owner chain, give the video-notes root a real shell, normalize a promoted backlink cursor to its stable entry before unmount.

Worth doing together rather than one at a time — the recurring shape is that a rendered location's *reachability* is implicit, and each surface re-derives it differently.

Credit: all three found by Codex review on #513.

title: Two fast j/k presses can collapse into one move while a model walk is uncached
description:
Found by review on #494 ([thread](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/494#discussion_r3687520573)). Real, narrow, and deliberately not fixed in that PR — the obvious fix regresses the hot path, and the good fix wants its own pass.

## What happens

`move_down` / `move_up` resolve their target with `await nextVisibleBlock(...)`. On an uncached `childIds` that's a DB round-trip. Two presses inside that window both capture the same starting row, both resume, both read focus as still on A, and both write B:

```
press 1  ──walk(A)────────────► focus := B
press 2      ──walk(A)────────► focus := B      (wanted: C)
```

Two keystrokes, one row moved. The staleness guard added in 51f0aa25b doesn't catch it — neither invocation has written yet when the other checks, so focus legitimately still reads A for both.

## Why it's narrow

Bounded by the uncached-walk window. The steady state is handle-cached (same parent's `childIds`), so repeat presses resolve in a microtask and can't overlap. It needs a cold page, or a slow device, plus presses closer together than the walk.

## Why the obvious fix is wrong

Serializing the walks and awaiting the write would make every `j` wait for a transaction commit. `focusBlock` is `void`ed at these call sites on purpose (`src/plugins/vim-normal-mode/actions.ts`), and `invokeAction` doesn't await handlers — held-key repeat feeling instant depends on both. Trading that on every page to fix a cold-page case is a bad deal.

## The shape that probably works

An optimistic per-panel cursor: remember the location the in-flight move is heading to, and start the next walk from there rather than from the panel's not-yet-updated focus. Keeps writes fire-and-forget. The design work is the lifecycle — what clears it when a click lands mid-flight, when the write fails, when the panel swaps pages — which is exactly what shouldn't be bolted on at the end of a long review loop.

Whatever the fix, it should be pinned with a test that overlaps two walks with a deferred resolution; today's `staleFocusWrite.test.ts` only covers a single handler against already-moved focus.

title: readwise.tsx: no force resync, dead checkpoint-clear code, inert sync-since picker
description:
Found while retiring the superseded `agent-extensions/readwise.js` prototype (#492). The prototype had two purpose-built escape hatches — `user.readwise.sync-full` and `user.readwise.reset-checkpoint` — with no counterpart in `readwise.tsx`. All three problems below are pre-existing in `readwise.tsx` and independent of that deletion.

### 1. The Disconnect button's checkpoint clear is dead code

[`readwise.tsx:1614-1621`](../blob/master/agent-extensions/readwise.tsx#L1614): the comment `// also clear sync checkpoint so a reconnect starts fresh` is followed by

```js
void block
void repo
```

`git blame` puts both `void` statements in the file's first commit (`ec34cc380`, 2026-05-23) — dead from day one, never touched by any of the ~23 later commits, including two that reworked the disconnect/dialog flow. So Disconnect clears the token but silently not the checkpoint, contrary to its own comment.

### 2. No force-resync path

`runSync`'s signature is `(repo, {silent = false} = {})` ([`readwise.tsx:1444`](../blob/master/agent-extensions/readwise.tsx#L1444)); all three call sites pass only `silent`. There is no way to ignore the checkpoint and re-pull, and only three actions are registered (configure, sync, connect).

### 3. The `readwise:syncSince` picker is inert once you've synced

`updatedAfter = lastSynced ?? syncSince?.toISOString() ?? null` ([`readwise.tsx:1462`](../blob/master/agent-extensions/readwise.tsx#L1462)), and `readwise:lastSyncedAt` is set after every **successful** sync — a run that finds nothing new included, since `prefs.set(lastSyncedAtProp, finishedAt)` sits outside the per-book branch. (A sync that errors partway skips it: the `set` is inside the `try`.) So the user-facing "sync since" date picker silently does nothing from the second sync onward.

**It is not literally unresettable**, and the issue should not be built on that premise: `readwise:lastSyncedAt` is `ChangeScope.UserPrefs`, isn't hidden, and isn't in `INTRINSIC_READ_ONLY_PROPERTY_NAMES`, so `rowReadOnly` is false and `canDelete` is true — the prefs block's generic property row renders a working trash control ([`PropertyRow.tsx:171`](../blob/master/src/components/propertyPanel/PropertyRow.tsx#L171), wired at [`BlockProperties.tsx:263`](../blob/master/src/components/BlockProperties.tsx#L263)). `LastSyncedEditor`'s read-only `<span>` replaces only the *value cell*, not the row's delete control (`Editor: rowReadOnly ? undefined : display.Editor`). So the recovery path today is: open Readwise settings → hover the "Last synced" row → trash icon → Sync now. This is verified at code level across those call sites, not by clicking through the live UI.

This makes it a **discoverability** bug, not a hard stall — hence P2 rather than P1.

### Minimum fix

- `ConnectedEditor`'s Disconnect handler: actually unset `lastSyncedAtProp` on the prefs block instead of `void block; void repo`.
- `runSync`: add `{full?: boolean}` forcing `updatedAfter = null`, exposed as a "Full resync" control beside "Sync now" ([`readwise.tsx:1630`](../blob/master/agent-extensions/readwise.tsx#L1630)).
- Optionally give `LastSyncedEditor` an explicit Reset affordance rather than leaving the generic hover-only trash icon as the only lever.

### Worth knowing

Nothing in `readwise.tsx` records that `readwise:lastSyncedAt` must stay non-hidden and non-read-only for that escape hatch to keep working. Someone tidying the settings panel with `hidden: true` would silently remove the only working reset path. A one-line comment at the property declaration ([`readwise.tsx:107`](../blob/master/agent-extensions/readwise.tsx#L107)) would prevent that.

title: Decide ownership of agent:*/claude:* property keys before any props-as-blocks flip (21 keys, 525 cells, invisible to audit-extension)
description:
Surfaced by [PR #500](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/500)'s workspace-wide property audit.

## Finding

On the prod graph, 21 property keys resolve to no schema and are written by the claude-tasks daemon:

- `agent:*` — 12 keys, 369 cells: `executor`, `watcher`, `updated-at`, `status`, `attempts`, `session`, `reply`, `subtreeKey`, `activity`, `cancel`, `error`, `resume-options`
- `claude:*` — 9 keys, 156 cells: `watcher`, `updated-at`, `status`, `reply`, `attempts`, `session`, `activity`, `cancel`, `error`

They sit on `matrix-message` + `todo` + `srs-sm2.5` blocks (the daemon reacting to matrix messages), plus some untyped blocks.

Two things worth separating:

**1. They're invisible to the existing audit.** `grainAudit.isSystemProperty` blanket-exempts any name starting with `agent:` as "the app's own namespaced UI state". These aren't UI state — `agent:status`, `agent:reply`, `agent:session` on ~37 blocks are real records. So `audit-extension` cannot report them, and neither could the pre-write warning. Worth revisiting whether the `agent:` exemption should be narrowed to the specific keys that really are UI state.

**2. Nobody declares them, so a flip can't carry them.** Property migration skips unregistered keys silently. Before any workspace flips to child-backed properties these need an owner — either the daemon declares them as seeds (preferred: then the definitions are seed-origin and rename-stable) or §9 orphan synthesis mints user-origin definitions for them. Order matters: synthesizing first and declaring seeds later collides in the winner machinery and strands field rows on the loser's fieldId.

Note the `agent:` / `claude:` duplication looks like a rename mid-flight (same 9 leaf names in both namespaces) — probably worth resolving into one namespace as part of this rather than declaring both.

Related: the claude-tasks daemon work is currently stopped with ~90 lines uncommitted; whoever picks that up should fold the declarations in.

## Verification

`pnpm agent audit-properties` (PR #500) lists all 21 with counts, sample blocks and carrying types.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
close_reason:
Ownership resolved; the audit half is split out.

agent:* (12 keys + agent:asked-at) was never actually unowned: seed declarations landed 2026-07-21 in the agent-dispatch-companion and agent-runtime schemas, wired via staticDataExtensions — nine days BEFORE this issue was filed. All 13 resolve live as seed-origin definitions, so the preferred option (declare as seeds, before any orphan synthesis) is already satisfied and the ordering hazard never materialized.

claude:* (9 keys, 156 cells, 44 blocks) was the residue of a completed rename (2026-07-05), whose documented copy-forward deliberately left the originals in place. Verified before deleting: every one of the 156 cells had an agent:* twin and every twin was value-identical — zero divergence, zero orphans. Dropped 2026-08-18 through repo.tx, re-checking the twin condition inside the writing tx per row. Post-state: 0 claude:* cells, agent:* unchanged at 396 cells / 132 blocks.

Net: this is no longer a flip blocker. Property migration has an owner for every agent-namespace key.

The audit blindspot (grainAudit.isSystemProperty) is genuinely open and is now its own issue — it needs a design decision, not the one-line prefix removal proposed here.

title: Content promotion mints definition-less property keys (matrix:timestamp/url) — needs a register-first pass like the roam importer's
description:
Split out of the [PR #500](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/pull/500) investigation, which built the *reporting* half only.

## The seam

`computePromotedFromChildren` ([src/plugins/roam-import/promotion.ts](../blob/master/src/plugins/roam-import/promotion.ts)) is a pure function: it turns `key:: value` children into a namespaced property bag and **registers nothing**. The roam importer pairs it with a classify-then-`userSchemas.addSchema` pass ([schemaReconciliation.ts](../blob/master/src/plugins/roam-import/schemaReconciliation.ts)) that runs *before* content blocks are written — which is why all 385 `roam:*` keys in the prod graph have definition blocks.

The matrix extension reuses the promotion function with `namespacePrefix: 'matrix'` and **skips reconciliation**. Result on live data:

- `matrix:timestamp` — 258 cells, no definition
- `matrix:url` — 174 cells, no definition
- `matrix:status` — 1 cell, no definition

These are NOT the extension's declared properties (all 9 of those are properly seeded). They're a different property that shares a leaf name: `matrix:timestamp` is `"13/06/2026 13:39:23 UTC"` promoted from a bot's `timestamp::` line, while the declared `matrix-event:timestamp` is epoch ms. Same for `matrix:url` (array of Readwise/source URLs) vs `matrix-event:url` (matrix.to permalink).

## Why it matters

An unregistered key is skipped silently by property migration (`propertyChildrenProcessor`: `resolveNameSchema` → `continue`), so it's the one class of property data a child-backed workspace can't carry. §9 orphan synthesis is the intended converter, but the migration doc requires extension-owned keys to be claimed by their owner *first* — synthesizing first mints a user-origin definition that collides with a later seed and strands field rows on the loser's fieldId.

Promotion is structurally a definition-less key minter: the key names come from message text, so no `seedProperty` list can cover them. Any consumer needs the register-first pass, not just a one-time cleanup.

## Options

1. **Fold registration into the promotion helper** — have it return the keys it minted (or take a repo and register them) so no consumer can forget. Strongest, and it makes the roam pass the default rather than a thing you remember.
2. **Call reconciliation from the matrix extension** — smallest change, leaves the next promotion consumer exposed.
3. **Leave promoted keys to §9 synthesis** — acceptable only if the flip runbook explicitly enables/claims first; note synthesis mints *user-origin* definitions, so a later `seedProperty` for the same name collides.

## Live trap already present

`matrix:audio-url` / `matrix:audio-file-name` (182 cells each) are also promoted, but DO have definitions with random v4 ids, no `seed:key`, no change-scope — hand-registered via `addSchema`. So if anyone later adds `seedProperty({name: 'matrix:audio-url'})`, the seed collides with that existing user-origin definition. Worth resolving alongside whichever option is chosen.

## Repro / verification

`pnpm agent audit-properties` (PR #500) lists these with counts and per-key reasons.

title: Canary/detection gaps: plugin-disable can silently stop deriving data; only 1 of 4 trigger-maintained index tables is mirror-checked
description:
## Origin

A note-to-self, paraphrased: after some staleness/breakage was noticed late, "how could we have detected that something like that was happening?" — could a canary, periodic check, or data-integrity check have caught it sooner? A sibling note in the same bullet: "we need to resolve the 'disabling plugins makes bad things happen' situation."

This issue grounds both halves in the current code, separating what's already built from what's still a gap. **CONFIRMED** = verified by reading the code; **HYPOTHESIS** = plausible but not verified for every case.

## What already exists (so this isn't proposing from zero)

This repo already has a mature, documented defense system — `docs/data-integrity-defense.html` (layers L1–L6), built out of a prior incident cluster:
- **Client-side consistency audit** (`src/plugins/data-integrity/audit.ts`): a lean subset runs on a 30-min idle cadence per workspace (`schedule.ts`, `CADENCE_MS`), surfaced via a status-chip diagnostic; a richer `full` superset runs on demand (in-app action, or the bridge eval `scripts/data-integrity/consistency-check.eval.js`).
- **Server-side probe** (`scripts/supabase-health.mjs`, hourly via `.github/workflows/supabase-health.yml`): DB health thresholds plus L5 data-integrity anomaly detectors over `blocks_history`.
- **Local DB corruption detection** (`src/utils/localDbCorruption.ts`, `src/data/localDbCorruptionSignal.ts`): both open-time and runtime SQLite corruption, routed to a recovery UI (export + reset, never auto-wipe).
- **Trigger-freeze protection** (`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:1155-1176`): every `CREATE TRIGGER` is prepended with `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS` on every boot, specifically because `CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS` silently freezes an old trigger body forever otherwise (this is documented as the exact mechanism behind a past incident).
- **Add-only/retain-on-source policy** for derived refs (`isRetainableAbsentRef`) — when a property's schema is absent (e.g. its owning plugin isn't loaded), *existing* derived refs are retained rather than stripped. This is the fix for the historical ~10k-backlink mass-strip incident that the design doc's "Class A" names as caused partly by "a schema toggled off."
- Extension-authoring side: `pnpm agent audit-extension` + `install-extension --verify` already catch the analogous problem for **user-authored** extensions (block ids in non-ref properties, records in JSON cells, properties with no registered schema) — precedent for an operator-run audit command.

So the "can we detect this" instinct is already largely built for the failure classes that caused past incidents. The gaps below are specific and narrower.

## Gap 1 (CONFIRMED): disabling a built-in plugin can silently stop deriving data for new edits — not just degrade UI

Toggling a non-essential plugin off doesn't just hide UI — it prunes the **entire** extension subtree, including data-layer schema and post-commit processors:

> "a togglable boundary array is pruned when its handle resolves to off" — `src/facets/resolveAppRuntime.ts:78-89` (`resolverVisitor`/`shouldKeepBoundary`)

Two concrete, code-confirmed examples:
- `references` plugin (`src/plugins/references/index.ts`) is a non-essential `systemToggle`. Its `referencesDataExtension` (`dataExtension.ts`) bundles the `block_references` local schema **and** `parseReferencesProcessor` (`referencesProcessor.ts`) — the post-commit processor that parses `[[wikilinks]]`/`((block-refs))`/ref-typed properties out of `content`/`properties` into the `references` column — under the *same* toggle boundary.
- `alias` plugin (`src/plugins/alias/index.ts`) bundles `aliasDataExtension`'s sync processor the same way.

Consequence: while `references` (or `alias`) is disabled, a block edited or created with a `[[wikilink]]` in it gets **no reference derived at all** — not stripped, never computed. This is distinct from the already-fixed mass-strip class: retain-on-source protects *existing* derived refs from deletion when a schema is absent; it does nothing for *new* content authored while the owning processor isn't registered. The gap persists until some *other* edit re-touches one of the processor's watched fields (`content`/`properties`/`references`/`deleted`) on that same block — or indefinitely, if it never is.

The one check that would catch this — `content_link_recompute` (R1/R3 in `audit.ts`, flags a block with marks in content but no matching stored ref) — only runs in **`full` mode**, which is on-demand only (`schedule.ts` never passes `opts.full`). So the always-on 30-min cadence does not surface it; a human has to know to run "Run data integrity audit" in full mode. There's also no warning in the Extensions settings UI (`src/plugins/extensions-settings/ExtensionsSettings.tsx`) when toggling off a plugin that owns data derivation — it's a plain checkbox.

**HYPOTHESIS**: this generalizes to other data-extension plugins that bundle a `postCommitProcessorsFacet` contribution under their own toggle (daily-notes, grouped-backlinks, etc.) — not verified per-plugin here, but the toggle mechanism (`resolveAppRuntime.ts`) applies uniformly, and issue #150 independently confirms disabling a data-extension plugin is a recognized, distinct runtime state (there, causing a perf regression rather than data staleness).

## Gap 2 (CONFIRMED): the consistency audit's mirror check covers only one of four trigger-maintained index tables

`block_references`, `block_types`, `block_aliases`, and `blocks_fts` are all trigger-maintained mirrors of `blocks` (triggers defined in `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts` — `blocks_type_*`, `blocks_alias_*`, `blocks_fts_*` — plus `blocks_references_*` in `src/plugins/references/localSchema.ts`). Only `block_references` has a mirror-consistency check (`references_index_mirror` in `audit.ts`, diffing `blocks.references_json` against the `block_references` rows in both directions, plus dupes/malformed JSON). Nothing in either lean or full mode compares `block_types`/`block_aliases`/`blocks_fts` content against their source `blocks` columns.

To be clear about what's *not* the gap: trigger-body drift itself (a client's installed trigger silently keeping a stale definition) is already handled by the boot-time `DROP TRIGGER`+recreate in `clientSchema.ts` — that's a different, already-solved problem. The gap here is that nothing verifies these tables' *content* stays in sync with `blocks` at runtime the way `block_references` is verified (e.g. a future bug in one of these triggers, or a manual DB-surgery script that forgets one of the four, would go undetected).

## What a canary could look like

Detection and manual, well-warned repair only — nothing here should auto-repair or auto-wipe live user data.

- Promote `content_link_recompute` (or a cheap bounded variant, mirroring how `property_ref_at_rest` already has a curated lean subset vs. a full schema-aware superset) into the always-on lean cadence, so a plugin-disabled staleness window gets flagged without a human remembering to run the full audit.
- Add mirror-consistency checks for `block_types`/`block_aliases`/`blocks_fts` analogous to `references_index_mirror` — same shape, different table.
- Surface a warning in the Extensions settings UI when disabling a plugin that owns a `postCommitProcessorsFacet`/`localSchemaFacet` contribution (data-owning, not purely UI) — the built-in-plugin toggle path currently has no analogue to the `audit-extension`/`install-extension --verify` precedent that already exists for user-authored extensions.

## Related, not duplicates

- #209 (meta correctness-audit epic) — different failure-class taxonomy (stale inputs, per-column desync, non-atomic sequencing); doesn't cover plugin-toggle-caused non-derivation or the four-table mirror-coverage gap.
- #460 (two blocks claiming the same alias) — a different, already-filed silent-drift class; same spirit ("detection is independently useful"), different mechanism.
- #150 (cold-start re-resolve storm for disabled data-extension plugins) — confirms plugin-disable is a recognized distinct runtime state, but the bug there is performance, not data staleness.

## Priority

Proposing **P2**: this is a detection/observability gap in an already-mature, actively-maintained defense system, not an active corruption incident — no evidence anyone has hit the plugin-disable staleness gap in practice, and the mirror-coverage gap is a coverage hole, not an observed failure. Happy to defer to a different call.

title: Mobile UX: WorkFlowy-style touch-and-hold selection, movement toolbar, drag-reorder, and bullet context menu
description:
## Motivation

WorkFlowy's mobile outliner UX is worth studying and partially copying. The specific affordances worth of note:

- touch-and-hold enters a visual "selection mode" for the bulleted item
- a bottom bar focused on movement (indent/outdent/move up/down) appears once something is selected
- bullets support drag-and-drop to rearrange directly
- a context menu on the bullet offers actions like move, embed, etc.

This issue is a design/scoping starting point, not a single monolithic ask — see the breakdown below.

## What already exists (so this doesn't duplicate work)

The app already has a fair amount of the underlying plumbing; most of what's missing is the touch *entry point* into it, plus net-new drag-and-drop.

- **Multi-select mode already exists as an action context** (`ActionContextTypes.MULTI_SELECT_MODE = 'multi-select-mode'`, `src/shortcuts/defaultContexts.ts`, `modal: true`), and it already has a "movement bar's" worth of actions wired up — indent/outdent, move up/down, toggle-collapse, delete/cut, copy, paste-before/after (`multiSelectModeActions` in `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts`, ~L1213). It's entered today only via desktop-only triggers: `Shift+ArrowUp/Down` (keyboard) and `Shift`/`Ctrl`/`Cmd`-click (`src/extensions/blockSelectionAction.ts`, `pointerBinding: {kind: 'mouse', ...}`). **No touch path reaches it at all today** — `pointerBinding` supports a `kind: 'touch'` variant elsewhere in the codebase, but nothing binds it for selection.
- **A gesture-recognizer framework already exists and is live**, not just designed: `src/extensions/continuousGestures.ts` unifies Pointer Events into a per-block recognizer loop with arbitration (last-active-wins), an enablement gate, and non-passive-listener/`touch-action` handling for scroll suppression. Existing recognizers built on it: swipe-quick-actions (`src/plugins/swipe-quick-actions/swipeRecognizer.ts`) and daily-notes' two-finger date-scrub (`src/plugins/daily-notes/dateScrubGesture.ts`). This is the extension point a new long-press recognizer would plug into. See also `docs/continuous-gesture-triggers.md` for the trigger-unification design (the generic `gestureBinding` on the action-dispatch spine is still pre-implementation; the recognizer loop itself is not).
- **Long-press is explicitly reserved in a code comment for exactly this idea already**, and explicitly *not yet built*: `src/plugins/daily-notes/dateScrubGesture.ts` (top-of-file doc comment) says long-press is intentionally not used for date-scrub because "that gesture belongs to selection / bullet drag (Workflowy convention)." So this proposal isn't a new idea to the codebase — it's an acknowledged placeholder nobody has filled in yet.
- **Two mobile-specific fixed bottom bars already exist** as precedent for a third: `src/plugins/mobile-bottom-nav/` (global nav: sidebar/new-node/today/search/undo/command-palette) and `src/plugins/mobile-keyboard-toolbar/` (shown above the on-screen keyboard while a block is being text-edited; its default items already include outdent/indent/move-up/move-down/undo/redo, `src/plugins/mobile-keyboard-toolbar/defaultItems.ts`). Both use a facet-of-action-refs pattern (`mobileBottomNavItemsFacet` / `mobileKeyboardToolbarItemsFacet`) so other plugins can contribute buttons, and both gate visibility on `usePointerCoarse()` (touch-primary device detection, `src/utils/react.js`). A selection-mode movement bar is a natural third instance of the same pattern.
- **A bullet context menu already exists on desktop** (`src/components/renderer/DefaultBlockRenderer.tsx`, the `BlockBullet` component, using Radix `ContextMenu`): Copy ID, Copy Block Ref, **Copy Block Embed**, Zoom In, Show/Hide Properties. "Copy Block Embed" already covers the "embed" idea from the notes. Whether this menu is currently reachable via long-press on mobile is **unverified** — Radix listens for the native `contextmenu` DOM event, which mobile browsers fire on a long-press of some elements but not reliably across iOS/Android/element types. Worth device-testing before assuming it's a gap. "Move" is not currently a menu item (there's no destination-picker UI anywhere in the app) — that part would be net new.
- **Block drag-and-drop reordering does not exist at all**, desktop or mobile. No `draggable`/`onDragStart`/`onDrop` handling on blocks/bullets anywhere in `src/components` or `src/editor`, and no drag-and-drop library (`dnd-kit`, `react-dnd`, `sortablejs`, etc.) in `package.json`. This would be entirely new infrastructure.

## Proposed breakdown (independently shippable)

**1. Touch-and-hold enters multi-select-mode** — *needs design*
A new long-press recognizer (via `continuousGestures.ts`) that arms selection on a held block, wired to the existing `MULTI_SELECT_MODE` context. Design questions: hold-then-drag-to-extend vs. hold-then-tap-more-blocks; how it arbitrates against the existing swipe-quick-action and date-scrub recognizers on the same block surface; what the visual "now selecting" affordance is (WorkFlowy shows a highlight + drag handle); duration/movement thresholds. This is the gating piece — 2 and 4 partly, and 3 possibly, depend on how this is designed.

**2. A movement-focused bottom toolbar while multi-select is active** — *small-to-medium, mostly plumbing*
The underlying actions already exist (see above). This is largely "build a `mobile-keyboard-toolbar`-shaped component gated on `MULTI_SELECT_MODE` + `pointer:coarse` instead of `EDIT_MODE_CM`." Must reuse the existing iOS keyboard/viewport machinery — see risk note below — though since selecting blocks doesn't require the on-screen keyboard, the positioning math here is likely simpler (mostly `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`, like `mobile-bottom-nav` already does) and should be verified on-device rather than assumed identical to the edit-mode toolbar's case.

**3. Drag-and-drop bullet reordering** — *needs design, largest piece, worth scoping/shipping separately*
Entirely new. Open questions: hand-rolled on `continuousGestures.ts` pointer-event primitives vs. pulling in a DnD library (none currently a dependency); mouse support or touch-only; single-block drag vs. dragging an active multi-selection; how it composes with (1) (does drag require selection mode first, or is a direct press-and-drag on one bullet independent of it — this mirrors WorkFlowy's own UX, which has both a plain bullet-drag *and* a separate multi-select flow, so the notes may be describing two distinct affordances rather than one). Also: the data layer has had real bugs from tied/duplicate `order_key` values on concurrent reorders (e.g. issues #182, #198) — any new order-writing code on the drag-commit path needs to go through the existing move/reorder primitives, not hand-roll `order_key` math.

**4. Extend the existing bullet context menu** — *small*
Add "Move" (needs a destination picker, which doesn't exist yet — could piggyback on whatever UI (3) builds) to the existing Radix `ContextMenu` in `DefaultBlockRenderer.tsx`; "Copy Block Embed" already exists. First, device-verify whether the existing menu already surfaces via long-press on iOS/Android before assuming this needs new gesture wiring — if (1) ships a long-press recognizer, wiring this menu to it explicitly (rather than relying on the native `contextmenu` event) would also make it consistent across platforms.

## Risk to flag: iOS fixed-positioning + keyboard hazard

This codebase has hard-won, non-obvious prior art here (`src/utils/keyboardViewport.ts`, `src/utils/keyboardAwareScroll.ts`) from getting the *existing* two mobile bottom bars right: iOS Safari keeps the *layout* viewport full-height while the *visual* viewport shrinks under the on-screen keyboard (Android Chrome instead resizes the layout viewport), so a naive `position: fixed` bottom element can end up positioned against the wrong viewport, and reacting to the resulting `scroll` events by re-scrolling can create a self-feeding 60fps scroll loop (there's an explicit guard against this, `shouldReassertCaret`, in `keyboardAwareScroll.ts`). A new selection-mode bottom bar sits in exactly this hazard zone and should reuse the existing viewport utilities rather than re-deriving the positioning math from scratch — and should be verified on a real iOS device, not just Chrome DevTools emulation (the existing fixes were device-verified against real iPad/iPhone Safari quirks that don't reproduce in emulation).

## Related open issues
- #78 — swipe-quick-action invocation bypasses the action dispatcher (tech-debt on the existing touch-gesture path this would sit next to)
- #124 — integrate pointer dispatch into the context lifecycle (retire the pointer modal-shadowing bypass)
- #348 — iPad Safari normal-mode block-copy failures (existing mobile/touch papercut in the adjacent normal-mode/selection area)

No existing issue covers this specific WorkFlowy-mobile-UX proposal; a repo-wide issue search (mobile, touch, drag, long-press, workflowy, multi-select, toolbar) turned up no duplicate.

title: Design question: seam for replacing a system plugin's implementation, not just toggling it off
description:
## Idea

Raised as a rough, open design question (from a voice note, so treat the framing as approximate): **how could someone replace a system plugin with their own version, and have things that depend on it keep working?**

The problem as framed: other plugins currently depend on plugins at the *reference* level — they import parts of a plugin or contribute to its facets directly — so there's no seam that lets a dependency be retargeted at a substituted implementation. Two rough directions were sketched:

1. An abstraction/module-resolution layer that lets modules resolve from a default location but be overridden.
2. "Materialize everything" — put the live plugin source in the database, edit it there, and resolve from that (noted this would probably need a service worker).

Also raised, and related: **"every theme should be an example plugin (vend system plugins via API)."**

This issue is meant to capture the question with grounding, not to resolve it.

## Grounded problem

`docs/extensibility-axes.md` already has the right vocabulary: **infill seam** (facet — fixed architecture, contribute slot fillers) vs. **substrate seam** (module — replaceable architecture, importable parts, expensive, few seams). Facet-mediated composition is the infill axis and works well for what's routed through it — including same-id override on Map-keyed facets (e.g. `blockRenderersFacet`): a user plugin can already register under an existing key and silently win. That's real, working substitution, but only for the slice of behavior a plugin chose to expose as a facet contribution.

The toggle mechanism (`systemToggle`/`userToggle` + `isEnabled` in `src/facets/togglable.ts`) only gates whether a plugin's `AppExtension` tree is walked into the runtime when the facet graph is resolved. It doesn't touch the module graph — every plain export (functions, constants, components, types) a plugin has stays live and importable regardless of its toggle state.

Cross-plugin dependencies routinely go straight at those exports, bypassing facets entirely. Concrete examples in the tree today:

- `src/plugins/daily-notes` is imported directly (no facet involved) by at least 8 other plugins — `srs-rescheduling`, `srs-review`, `roam-import`, `references`, `colemak-keybindings`, `quick-find`, `left-sidebar`, `backlinks-view` — for functions (`getOrCreateDailyNote`), constants (`DAILY_NOTE_TYPE`, `dailyNoteBlockId`, `OPEN_TODAY_ACTION_ID`), a type (`BlockDateAdapter`), and even a React component (`ReschedulePicker`).
- `src/plugins/birthday/wolfTheme.ts` imports `THEME_STORAGE_KEY` from `theme-toggle` directly; `src/plugins/app-intents/appIntents.ts` imports `QUICK_FIND_ACTION_ID` from `quick-find` directly.
- `src/extensions/apiCatalog.ts` replaced the old `@/extensions/api.js` re-export barrel specifically so "the import graph stays honest" — but by its own header it is "DATA, not a re-export surface," a discovery catalog, not an enforced boundary. Nothing stops any module from importing any other module's real path, and `src/extensions/exampleExtensions.ts` documents this as intentional: extension source "resolve[s] through the page-global importmap to the same module instances the running app uses."

Net: disabling a system plugin removes its facet contributions, but every direct importer keeps compiling against and calling the original module. There's no seam today that lets a user say "resolve `@/plugins/daily-notes` to my fork" and have those ~8 dependents pick it up.

## What already exists nearby (adjacent, not the same thing)

- **Toggle on/off** — binary presence, not substitution.
- **Runtime extension blocks** (`type:'extension'` blocks compiled by `src/extensions/dynamicExtensions.ts`, scaffolded by `pnpm agent new-extension`) — lets a user *add* a plugin from data. Doesn't make existing bundled plugins resolve their imports to it.
- **Map-keyed facet override** — real substitution, but scoped to whatever a plugin chose to expose as a facet contribution.

## The two sketched directions, against the grounded architecture

**(a) Indirection / module-resolution layer** (resolve a specifier from a default location, overridable)

- Partial precedent: the page-global import map (`index.html`) already remaps bare specifiers (`react`, `@/`) for Blob-instantiated dynamic-extension modules, and `docs/plugin-module-url-sw-hybrid.md` (tracked by open issue #253) designs a service-worker-mediated `${BASE_URL}module/<id>` fetch-interception point — architecturally the kind of place a "default → override" resolver would need to hook.
- Against that precedent, `docs/extensibility-axes.md` explicitly treats facet vs. module replacement as two deliberate axes and pushes back on a general answer: "Not a proposal for arbitrary function-level monkey-patching... JS module imports don't structurally support this without build-time AOP." It scopes "substrate seams" to a short, deliberately-chosen list (renderer — built; action dispatcher — proposed next; repo/bootstrap/runtime construction — explicitly deferred pending real demand) and calls each new substrate seam "a long-term commitment to a contract," requiring the replaced layer's parts to be "decoupled enough to be re-imported and re-composed." A general "any system plugin is swappable" resolver would be a substantially broader substrate commitment than anything considered there so far.

**(b) Materialize plugin source into the DB, resolve from there**

- Precedent already exists for user extensions: `dynamicExtensions.ts` compiles `type:'extension'` blocks at runtime today (Babel transpile → Blob-URL `import()`), no service worker involved.
- The service-worker piece maps onto #253 / `plugin-module-url-sw-hybrid.md`, but that design is explicitly scoped to letting one *user extension block* import another — the doc states built-in plugins "are ordinary bundled ES modules that never touch [the `/module/` path]" by design, and #253's own trigger condition is "do this only when we want cross-block plugin→plugin imports," not yet met.
- Materializing a *system* plugin's source into a block and compiling it the same way produces a running module instance, but doesn't by itself make the ~8+ static `import ... from '@/plugins/daily-notes'` call sites elsewhere in the bundle resolve to it — that retargeting is (a)'s problem. So (b) alone fully substitutes a system plugin only when that plugin happens to have zero non-facet-mediated dependents, which is the exception rather than the rule per the examples above.
- Costs worth naming if pursued: the "require a controlling service worker" question is already open and undecided for the narrower #253 scope (user extensions only); requiring it for *system*-plugin substitution is a materially bigger commitment, since today the app boots and runs fully with no controlling SW at all. There's also a bundling cost: a plugin whose dependents must resolve it dynamically (to stay substitutable) can no longer be a plain statically-imported, tree-shakeable module in `staticAppExtensions.ts` the way every system plugin is today.

## Theming note ("every theme should be an example plugin")

Partly already true, partly not:

- Default color themes (`src/plugins/default-themes`) are already an ordinary system plugin — `systemToggle` plus contributions to `themesFacet` (a Map-keyed facet). A user extension can already add a competing theme, or override a built-in one by contributing under the same id. This is a working infill-seam example today, not hypothetical.
- But it isn't vended/discoverable as one: `src/extensions/apiCatalog.ts` — the blessed, discoverable extension-authoring surface — doesn't list `default-themes` or `theme-toggle` among its entries, so nothing today points a plugin author at the real built-in theme source as a forkable template (contrast `src/extensions/exampleExtensions.ts`, which ships copyable starter source for a custom renderer).
- The facet's contract is also narrower than "a theme": tokens are HSL colors only (separately flagged in `docs/extension-seam-gaps.md` R10 — indent width, bullet size, fonts, density are hardcoded outside the token set). `src/plugins/birthday/wolfTheme.ts` is a real, in-repo illustration of hitting that ceiling: it deliberately bypasses `themesFacet` and instead sets the `data-theme` attribute / `localStorage` / a raw injected `<style>` element directly, specifically because the facet can't carry the bullet-glyph CSS and "restore only if untouched" behavior it needs.

## Open questions (deliberately not resolved here)

- Is the real target a couple of high-value, deliberately-chosen substrate seams (extending `extensibility-axes.md`'s list — action dispatcher is its next-ranked candidate) — or a general "any plugin is swappable" mechanism?
- If general: is a controlling service worker an acceptable requirement, for a broader and riskier surface than #253's user-extension-only scope?
- Is "materialize into the DB" motivated by *editability* (edit source in place, see your own fork) or *substitutability* (retarget other plugins' existing references)? These want different mechanisms — the first is close to what `dynamicExtensions.ts` already does; the second needs (a)'s resolution layer regardless of where the source physically lives.
- Independent of any architecture decision: should the "vend system plugins via API" half start now as a docs/catalog change — listing plugins like `default-themes` in `apiCatalog.ts` as forkable examples — since that part doesn't depend on resolving the substitution question?

## Related

- #253 — stable `/module/<blockId>` URLs for user extensions (narrower: block-to-block imports only; explicitly not triggered yet)
- `docs/extensibility-axes.md` — infill vs. substrate vocabulary, the substrate-seam candidate list, and its "high bar" discipline for adding one
- `docs/extension-seam-gaps.md` — R1 (renderer-resolution policy) is today's closest built substrate-seam precedent; R10 (theme tokens are colors only)
- `docs/plugin-module-url-sw-hybrid.md` — the service-worker/module-URL design #253 tracks
