title: Grouped backlinks: groupWith needs a discovery/authoring UI (and a look at how it competes with other groups)
description:
## Summary

`groupWith` is the intended mechanism for manually steering grouped backlinks ("Grouped References") into a meaningful bucket, but today it's an undiscoverable, hand-typed property with no dedicated UI. Separately, there's a report that backlinks aren't landing in the intended group even when `groupWith` is set. This issue tracks the discovery/authoring gap (confirmed in code) and the correctness concern (grounded hypotheses, not yet reproduced), plus what a "group with + types" direction would concretely mean.

## How grouping works today (confirmed in code)

`groupedBacklinksForBlockQuery` (`src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/query.ts`) builds each backlink's group candidates from:
1. every reference on the backlink source itself and on each of its ancestors, up to the root page (`SELECT_GROUPED_BACKLINK_CANDIDATES_SQL`)
2. the root ancestor block itself (`context_kind = 'root'`)
3. `groupWith` expansion: for each context block found in (1)/(2), its `groupWith` targets (a `refList` property, projected into `block_references` with `source_field='groupWith'`) become additional group candidates for every source whose context chain reached that block (`SELECT_GROUPED_BACKLINK_ATTRIBUTE_CANDIDATES_SQL`)
4. type enrichment: the types of each context block from (1)/(2), plus the types of anything that context block references one hop out (`SELECT_GROUPED_BACKLINK_TYPE_CANDIDATES_SQL`)

`buildGroupedBacklinks` (`src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/grouping.ts`) then assigns each backlink source to **exactly one** surfaced group: within a priority tier (`high` > `default` > `low`, tiers set by label-matching in the "Grouped backlinks defaults" settings), it repeatedly picks whichever candidate group currently has the most unclaimed members and consumes those sources — so a source ends up in the largest group covering it, not necessarily the most specific or most relevant one. Leftovers (or groups below `minGroupSize`, default 2) fall into an "Other" bucket.

## 1. Discovery / authoring gap for `groupWith` (confirmed)

`groupWith` (`src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/config.ts`) is a plain `refList` property with no dedicated UI anywhere:
- No command, action, or dialog sets it. Compare with tagging: block-tagging registers an "Add tag" action that shows up as a button in the grouped-backlinks group header, letting you bulk-tag every block in a group. There is no equivalent "Group with" action, either for a single block or for a group's blocks in bulk.
- The only way to set it today is the generic block "+ Field" property picker, and only if the user already knows to type the literal property name `groupWith`.
- The knobs that decide whether a `groupWith` group actually wins over competing groups (`highPriorityTags` / `lowPriorityTags` / `excludedTags` / `excludedPatterns`) live in a separate, global "Grouped backlinks defaults" settings block, edited by typing the exact group *label* as free text. There's no link from a `groupWith` target back to "make this win."

Net effect: using `groupWith` for anything beyond the automatic ref/root/type candidates requires knowing an undocumented property name, and — if you want the resulting group to reliably surface — a second, disconnected settings step. There's no in-context affordance to say "backlinks like this one belong under group X."

## 2. "Not grouping with my group" — investigation (unconfirmed; awaiting repro)

I don't have a concrete repro to root-cause the report against, so nothing below should be read as *the* explanation — these are mechanisms I could confirm exist in the code that could plausibly produce "this isn't grouping where I expect":

- **`groupWith` doesn't chain.** Expansion is one hop only, by design, and covered by an explicit test (`does not chain groupWith transitively`, `src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/test/query.test.ts`). If `A groupWith B` and `B groupWith C`, a backlink that only reaches `B` through `A`'s expansion does **not** also pick up `C`. A `groupWith` hierarchy that's expected to compose will silently stop partway up the chain.
- **Groups compete by raw member count, not specificity.** `groupWith` ("attribute" kind) and type ("type" kind) candidates are treated the same as plain ref candidates for priority — a `groupWith` group only wins if it happens to have more currently-unclaimed members than every other candidate group in its tier at the moment it's picked. A broader, incidental ref-based group (e.g. a shared ancestor page) can claim the same sources first purely by being bigger, leaving the intended `groupWith` group under `minGroupSize` and folded into "Other."
- **Ties favor ref/root candidates over `groupWith`/type candidates.** The pick-largest step takes the first strictly-larger group it encounters; candidates are inserted in the order ref/root → field → `groupWith` → type, so an exact tie in member count silently favors the ref-based group.

Next step if/when this reproduces: capture which blocks, which `groupWith` values, and the expected vs. actual grouping, so these hypotheses can be checked against real data instead of guessed at.

## 3. "group with + types" — what it would concretely mean

The idea is to key grouping off types more directly, as a follow-on to fixing discovery. In the current architecture that could mean:
- Making `groupWith` settable/suggestable from a type definition (e.g. "instances of this type default to `groupWith` X") instead of requiring it to be hand-set per source block.
- Letting type-enrichment candidates participate in `groupWith` expansion the way ref/root context blocks do today — currently a block reached only via `groupWith` expansion does not contribute its own types as further candidates (type enrichment runs only over the original ref/root context set), so `groupWith` and type enrichment don't compose with each other either.
- Prioritizing type-based and `groupWith`-based groups over incidental ref-based ones by default, instead of relying on hand-typed label matching in the global settings block.

This needs its own design pass — flagging the concrete gap here rather than prescribing the fix.

## Scope note

Per the source note, parent-based grouping is explicitly lower priority right now — this issue is scoped to `groupWith` + types.

title: Readwise: ingest Reader documents directly, not only via highlights
description:
## Summary

Bring Readwise **Reader** documents into the app directly, instead of only ever seeing a document once it has a highlight. Ingest the document itself, then attach highlights later if/when they show up.

## Current behavior (verified in code)

The active integration is `agent-extensions/readwise.tsx` (`agent-extensions/readwise.js` is an older, unmaintained draft of the same idea that stopped receiving commits right after the extension's initial version, while `readwise.tsx` picked up ~20 further feature commits — worth cleaning up separately, not part of this issue).

- The only Readwise endpoint called today is the classic Highlights export API: `GET https://readwise.io/api/v2/export/`, paginated via `pageCursor`/`updatedAfter`. There is no call into any Reader-specific endpoint.
- That endpoint returns "books" bundled with their highlights, and a `readwise-document` block is created for every book it returns. Since `/export/` is a highlights export, a book only appears in it once it has at least one highlight — **this confirms the premise that a document currently only exists in the app once it's been highlighted.** (That grouping behavior is a property of Readwise's API rather than something asserted in this repo's code, so it's worth reconfirming against Readwise's docs, but it's consistent with what the sync loop implements and observes.)
- Block shapes created by `syncBookToBlocks`:
  - `readwise-library` — singleton root page.
  - `readwise-document` (one per Readwise `user_book_id`) carrying `readwise:user_book_id`, `readwise:title`, `readwise:author` (a `ref` to an author page), `readwise:category`, `readwise:source`, `readwise:source_url`, `readwise:readwise_url`, `readwise:cover_image_url`, `readwise:document_note`, `readwise:num_highlights`, `readwise:last_highlight_at`, `readwise:asin`, `readwise:tags`.
  - `readwise-highlight` (one per highlight `id`), nested under a deterministic "Highlights" section block on the document, carrying `readwise:highlight_id`, `readwise:user_book_id`, `readwise:readwise_url`, `readwise:location`, `readwise:location_type`, `readwise:color`, `readwise:highlighted_at`, `readwise:updated_at`, `readwise:created_at`, `readwise:tags`, plus app-owned review state (`readwise:review_date`, `readwise:reviewed` — initialized once, never overwritten by sync).
  - `readwise-note` (one per highlight that has a note), carrying `readwise:note_for_highlight_id`.
- Dedup/idempotency today is **not** a property lookup — it's a deterministic block id: `pluginBlockId(workspaceId, READWISE_NS, "book:${user_book_id}")` for documents and `"hl:${highlight.id}"` for highlights. Re-syncing the same `user_book_id`/highlight id always resolves to the same block id.
- Imported fields refresh source-mirror style (`applyManagedProperties` overwrites the listed `readwise:*` properties every sync and deletes ones no longer present) without touching unrelated properties — consistent with the repo's convention that a typed property gets written *alongside* the `readwise:*` source-mirror property, never in place of it. Any new write path this feature adds needs to keep that shape.

## What the Reader API adds

Readwise's Reader product has its own document list/content API surface, separate from the `/export/` endpoint this integration calls. Nothing in this repo references it yet, so before implementing, these need checking against Readwise's current API docs (not guessed at here):
- The actual Reader document-list and document-content endpoint paths/params.
- Whether a Reader document's id in that API lives in the same identifier space as `user_book_id` from the highlights `/export/` API, or is a separate id that would need reconciling.
- What "document content" the Reader API actually returns (HTML vs. plain text vs. summary-only) and its typical size.

## Main open question: ingestion-ordering / idempotency

If a document is ingested first (from Reader, before any highlight exists) and highlights for it arrive later (from `/export/`, once the user highlights something), the highlight sync must attach to the *same* `readwise-document` block rather than creating a duplicate — and the reverse (a document that already exists from highlight-sync later gets its full content backfilled from Reader) has to land on that same block too.

Today's dedup only works because both document and highlight ids are derived from one shared `user_book_id` known at write time. Reader-first ingestion breaks that assumption unless Reader's document id turns out to be that same id:

- If Reader's list API also exposes `user_book_id` (or an equivalent shared id) per document, the existing deterministic-id scheme extends cleanly — reuse `book:${user_book_id}` for Reader-only ingestion too.
- If it doesn't, the importer needs an explicit reconciliation step: look up an existing `readwise-document` block by a Reader-specific key (a new `readwise:*` property) before minting a new deterministic id, and merge in `user_book_id` once highlights show up for it — including a plan for what happens to any block id/properties/children already written under the "wrong" key.

This needs to be worked out before implementation; the rest of the feature (calling the Reader endpoints, deciding what to render) is comparatively mechanical once the id story is settled.

## Data volume

Full document content (article text/HTML) is materially larger per item than highlight metadata. Since this would land in `blocks` like everything else, it's meaningfully more data moving through sync (PowerSync) and OPFS storage per document than the current integration incurs. Worth sizing before deciding whether full content is a normal block property, a separate/lazy-loaded piece, or fetched on demand rather than eagerly synced.

## Constraint

Preserve the "typed property written alongside the `readwise:*` source-mirror property, never instead of it" convention the importer already follows (see `applyManagedProperties` / `documentPropertyEntries` in `agent-extensions/readwise.tsx`). Any new Reader-content properties should use the same source-mirror naming (`readwise:*`) rather than replacing the existing highlight-derived fields.

title: View precedence for blocks with multiple view-owning types: type order vs. explicit priority
description:
## Idea (from a rough voice-note capture)

When a block carries multiple types and more than one of them wants to own the block's rendering (e.g. a block tagged as both a "table" type and a "map" type), something has to pick a winner. The rough proposal: let the **order of the types on the block** decide precedence — first (or last) listed wins — and let the user reorder types to control which view takes over.

A related idea from the same voice-note session: add a side table materializing **both user-defined and system types** into one place, because at the time system types were code-declared and had no referenceable block, which made "give me a block reference for this type" paths special-case around them.

This issue captures both ideas, grounded against the current code, and flags what's already been overtaken by later work.

## What actually happens today (checked against code)

Renderer selection is **not** type-order-driven at all right now. `useRenderer` (`src/hooks/useRendererRegistry.tsx:14-43`) runs every registered `blockRenderersFacet` contribution's `canRender` predicate, then sorts survivors by a numeric `.priority()` (descending) and takes the first — a flat, global priority tournament, unrelated to the target block's own `types` array. Kernel renderers use priority `1`/`5`/`10`/`20`; a few type-specific renderers (`RecentsPageBlockRenderer`, `ReviewDeckRenderer`, `PropertySchemaBlockRenderer`, `BlockTypeBlockRenderer`) all register at priority `100`. Since `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, ties between equal-priority renderers resolve by **facet/extension registration order** (`Object.values(registry)` insertion order from `createRendererRegistry`, `src/extensions/core.ts`) — not by anything on the block. So today: undefined-by-design from a user's point of view, priority-number based, with silent registration-order tie-breaks.

The one place the codebase already resolves a two-type conflict is `src/plugins/geo/geoContentDecorator.tsx` (Place vs Map): it's hardcoded in code ("Place trumps map"), independent of the block's own `types` array order. It composes rather than replaces though — it's a *decorator* stacking on top of the normal body renderer, not a full-renderer takeover, precisely so an exclusive-view choice isn't needed there. Its own comment notes it *replaced* an earlier `blockRenderersFacet`-based per-type override for exactly this class of problem.

## Is `types` order stable / user-controllable today?

Order is stable in storage: `TypeTagger.addType` appends (`src/data/typeTagger.ts`), `removeType` filters in place, and there's already a `setBlockTypes(blockId, typeIds)` primitive that accepts and persists an arbitrary explicit order (`typeTagger.ts`, wired through `Repo.setBlockTypes`).

But there is **no reorder UI**. `TypesPropertyEditor.tsx` (the block's Types picker) only supports appending a new type and removing one via its chip's "x" or Backspace — chips render in stored order but aren't draggable. A user can only change order today by removing types and re-adding them in the desired sequence.

## This is already half-designed — see `docs/renderer-resolution.md`

That doc (status: Proposed, not yet implemented) sketches a `body:byType` dispatch slot that resolves *exactly* this way: resolution walks the block's `typesProp` array in order, and the first type id with a registered `body:byType` contribution wins — "if a block has `types = ['todo', 'video']` and both register a body, `'todo'` wins because it's listed first — the type system's 'earlier types take precedence' convention applies here naturally" (its own words). So "type order picks the view" is already the leading candidate mechanism in the proposed redesign — it just doesn't yet ship, doesn't discuss first-vs-last as an explicit choice, and (per the point above) has no reorder UI to go with it.

`docs/type-system.md` §4b also already recorded the counter-argument against the alternative (an explicit `priority`/`defaultRenderer` field on `TypeContribution`): it would "duplicate the existing facet's job, leak behavior into the membership layer … and pre-commit to single-winner dispatch" in a way that constrains a future multi-view (Embark-style, simultaneous presentations) model. That's a real, already-recorded reason to lean toward order-as-lever over a new priority field on the type definition — but it trades away explicitness: which type "wins" becomes whatever the block's `types` array happens to contain, in whatever order it was built up, with no visible affordance today for a user (or a type author) to see or reason about that order without opening the Types picker and reading chip order.

## Open questions

1. **First-wins or last-wins?** The `renderer-resolution.md` sketch assumes "earlier type wins," matching the append-only `addType` order (oldest tag = highest precedence) — arguably surprising, since the type someone adds *last* (often "make this a table now") feels like the one that should take over. Needs a decision either way, plus reasoning recorded somewhere durable.
2. **Order-as-lever vs. explicit priority on the type definition.** Order is cheap (no schema change, already the direction `renderer-resolution.md` leans) but invisible/accidental — nothing surfaces *why* a given type is winning, and reordering today means remove-and-readd. An explicit priority field on `TypeContribution` is more legible and stable but is the exact shape `type-system.md` §4b already argued against, for architectural reasons (see above). Any implementation needs to pick one, or explain why order needs a visible/reorderable affordance (e.g. drag handles in `TypesPropertyEditor`) to be legible enough to use as the lever.

## Re: the "side table for user + system types" idea — mostly resolved since the voice note

Since that note was captured, `seedType`-based definition seeds landed (`src/data/definitionSeeds.ts`, `src/data/blockTypes.ts`). Every kernel/plugin type is now declared via `seedType(...)` and gets a deterministic per-workspace backing block id (`typeDefinitionBlockId`), materialized as a real block just like a user-defined type. `getTypeBlockId` (`src/data/typeDefinitionRegistry.ts`, `src/data/userTypesService.ts`) is now total for essentially all registered types — so "system types have no block to reference" is **no longer generally true**. The one residual gap: `getTypeBlockId` still stays `undefined` for a type whose seed key is *contested* (two seeds racing for the same membership id) until that's resolved (`typeDefinitionRegistry.ts`) — a narrow edge case, not the general "system types are unreferenceable" problem the original note described. Worth closing that framing out rather than carrying it forward into any implementation of this issue.

## Suggested scope

This probably isn't worth building standalone — it's the same decision `docs/renderer-resolution.md`'s `body:byType` slot already needs to make, and there's no live trigger yet: no shipping type actually competes for a block's body renderer today, and the one real multi-type-view case in the codebase (geo Place/Map) deliberately sidesteps the conflict via decorator composition rather than an exclusive-renderer takeover. Suggest resolving the two open questions above as part of implementing `renderer-resolution.md`, once there's an actual second view-owning type (e.g. a hypothetical table view) providing a real trigger, rather than speculatively building reorder UI + precedence logic now.

## Related, not duplicate

Checked #89 (data-defined type-definition blocks) — that's about the authoring-friction of *defining a new type* without writing extension code; this issue is about *resolving which already-assigned type wins* the block's view once a block carries several. Different problem, not a duplicate.

title: Backlinks default filter: let reviewed/archived items resurface later (and centralize the done/archived/reviewed policy)
description:
## Problem

The backlinks panel's default filter hides an item from a daily note's backlinks once it's marked resolved — `todo` `status: done`, SRS `archived: true`, or (in the Readwise extension) `readwise:reviewed: true`. That's the desired behavior for a first pass, but it has no way to *resurface* an item later: once `readwise:reviewed` flips to `true`, the highlight is excluded from every daily note's backlinks forever, even if the intent was "I've done a first pass, come back to this on a future date." There's currently no way to schedule that comeback.

This is most visible with Readwise highlights (`agent-extensions/readwise.tsx`), which use a plain boolean (`readwise:reviewed`, line 375-382) with no forward-looking date — `readwise:review_date` (line 366-374) is stamped once at import/sync time (`reviewDateIsoForSync`, line 1115) rather than being a "next review" pointer. SRS cards don't hit this the same way, because `archived` really is meant to be terminal there, and `next-review-date` already gets pushed forward automatically on every grade — but the same boolean-flag shape could recur anywhere else "resolved" gets modeled as a one-way flag.

## How the filter resolves today (grounded in code)

- `src/plugins/backlinks/resolveFilter.ts` (`resolveBacklinksFilter`, lines 30-56) is the shared resolution entry point, used by both the UI and the agent CLI's `--filter stored|effective` flag (wired in `packages/agent-cli/src/cli.ts:732,746` → `src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts:1200-1204`).
- `'stored'` = the block's own saved `backlinks:predicates` property (`src/plugins/backlinks/filterProperty.ts`).
- `'effective'` = the daily-note defaults merged with the block's own filter, via `effectiveBacklinksFilterForBlock` (`src/plugins/backlinks/dailyNoteDefaults.ts:54-61`), only applied when the target is a daily note.
- The daily-note default itself (`dailyNoteBacklinksDefaultsProp`, `dailyNoteDefaults.ts:22-29`) is **user-configured data**, not a hardcoded default — the code-level initial value is the empty filter (`INITIAL_DAILY_NOTE_BACKLINKS_DEFAULTS = EMPTY_BACKLINKS_FILTER`, `dailyNoteDefaults.ts:20`). A user builds their own "hide done/archived/reviewed" filter by hand-authoring exclude predicates (generic `BlockPredicate` `{where: {<property>: true}}` entries, see `src/plugins/backlinks/propertyFilter.ts`) against whichever properties they want.
- The merge/normalize logic (`mergeBacklinksFilters`, `normalizeBacklinksFilter`, `hasBacklinksFilter`) is centralized in `src/plugins/backlinks/query.ts:119-152` and reused by both the flat and grouped backlinks queries — that part is *not* duplicated.

## Where "is this item done/archived/reviewed" gets decided today

What *is* spread out is the upstream, per-domain notion of "resolved," which has no shared abstraction — each plugin reads its own flag independently:

- **todo**: `readStatus()` in `src/plugins/todo/actions.ts:22-26` reads `status` (`'open' | 'done'`, `src/plugins/todo/schema.ts:12-23`). Note: `roam:todo-state` (`schema.ts:25-36`) is preserved *provenance* from Roam imports, not a second live "done" check — `status` is set at import time too (`src/plugins/roam-import/import.ts:107-113`) and is the only field anything actually reads for done-ness.
- **SRS**: `archived` (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/schema.ts:66-73` — the property name is just `archived`, scoped to `srs-sm2.5` blocks, not literally `srs:archived`) is read independently in two places for two different purposes: `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:602` (building UI indicator state) and `src/plugins/srs-review/dueQuery.ts:46-63` (a hardcoded `exclude` predicate on the due-cards query, deliberately *not* `archived: false` — see the comment there about NULL columns). Written by `archiveSrsCard()` (`src/plugins/srs-review/archive.ts:5-15`).
- **Readwise** (extension): `readReviewed()` in `agent-extensions/readwise.tsx:1146-1154` reads `readwise:reviewed`; `toggleHighlightReviewed()` (line 1156-1164) is the only writer.
- **Backlinks visibility**: a third, independent mechanism — the user manually authors one exclude `BlockPredicate` per property (`status`, `archived`, `readwise:reviewed`, ...) in their own daily-note default filter. Nothing maps "these three properties, across these three plugins, all mean roughly 'resolved'" into one place.

So there's no single `isBlockResolved(data)`-style policy (or facet/registry) that the backlinks filter, the SRS due-query, and any future consumer could all share — each caller re-derives "done-ness" from its own property, and a user wanting the combined "hide anything resolved" view has to know all three property names and hand-write three predicates.

## Two candidate directions (open — not decided)

**A. Make the filter date-aware.** Instead of excluding on a plain boolean (`reviewed == true`), exclude only when the item's own "next relevant date" property is not today-or-future. This would require giving flag-shaped properties like `readwise:reviewed`/`readwise:review_date` real forward-looking semantics (repurposing or replacing `readwise:review_date` from "date first reviewed" into an actual resurface-date pointer, the way SRS's `next-review-date` ref already works and is already comparable at filter time via the target-traversal path used in `dueQuery.ts`).
- Reuses an existing, working pattern (ref-to-daily-note + date comparison) rather than inventing new filter machinery.
- Requires a migration/semantic change to `readwise:review_date` (or a new property) so "date reviewed" and "date to resurface" don't collide.
- Still leaves each domain (todo/SRS/readwise) with its own idea of which property is "the" date, so doesn't by itself solve the centralization gap below.

**B. Go back to a nested review-todo.** Instead of a boolean flag on the highlight itself, represent "review this again on day X" as its own `todo` child block nested under the highlight (composing the existing `todo` type rather than inventing a parallel done-flag). Resurfacing is then just "the todo isn't done yet," and daily-note/backlinks/agenda machinery that already understands todos handles it for free.
- Matches the "a block is the unit of anything you'd want to see/link/undo/edit" data-model grain (see `AGENTS.md` data-model-grain guidance / `pnpm agent describe-runtime --guide record-grain`) more directly than a boolean+date pair bolted onto the highlight block.
- Costs a block per review cycle instead of a single property flip, and needs its own answer for what happens to old review-todos after each cycle (delete? keep as history? — a grain/GC question).

## Centralization sub-problem

Independent of which direction (A or B) wins, the "is this block done/archived/resolved" check is currently duplicated per-domain with no shared policy object or facet (see file:line list above). Worth deciding whether a shared abstraction (e.g. a facet plugins register into, mapping their type → "resolved" property/predicate) belongs in this fix or is a separate follow-up.

## Scope

This issue captures the idea and grounds it in the current code; it does not pick a direction. Filed as a design question — evaluate A vs. B (or something else) before implementing.

title: blocks.updated_by / created_by have no server-side check against the authenticated user
description:
## Summary

`blocks.created_by` / `blocks.updated_by` are plain client-supplied columns. Nothing on the server ties their value to the authenticated caller's identity, so any workspace member with write access can stamp an arbitrary string into either field — including another real user's id — and it will sync to every peer as that user's attribution.

## Where the value comes from

- The client stamps `ClientContext.user.id` (the Supabase auth session id, resolved in `src/services/supabase.ts` via `session.user.id`) into `created_by` / `updated_by` on every local write, in `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts`.
- PowerSync uploads the local SQLite row's `created_by`/`updated_by` verbatim as part of the CRUD payload (`src/services/powersync.ts`) to two Postgres RPCs: `apply_block_creates` (`supabase/migrations/20260709000000_add_apply_block_creates_rpc.sql`) and `apply_block_patches` (`supabase/migrations/20260527180103_add_apply_block_patches_rpc.sql`).
- Both RPCs are `SECURITY INVOKER` and write whatever `created_by`/`updated_by` is in the client-submitted JSON directly — there is no comparison against `auth.uid()` anywhere in either function.

## No server-side check exists today

- `public.blocks.created_by` / `updated_by` are plain `TEXT NOT NULL` columns (`supabase/migrations/20260510222352_consolidated_initial.sql`) — no CHECK constraint, no FK, nothing binding them to `auth.uid()`.
- The only RLS policy governing writes, `blocks_write`, checks only workspace membership:
  ```sql
  CREATE POLICY "blocks_write" ON "public"."blocks"
    USING (private.is_workspace_writer(workspace_id, auth.uid()::text))
    WITH CHECK (private.is_workspace_writer(workspace_id, auth.uid()::text));
  ```
  It never inspects `created_by`/`updated_by`.
- The `blocks_clamp_updated_at` trigger (added in `20260612000000_add_user_updated_at_monotonic_clamp.sql`) enforces monotonicity on the `updated_at` *timestamp* but explicitly leaves `updated_by` alone ("`user_updated_at`, `updated_by`, `created_*` are deliberately NOT in this test").

So: server-side enforcement of the "updated by" field does not exist. This is confirmed by reading the code, not assumed.

## Blast radius (please read before triaging severity)

This is **not** an unauthenticated or outside-attacker issue. Exploiting it requires an already-valid Supabase auth session with writer access to the target workspace — i.e. an existing legitimate collaborator (or someone who has compromised such a session/device). It does not grant new access to a workspace; it lets an already-privileged writer forge *attribution* within a workspace they can already edit.

Given the project's current usage is a small, trusted multi-user graph, there's no evidence of live exploitation and this isn't an active incident. It's a real trust-boundary gap worth closing (attribution is used for audit/blame/display and can be forged silently and undetectably today), but it should be treated as hardening, not an emergency.

## Enforcement options considered

1. **RLS `WITH CHECK` on `blocks_write`**, e.g. appending `AND updated_by = auth.uid()::text`. Because the RPCs are `SECURITY INVOKER`, RLS still applies to the INSERT/UPDATE they perform, so this would close the gap even through `apply_block_creates`/`apply_block_patches`.
   - **Caveat found while investigating**: `apply_block_creates`'s insert-or-TOUCH path (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET updated_at = blocks.updated_at`, added for the id-collision echo fix) deliberately does *not* touch `updated_by` on conflict — the resulting row keeps the *original* author's id while the statement can be executed by a *different* racing user's session. A naive `updated_by = auth.uid()` WITH CHECK would reject that UPDATE whenever the racing user isn't the original author, breaking the collision-echo mechanism that migration exists for. Any WITH CHECK approach needs a carve-out for that path (e.g. only enforce when the statement is actually assigning `updated_by`, not when it's preserved unchanged from `OLD`).

2. **DB trigger that overwrites `updated_by`/`created_by` with `auth.uid()`** unconditionally (mirroring the existing clamp trigger's shape). Simpler to reason about than a WITH CHECK carve-out, but must not be content-agnostic in the same way the insert-or-touch UPDATE is — forcing `updated_by := auth.uid()` on that touch would misattribute the row to whichever user's client happened to race the duplicate create, which is also wrong. Would need the same "did the row's real content change" gating the clamp trigger already uses for `updated_at`.

3. **Leave it advisory** — defensible short-term given the low current blast radius, but should be a deliberate decision, not silence.

I did not find any currently-legitimate write path that needs `updated_by`/`created_by` to diverge from the real authenticated user: the roam importer stamps the *importing* user's id (not the original Roam author) into both fields, and agent/bridge writes go through the same live browser session's `ClientContext.user`, so they already carry the real authenticated user's id. `ClientContext` (`src/data/clientContext.ts`) documents future "impersonation"/acting-as-another-user as a planned extension point, but it isn't implemented today — so no live feature currently depends on the field being spoofable. That means options 1/2 have no known legitimate case to special-case *today*, aside from the insert-or-touch interaction above; a future acting-as/impersonation feature would need to be designed as an explicit, server-recognized delegation rather than relying on this gap staying open.

## Suggested next step

Pick one of the enforcement options above (RLS WITH CHECK with the insert-or-touch carve-out looks the more surgical fit, since it reuses the existing RLS mechanism) and add a migration + pgTAP test, following the pattern of the existing `blocks_clamp_updated_at` work.

title: Build a composite rendering fixture (systems test page) for markdown/block rendering
description:
## Idea

A gwern.net/Lorem-style "systems test page" — a single fixture that exercises the full range of block/markdown rendering constructs, so a diff to the render pipeline can be eyeballed (or asserted) against one page instead of re-deriving coverage from memory each time.

## Why file this

There's currently nothing to compare against and nothing to plug a fixture into:

- No composite render fixture exists. Markdown tests are narrow per-construct unit tests (`src/markdown/test/renderMarkdownHtml.test.ts`, `src/markdown/test/defaultMarkdownExtension.test.tsx`, `src/plugins/references/markdown/wikilinks/test/*`, `src/plugins/references/markdown/blockrefs/test/*`) — none of them render a single page that exercises everything together.
- No visual-QA harness. `scripts/webkit-qa.mjs` takes one screenshot as a bootstrap smoke check with no baseline comparison. No Storybook/stories, no Playwright browser-assertion suite, no `toMatchSnapshot`/`toHaveScreenshot` anywhere in the repo.

Render path for reference: `src/markdown/extensions.ts` → `src/markdown/defaultMarkdownExtension.ts` (`remark-gfm`) → wikilink/blockref remark plugins → `src/components/renderer/MarkdownContentRenderer.tsx`.

## What the fixture should exercise

Constructs confirmed supported today (verified against the live pipeline):

- bold, `~~strikethrough~~`, headers, ordered lists, blockquotes, tables, `---`, URLs/autolinks
- `((id))` block refs, `!((id))` embeds
- `[text](((id)))`
- `[text]([[Page]])` page aliases, `![[Page]]` page embeds
- wikilinks with exotic titles (e.g. a leading backtick)

Constructs confirmed as gaps that the fixture should document, not silently omit:

- `^^highlight^^` — renders literally, no `<mark>` output. No `remark-mark` (or equivalent) is installed; `remark-gfm`/`remark-parse` are the only remark plugins in `package.json`. Spot-checked directly against `renderMarkdownHtml` in this investigation — confirmed unsupported.
- Roam's literal `{{embed: [[Page]]}}` syntax is only an import-time rewrite (`src/plugins/roam-import/content.ts`), not a render construct — it never reaches the render pipeline as literal text.
- `__emphasis__` renders as **bold** per CommonMark, not *italic* as in Roam's dialect (see open question below).

Note: this fixture intentionally excludes the `[[<taglike page>]]` wikilink bug — that's tracked separately as its own implementation task.

## Open questions to settle before/while building

1. **Does the fixture pin the unsupported constructs too?** i.e. does it assert `^^highlight^^` renders literally (locking in the current gap as documented behavior), or does it only cover what already works and leave gaps to be discovered independently? Silently omitting the gaps defeats part of the point — a future fix to `^^highlight^^` should show up as an intentional fixture update, not an untested surprise.
2. **What does the fixture plug into?** Two options, meaningfully different cost:
   - A DOM/HTML snapshot test (`toMatchSnapshot` or an equivalent string/DOM assertion) of the whole render pass — cheap, no new infra, fits the existing vitest setup used by `renderMarkdownHtml.test.ts` et al.
   - A real visual-regression harness (screenshot diffing) — catches CSS/layout regressions the HTML snapshot can't, but is new infrastructure (baseline storage, diff tooling, flakiness management) that doesn't exist in this repo today.

   This is the decision the issue is really forcing: pick one (or explicitly punt to the cheap option first and defer the expensive one).
3. **`__emphasis__` semantic mismatch — deliberate or not?** Content imported from Roam that used `__x__` for italics will now render as bold after import into this app, since CommonMark treats `__` as strong emphasis. This predates the fixture idea but the fixture is a natural place to pin whatever the answer is. Needs an explicit decision: keep CommonMark semantics (and note the Roam-import behavior change somewhere users will see it), or special-case `__..__` for imported content.

## Suggested scope for a first pass

- Land the composite fixture as an HTML-snapshot vitest test (cheap option) covering the supported-construct list above, with explicit assertions (not just a snapshot) for the two documented gaps (`^^highlight^^`, Roam embed literal).
- Leave the visual-regression-harness question and the `__emphasis__` semantics question as explicit follow-ups/decisions rather than silently resolving them inside this issue.

title: Design: user-global settings tier (settings are per-workspace, e.g. Vim mode resets per workspace)
description:
## Pain point

Settings are per-user-**per-workspace**, not per-user. Concretely: enabling "Vim normal mode" (`src/plugins/vim-normal-mode/index.ts`, a `systemToggle`) in one workspace has no effect in any other workspace — it has to be re-enabled every time you open/create a new workspace. Most of what's stored this way isn't actually about the *workspace's content* — it's a preference about how the editor behaves for this person, and should follow them everywhere.

## Current model

Every settings/UI-state block is rooted at a per-`(workspace, user)` "user page", built from deterministic ids over `(workspaceId, userId)` (`userPageBlockId` in `src/data/stateBlocks.ts`). `getUserPrefsBlock` and `getPluginPrefsBlock` walk down from that page, so *every* `ChangeScope.UserPrefs` (and `ChangeScope.UiState`) row a plugin writes is implicitly workspace-scoped — there's no user-level identity in the data model that spans workspaces.

Concretely, for the vim example: the toggle's on/off state lives in a shared `extensions:overrides` map (`src/plugins/extensions-settings/config.ts`), stored on a `getPluginPrefsBlock` row keyed by `(workspace, user, "extensions-prefs")`. Keybinding remaps (`src/plugins/keybindings-settings/overrideStore.ts`) work the same way — one prefs block per workspace. Theme is the odd one out: it lives purely in browser `localStorage` (`src/plugins/theme-toggle/theme.ts`), so it's already effectively "global" per browser profile, but as a tradeoff it does **not** sync across the user's devices the way the workspace-scoped prefs blocks do.

## Rough classification

**Plausibly workspace-scoped** (references this graph's own content): grouped-backlinks' tag priority/exclusion lists (`src/plugins/grouped-backlinks/config.ts`), block-tagging's configured tag list (`src/plugins/block-tagging/config.ts`) — these name tags/pages that only make sense inside one graph.

**Plausibly user-global** (about the editor, not the graph): vim normal mode and its Colemak sub-toggle, most other extension enable/disable toggles, keybinding overrides, theme.

**Ambiguous**: the `extensions:overrides` map bundles *every* togglable's on/off state into one per-workspace row, so splitting out "vim mode" means splitting that map by tier, not just relocating the whole block.

## Storage-location question (open)

The sync model is fundamentally workspace-partitioned: per `powersync/sync-config.yaml`, the only synced tables are `workspaces`, `workspace_members`, and `blocks` (every row of which carries a `workspace_id` and syncs only to members of that workspace). There's no `users`/`profiles`-style table synced independent of workspace membership today — so a tier that's genuinely global (synced across the user's devices, independent of which workspace happens to be open) has no existing home. Candidate approaches, none clearly right yet:

1. **New table**, e.g. `user_settings` keyed by `user_id`, with its own PowerSync stream scoped to `auth.user_id()` instead of workspace membership, plus a client-side table/read-path outside the `blocks`/`Repo` abstraction. Matches the semantics but is the biggest lift and a new parallel storage substrate.
2. **A designated "home" workspace** whose blocks are special-cased to always sync regardless of the active workspace. Reuses the whole `Block`/`Repo`/typed-property stack (including `getPluginPrefsBlock`), but needs a rule for unavailability (offline before first sync, revoked membership) and a way to keep it from showing up as a normal graph in workspace-switcher UI.
3. **localStorage, best-effort** — what theme already does. Cheapest, but explicitly device-local, not synced — which undercuts the actual ask if "follow me everywhere" includes new devices.

## Migration question (open)

Whichever tier wins, users already have per-workspace values set today. Needs a precedence rule (global default with per-workspace override winning when present?) and a decision on what happens to values already stored per-workspace: backfill the global tier from somewhere, leave them all as silent overrides of a fresh global default, or require a one-time re-pick.

## Ask

This needs a design decision before implementation: (a) which specific settings/toggles move to a global tier (vim mode is the clear motivating case), and (b) where a global tier's storage lives, per the three options above (or another one). Opening as a design/architecture issue rather than a ready-to-build ticket.

title: Agent memory: inject durable, graph-stored instructions/preferences on agent connect
description:
## Idea

When an external agent connects to a knowledge-medium graph, it currently receives a fixed, hardcoded briefing (data-model guide, authoring catalog, runtime description) plus whatever local device config it has. Nothing about that briefing comes from the graph itself, and there's no way for the graph's owner (or the agent, over time) to leave durable notes that shape how future agent sessions behave.

The idea: on connect, an agent should also receive an injected "memory" — durable instructions/preferences stored *in* the graph — along with guidance for how to update that memory going forward. This would need to be scoped per project/context, since a single graph can hold multiple unrelated contexts.

This is directly inspired by Tim Kellogg's "Agent Memory Patterns" (https://timkellogg.me/blog/2026/04/27/memory-patterns), specifically the framing that always-visible context blocks function as a *learnable system prompt* — content the agent cannot ignore and can also revise, unlike a chat log the agent might skim past.

## Relevant current state (for orientation, not a spec)

- Two connect paths exist: the HTTP long-poll bridge (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/bridge.ts`, `packages/agent-cli/`) and the MCP server (`packages/agent-cli/src/mcpServer.ts`, `packages/agent-cli/src/mcpShared.ts`, registered via `packages/agent-dispatch/src/mcpServerDef.ts`).
- Everything an agent receives today is hardcoded in the repo (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/dataModelGuide.ts`, `authoringCatalog.ts`, `describeRuntime.ts`) or local device config (`src/plugins/agent-runtime/tokens.ts`, `packages/agent-dispatch/src/config.ts`). Nothing is sourced from the graph, and there's no agent-memory concept anywhere.
- The MCP server's `instructions` field is already plumbed through but static (`packages/agent-dispatch/src/mcp.ts`, around lines 19-26) — it's delivered at `initialize` time, which makes it a natural hook for injecting something dynamic, if this gets built.
- The closest graph-stored precedent to follow (if memory ends up living in a block) is `getUserPrefsBlock` / `getPluginPrefsBlock` in `src/data/stateBlocks.ts` — deterministic-id blocks scoped per workspace+user, using `ChangeScope.UserPrefs`.
- Agents can already create/update blocks generically; there's no dedicated "memory" verb or block kind.
- Issue #71 (closed) deliberately moved agent auth tokens *out* of the graph and into localStorage. That's a different kind of data (credentials) than what's being proposed here (content/instructions), but it's worth keeping the distinction explicit rather than assuming graph-storage is obviously right for everything an agent touches.

## Open design questions (this issue is about these, not a settled plan)

1. **What counts as a "project"?** Today the only scoping concept that exists is `workspaceId`. Is a "project" just a workspace, or does it need a finer sub-scope (e.g. a page or subtree the agent is working under)? And however it's defined, how would a connecting agent declare or discover which project/context it's in?

2. **Where does memory actually live?** A per-(workspace, user) prefs-style block (private to that user) vs. a workspace-global block (shared across every agent and user working in that graph) have very different implications — the first doesn't help multiple agents/humans converge on shared conventions, the second means one agent's edits affect everyone's sessions.

3. **Precedence and composition with existing instruction sources.** Dispatched agent runs already combine filesystem-level `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` with the dispatch prompt templates (`packages/agent-dispatch/src/prompt.ts`). Adding graph-sourced memory as a third source raises the question of ordering, conflicts, and whether/how they should be merged rather than just concatenated.

4. **Safety.** An agent that can rewrite the same instructions that get auto-injected into its own (and future agents') sessions is a prompt-injection amplification vector — especially since dispatched runs already have WebFetch access, so untrusted web content could steer an agent into planting persistent instructions for itself or others. This needs a trust story before it ships: options could include review-before-apply, a distinct scope/audit trail for memory writes vs. ordinary content writes, or restricting which callers can write to memory at all. None of that is decided yet.

## Scope of this issue

This is a design/exploration issue, not an implementation ticket. The goal is to work through the four questions above (and any others that surface) before committing to a shape for "agent memory."

title: Two residuals from the rename same-tx conversion: alias.sync re-run gap, asymmetric undo on the invalidation paths
description:
Two residuals from the same-tx conversion ([#461](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/issues/461), merged in #444). Both were raised as open decisions in that PR's description and merged without an answer, so filing them here rather than leaving them in merged-PR history. Neither is urgent; both are documented at their declarations in code.

## 1. `alias.sync` no longer sees rename's own content rewrites

The one behaviour regression of the conversion. Post-commit, the rename rewriter wrote in a transaction of its own, so `alias.sync` fired over its writes for free. Same-tx, rename runs *after* sync in the same pass and sync does not opt into `rerunOnDirtyRows`, so it gets no second look.

**Reachable case:** an *aliased* block whose title embeds the renamed wikilink — a page literally titled `See [[Foo]]`, with alias `See [[Foo]]`. Renaming `Foo` → `Bar` rewrites the title to `See [[Bar]]` but leaves the alias reading `See [[Foo]]`, until that block's next edit heals it via rule 1.

Obscure (it needs a page title that is itself a wikilink), and it self-heals rather than losing data.

**Fix if wanted:** opt `alias.sync` into `rerunOnDirtyRows`. Not done because that means taking on the re-run's merged-baseline `before` semantics for a content↔alias reconciliation — `planSync` diffs `before`/`after` internally to pick its rule, and the merged baseline is exactly where PR #428 found three subtle misreads in other processors. Bigger than the case warrants without a reason to touch it.

Noted in `src/plugins/alias/syncProcessor.ts`' placement docblock.

## 2. Undo is asymmetric across the rename's branches

The conversion's headline win is that a rename and its backlink rewrites are one commit and one undo entry. That holds for the **common** path.

The **invalidation** paths do not have it: handoff, unrenderable replacement, and surviving-embed all deliberately leave the content alone and *drop* the stale edge, precisely so the post-commit `parseReferences` rebuilds the binding. That rebuild is a second write in its own `ChangeScope.References` tx — a second undo entry. So one undo can leave the rebuilt edge behind.

Not a regression: before the conversion, *every* rename produced that second entry. But it is no longer uniform, which is the kind of thing that reads as a bug later.

**Fix if wanted:** for the **handoff** case specifically, same-tx makes the clean option available — a live claimant exists, so `tx.aliasLookup` resolves the new target in-tx and the edge can be rebound directly instead of dropped. No seat has to be minted, so nothing expensive moves onto the commit path.

The other two branches genuinely need the re-parse: with the alias released there is no claimant, so rebinding requires *minting a seat*, which is a create we should not put on the user's commit path.

Not done because it adds a second alias-resolution implementation alongside the re-parse's, and keeping the two in agreement is its own maintenance burden. The drop-and-reparse path is correct and self-healing today.

Noted in `renameProcessor.ts` at `collectTargetPlans`' stale-edge branch.

---

Also still open from group 2, tracked on #443 rather than here: the doc's **marked-row arm** (a marked name row's lossy-name fallback should be canonical `::((A))`, never a pinned label). Noted at `replacementFor`.

title: Re-resolve kernel-page parents inside the write tx (#378/#468 follow-up)
description:
Codex review on #468 raised four findings of one shared shape, all P2, all deliberately deferred there. Recording them here so they aren't lost with the review thread.

## The pattern

Three of the #468 fixes resolve a kernel page OUTSIDE the transaction that then writes a child under it:

| Site | Resolves | Writes child in |
|---|---|---|
| `src/data/definitionSeeds.ts` `materializeSeeds` | `config.ensureParent(...)` | a later `repo.tx` |
| `src/data/userSchemasService.ts` `addSchema` | `getOrCreatePropertiesPage(...)` | a later `repo.tx` |
| `src/data/typeExtraction.ts` `createTypeBlock` | `resolveTypesPageId(...)` | a later `repo.tx` (widest window — property-schema validation awaits in between) |

If alias ownership changes in that window — the adopted page loses `Properties`/`Types`, or is deleted, and another page becomes canonical — the captured parent is stale. The child then either fails loudly against a tombstone (`ParentDeletedError`) or lands permanently under a page that is no longer canonical, and no later pass repairs its parent.

`src/data/targets.ts` (`canonicalAliasReaderFromTx`) states the rule this violates: re-resolve canonical ownership with the tx-scoped reader before any dependent write.

### Why it wasn't fixed in #468

`getOrCreate*` opens its own tx, so it can't be called from inside the caller's tx. Doing this properly needs a **tx-scoped** sibling to `predictKernelPageId` — something like `resolveKernelPageIdInTx(tx, workspaceId, spec)` over `canonicalAliasReaderFromTx` — plumbed into all three call sites.

That carries a policy question worth deciding deliberately rather than in passing: **what should happen when the in-tx resolution finds no live page at all** (the page existed when `getOrCreate` returned, then vanished mid-window)? Abort the write, re-create inside the tx, or fall back to the outside-tx id and let the parent check fail loudly? Each is defensible and they differ in whether a seed pass can partially materialize.

Worth noting for prioritization: #468 already narrowed this considerably. Before it, these sites used the raw deterministic id, which is stale *unconditionally* after any adoption — not just inside a race window.

## Related, separate: repatch references on a daily-note divergence

`src/plugins/roam-import/import.ts` — `retargetDailyReconciliations` corrects a daily page's `finalId` against `getOrCreateDailyNote`'s actual return, but does **not** repair `references[]`, which step 3 already patched from `resolveAliases`' own independent prediction. So if a claimant holds an imported daily page's alias during steps 1–3 and releases it before step 4, the page's aliases/attrs/descendants move to the real note while imported wikilinks to that date stay bound to the old claimant — a stable-wrong binding that no re-parse heals.

#468 emits a diagnostic naming the divergence, and its docblock now records that this is a gap rather than an impossibility: descendants aren't written until phase 5d, so a repatch at step 4 is reachable. It needs `aliasIdMap` updated for the date's aliases plus a **rewrite** of the already-patched refs on every planned block — `patchAliasReferences` appends and dedups, so it cannot replace a stale entry. "Rewrite an existing derived ref" has its own blast radius, hence deferring.

## Status

All four are read-and-reasoned from the Codex review plus the surrounding code; **none has a repro**. First step for any of them is a failing test in the shape #468 used: drive the write path with the alias ownership changed underneath it.

title: SRS stores raw dailyNoteBlockId as a ref/history value — dangles when the note is adopted (#378 follow-up)
description:
Follow-up from the #378 sweep in #468. Those PRs fixed the sites where a raw deterministic id was used as a **write target** (a `parentId`, a nav target, a reconcile `finalId`). This issue covers a remaining class the sweep found but deliberately left alone: raw `dailyNoteBlockId(...)` stored as a **ref / pointer value** in SRS data.

Since #466, a daily note resolves alias-first and can be ADOPTED at a different block's id, in which case nothing is ever minted at `dailyNoteBlockId(workspaceId, iso)`. Any id computed that way and then *stored* becomes a dangling pointer.

### Sites

| File | Field | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| `src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/index.ts:192` | `reviewedAt` | id inside the `srsSnapshotHistoryProp` JSON (typed `string`) |
| `src/plugins/roam-import/roamMemo.ts:112` | `reviewedAt` | same |
| `src/plugins/roam-import/roamMemo.ts:120` | `nextReviewDateId` | feeds `srsNextReviewDateProp` |
| `src/plugins/roam-import/srsMarkers.ts:74` | `nextReviewDateId` | feeds `srsNextReviewDateProp` |

`srsNextReviewDateProp` is a `ref` preset with `config: {targetTypes: [DAILY_NOTE_TYPE]}` (`srs-rescheduling/schema.ts:37`), so the last two write a **real typed ref** at an id that may hold no row at all. `reviewedAt` is a plain stored string in review history — a dangling history pointer rather than a validated ref.

### Status: read, not reproduced

These were found by reading during the #468 sweep. **I have not written a repro**, so treat the severity as hypothesized: the reasoning is that an adopted daily note leaves these ids naming nothing, but I have not confirmed how the ref codec, `targetTypes` validation, or the review-history UI actually behave against a nonexistent target. First step is a failing test, same shape as the ones in #468 (pre-create a live claimant of the date's alias, then drive the SRS path).

### Why not fixed in #468

All four are **pure synchronous** functions in planning paths (`snapshotForPlan`, the Roam-memo planner, `srsMarkers`). Alias-first resolution is async, so fixing properly means threading a resolver — or a pre-resolved iso→id map — through SRS scheduling and the Roam-memo planner. That carries its own design question worth deciding on purpose rather than in passing: whether a daily-note ref should be resolved at **write** time (snapshot the id, risk staleness) or left to **read** time (resolve the iso through the alias, which the data already carries as `reviewedAtIso` / `nextReviewDateAlias`). The read-time option is attractive precisely because both records already store the iso/alias next to the id.

### Not affected (checked)

- `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts` — uses `dailyNoteBlockId` only as the key to retarget *from*, then rewrites to the claimant/ensured id.
- `src/plugins/geo/createOrFindPlace.ts`, `src/plugins/srs-review/index.ts` — both already use the `getOrCreateX(...)` returned block's `.id`.

title: Audit: call sites that recompute a deterministic block id instead of using the getOrCreate return value
description:
Surfaced by the caller audit in PR #466 (issue #378). Filing as a GitHub issue because the implementing agent recorded it as a task chip, which does not survive an app restart — and at least one of these sites looks like a data-integrity risk.

**The pattern.** A `getOrCreate*` helper returns the id of the block it actually resolved to. Several call sites discard that return value and recompute the deterministic id instead (`journalBlockId(ws)`, `dailyNoteBlockId(...)`, etc.). Before #466 those were always equal, so the bug was latent. **Once #466 lands, they can differ** — the helper may adopt a live alias claimant — and a caller using the recomputed id then reads or writes the WRONG block, or a block that doesn't exist.

**Fixed inside #466** (in scope there): `deletionGuard.ts`, `landing.ts`, `roam-import/report.ts`, `roam-import/import.ts`, `attachments/mediaCapture.ts`, `agent-runtime/commands.ts`.

**Found and deliberately NOT fixed there** — higher blast radius, wanted its own change:
- **`src/plugins/roam-import/…` daily-*page* reconciliation pipeline** — flagged by the audit as the most severe. Bulk import writing against a recomputed id rather than the resolved one could mis-target writes across many blocks in one run.
- `src/data/definitionSeeds.ts` — property/type seed bootstrap.
- `src/plugins/…/userSchemasService.ts` and `typeExtraction.ts` — user schema authoring.
- Recents navigation.

**Sequencing note:** this is only *reachable* once #466 merges (adoption is what makes the ids diverge). So it isn't urgent today, but it becomes real the moment #466 lands — worth doing in the same window rather than leaving a known live-data hazard behind an adoption feature.

**Suggested approach:** grep for every call of a `getOrCreate*`/`ensure*` helper whose return is dropped, then either use the returned id or, where a raw id is genuinely wanted, add a comment saying why it's safe. A lint rule (no-unused-return on those specific helpers) would prevent regression better than a one-time sweep.

Attribution/confidence: the site list and the severity ranking come from the #466 agent's audit; I verified the resolver's design and the in-PR fixes, but have not independently re-audited each of the deferred sites. Treat the list as a starting point to verify, not a finished inventory.

title: Convert references.renameBacklinks from post-commit to same-tx (deletes the whole rename race surface)
description:
## Goal

Move `references.renameBacklinks` from `definePostCommitProcessor` to `defineSameTxProcessor`, so alias changes and the backlink rewrites they imply commit atomically.

## Why

The processor has been post-commit since it was added (`820c9311`, 2026-05-13) — read phase outside any transaction, then its own write transaction. **That gap is the sole source of the entire race surface** the PR #444 review rounds kept finding: six rounds, four of them in the seat-classification predicate that exists only to reason about what happened inside that gap.

Its sibling was already converted: `c236082a` — *"Move alias sync to same-tx + add collision rejection"* — and that commit is also where rename's `serializeRename` FIFO came from, since same-tx sync stopped collapsing rapid edits and exposed rename's pre-tx SELECT racing its own writes. The asymmetry is an accident of sequencing, not a design.

Feasibility is confirmed: `SameTxCtx.db` is documented as a *"read-only active-transaction SQL surface … for plugin-owned projection tables that must be queried atomically with tx writes"*, and the same-tx merge processor already queries `block_references` through it — which is the enumeration rename needs.

## Decisions already made

- **No sync-arrival counterpart.** Same-tx processors are bypassed by sync (`arrivalProcessors.ts:199`). We accept that a rename applied from another device does not re-run backlink rewriting locally — we trust the originating device to have done it and synced the result.
- **Latency is acceptable.** Renames are rare; splicing N backlink sources inside the user's commit is fine, as is the fact that a throw rolls the user's rename back (`SameTxCtx` contract).
- Unrelated but settled in the same discussion: the delete-flow release rewrite stays **definition-scoped**, nothing beyond what props-as-blocks needs. No generalized page-delete rewrite.

## What the conversion deletes

The window becomes zero-width — seats are minted by post-commit `parseReferences` and the arrival seam, never inside our tx, and SQLite serializes write transactions — so *"did my own window mint this claimant?"* stops having a referent. The claimant test collapses to **"does anything else claim α? → hands off."**

Deletable, all in `renameProcessor.ts`:
- `seatMaterializedAt`, `renameCommitStamp`, `mintedAfter`, `seatClassificationCtx`, `isWindowMintedAliasSeat`, `isWindowMintedSeat`, `hasDeepUserContent`, `hasBlockingChildrenInTx` — the whole timestamp apparatus, including the strict-tie rule and the duplicate-field-row rule
- `aliasStillReleased`, `isWindowMintedSeatInTx`, the release cache (and the cache-key bug it had)
- the stale-plan content guard (content cannot change mid-tx)
- `serializeRename`
- `Tx.aliasClaimants` may become unnecessary if the check reads `block_aliases` via `ctx.db` instead

## What it does NOT resolve — still needed afterwards

- **Round-trip / markdown guards** (`pinnedSpanReplacement`, `faithfulWikilinkReplacement`, `MARKDOWN_UNSAFE_LABEL_RE`). Grammar concerns, no timing component.
- **The claimant check itself**, simplified. Another block genuinely can claim α via sync — see #460.
- **Stale-edge invalidation** on handoff / unrenderable replacement. Becomes atomic, still required.
- **Single-pass splice** (`rewriteWikilinksMulti`). Two renames in one commit stays possible.
- Merge path — already same-tx, untouched.

## Open question to settle FIRST

**Undo interaction with post-commit processors.** Today rename writes under `ChangeScope.References`, which is `undoable: true` with its **own undo bucket** (*"parseReferences bookkeeping. Separate undo bucket; uploads."*), so backlink rewrites are already a second undo entry. Same-tx amends the user's transaction instead, so they'd join the user's entry under the user's scope — one undo restores both, which is the improvement.

The thing to verify is what `parseReferences` does *afterwards*:

1. Same-tx rename writes `content` + `references` in lockstep (`applyRefRewrites` exists so the follow-up parse re-emits an identical list). If that holds, the post-commit parse is a no-op, writes nothing, and creates **no second undo entry**. Confirm it actually holds.
2. **The stale-edge invalidation path deliberately relies on the parse writing** — it drops the edge precisely so the re-parse rebuilds it. That path *will* produce a second `ChangeScope.References` entry, so undoing the rename once could leave the rebuilt edge behind. Needs a decision: rebind in-tx instead of dropping (now possible, since same-tx can resolve the alias atomically), or accept the extra entry.

Also worth checking: whether a same-tx processor can choose its own `ChangeScope`, or inherits the user tx's — the References bucket's separate identity is described as intentional.

## References

- PR #444 — the guards this subsumes, and the six review rounds that motivated it
- #443 — §11 lifecycle work items
- #460 — duplicate live alias claimants (independent; makes the simplified claimant check load-bearing)
- `c236082a` — the alias-sync conversion, as a template

title: Two live blocks can claim the same alias indefinitely — no detection, no repair, and three things hide it
description:
## Problem

Two live blocks can claim the same alias in one workspace, indefinitely, and nothing detects, repairs, or even *surfaces* it. It is the root cause behind several findings in the PR #444 review rounds.

### How it happens

`block_aliases_workspace_alias_unique` (`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts`) only fires when `tx_context.source IS NOT NULL` — i.e. for local user transactions. **Sync-applied rows skip it entirely.** So two devices that each add the alias `Coffee` to a different page, offline, both land, and both claims live in `block_aliases` after they converge.

### Why it persists silently

Three separate things hide it rather than report it:

1. **The alias list collapses it.** `SELECT_ALIASES_IN_WORKSPACE_SQL` (`src/data/internals/kernelQueries.ts`) does `GROUP BY ba.alias`, so a doubly-claimed name shows up once. Nothing in the UI indicates two pages answer to it.
2. **Resolution silently picks one.** `SELECT_BLOCK_BY_ALIAS_IN_WORKSPACE_SQL` is `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1` — the oldest claimant wins and the other is ignored, with no signal.
3. **The one repair pass in this area deliberately doesn't cover it.** `core.aliasClaimRederive` (`src/data/internals/aliasClaimRederiveProcessor.ts`) repairs NULL-stamped `reference_target_id` when an alias is *gained*, and its docblock states that re-pointing already-stamped rows — the handoff/reclaim half — "stays deliberately out".

### Why it matters

Beyond being wrong on its own, a co-claim is the precondition for the alias-seat hijack documented on PR #444: releasing the alias from one co-claimant makes the rename pass evaluate the *other* claimant against a timestamp heuristic, and a re-dated long-lived seat can be misread as this rename's own machinery — after which backlinks that meant the seat get spliced onto the block that released the name. Removing co-claims removes that precondition.

Backlinks also split invisibly: some sources bind to one claimant and some to the other, so `[[Coffee]]` means different pages depending on which edge a given source happens to carry.

## What's wanted

1. **Detection** — an integrity/repair sweep that finds `(workspace_id, alias)` pairs with more than one live claimant. The query is cheap against the existing index:
   ```sql
   SELECT ba.workspace_id, ba.alias, COUNT(*) AS claimants
   FROM block_aliases ba JOIN blocks b ON b.id = ba.block_id
   WHERE b.deleted = 0
   GROUP BY ba.workspace_id, ba.alias
   HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
   ```
2. **A resolution policy.** Needs a decision, since neither option is obviously right:
   - auto-resolve (oldest claimant keeps the alias, the others have it stripped) — converges without asking, but silently removes a name a user typed on another device;
   - surface it and let the user pick — safe, but needs UI and can sit unresolved;
   - convert the loser into an alias-collision merge, reusing the existing `ALIAS_COLLISION_MERGE_MUTATOR` path.
3. **Stop hiding it.** At minimum, the alias list shouldn't collapse a conflict into one row without indication.

## Notes

- Whatever the policy, the *detection* half is independently useful — it turns a class of silent divergence into something observable.
- Related: PR #444 (rename/seat lifecycle), #443 (§11 lifecycle work items).

title: Add a legible deterministic regression suite for the upload-retry failure modes
description:
Recommendation out of PR #448's fourth review round, from the agent that built and then repeatedly extended that model-based fuzz harness. Recording it because the reasoning is worth keeping, and because the follow-up is genuinely separate work.

**Context.** `uploadTransactionsWithFallback` is guarded by a model-based fuzz suite that diffs the real orchestrator against an independently re-derived model (`predictPass`). Four review rounds added injectable failure dimensions until there are now six, combinatorially interacting across up to five transactions, with disambiguation rules about which `complete()` call site fired that require tracing closure state across an async call graph.

**The concern, stated by the agent that knows the file best.** Two concrete pieces of evidence, not speculation:

1. It introduced a real modeling bug during that round (conflating the batch-`complete()` failure site with the post-rejection one, since both occur deep in the per-tx loop) and caught it only because the differential oracle failed loudly. The harness worked — but the model is now complex enough to be wrong in non-obvious ways.
2. The new fixed-point pass-loop detector is **the first logic in that file cross-checked by nothing.** Every property there is validated by diffing against an independent model; the detector's correctness rests on a hand-written monotonicity argument in a comment. If its state signature ever omits a relevant component, the loop stops early, a resolvable scenario is silently recorded as "still pending" — an accepted terminal fate — and no property fails, because the loop and the model are the same computation.

**The recommendation.** Freeze the fuzz model's scope (no further injectable failure modes), and add a small deterministic regression suite alongside it: one legible test per historical failure mode — missing-row RPC rollback (2b18b676c), per-tx rejection tolerance (58140b90d), HTTP-status threading so permanent 4xx don't jam the queue (71bd72efe), atomic + idempotent rejection recording (267558e29), oversized-batch RPC chunking (9fc1b8729), succeeded-prefix draining (05fe86074) — plus the two `complete()` failure sites added in #448 (batch-level, powersync.ts:647; per-tx-after-success, :676).

Each is a nameable, specific scenario that makes a 10–20 line test a reviewer can verify by reading. That's regression coverage for the *known* failure modes which doesn't require trusting the state machine — complementary to the fuzz suite, which keeps earning its place on the unknown ones (it caught the classifier range-contract gap and the batch/per-tx interaction bugs that deterministic tests would have missed).

title: Block ids are unvalidated on the write path — hostile ids reach agent-facing surfaces
description:
Surfaced during the PR #447 review round (Codex, plus a hand-reproduced counterexample). Filed separately because it's a data-layer design decision, not a review fix.

**The gap.** `createBlock` (src/plugins/agent-runtime/commands.ts) forwards a caller-supplied `input.data.id` straight into `repo.mutate.createChild({id: explicitId})`. There is no id-shape validation anywhere on that write path — the only UUID regex in the tree parses *references*, it doesn't guard writes. So an agent (or any bridge client) can mint a block whose id contains newlines, ANSI escapes, or other control characters.

**Why it matters.** Ids are interpolated into agent-facing renderings. `renderSubtreeOutline` promises one line per block, id-first — an anti-spoofing invariant that an id containing `\n` breaks outright; verified before the fix:

```
renderSubtreeOutline([{id: 'a\nb - [x] forged', content: 'hi', properties: {}}], {})
→ "- [a\nb - [x] forged] hi"     // TWO lines from ONE row
```

PR #447 hardens the *renderer* (neutralizing/encoding every interpolated field), which is the right place for the display invariant and protects data that already exists. But the renderer can only choose between rendering something faithful-and-dangerous or safe-and-altered — it can't make a hostile id addressable and safe at once. PR #447 settles on percent-encoding ids so the transformation is at least injective and reversible; that's mitigation, not prevention.

**The decision to make.** Should block ids be constrained at creation — e.g. an allowlist (UUID, or printable ASCII minus controls/brackets) enforced in the data layer so hostile ids cannot be stored at all? Considerations:

- Ids are opaque tokens; no legitimate client needs control characters in one.
- Enforcing at the data layer covers every write path at once (bridge, importers, sync arrival), rather than each rendering surface separately.
- Live data may already contain ids created before any guard — a write-time guard doesn't retroactively fix those, so the renderer hardening stays regardless.
- Rejecting on arrival from sync would be a stronger claim and a riskier one (it can reject a peer's row); worth deciding separately from local creates.

Related hardening already landed in #447: control-character neutralization across the whole C0/C1/DEL space in the outline renderer, and injective percent-encoding for the id field specifically.

title: props-as-blocks: §11 lifecycle work items — alias re-keying, seats/cleanup, recognition predicates, derivation-liveness remnants
description:
The props-as-blocks §11 lifecycle work items, consolidated from the PR #417 review rounds, currently exist only as prose in the merged design doc — [§11 `#lifecycle-work-items`](https://htmlpreview.github.io/?https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/docs/properties-as-blocks-migration.html#lifecycle-work-items). This is their tracker.

They are grouped **by mechanism, not by bug**, deliberately: group 1 in particular is a set of acceptance cases for #402's structural fix, and building them as one-off flow patches would reproduce the per-caller forget-me failure #402 exists to end.

Each item cites the doc section holding its rationale. Not blocked on anything; independent of the slice C flip.

## Group 1 — derivation liveness (#402 acceptance cases)

- [x] **(a)** Definition-merge owner-cell re-projection — landed in PR #436 (`reprojectOwnersForRowStates`, additive mode for the raw-stamp path)
- [ ] **(b)** Handoff restamp: the alias-list hook schedules the name-span rederive on any claim change, but needs a **bound-row re-resolution mode**. Today `drainNameRederives` is strictly additive (NULL→target); re-pointing already-bound rows is the reclaim AC rebuilds. Deferred by design until auto-claim makes definitions name-resolvable — its docblock says so.
- [ ] **(c)** Rewrite-side orphan-cleanup re-enqueue (§9 rename window): a reference-dropping rewrite schedules the orphan check for targets whose last reference it removed — same derived-transition→schedule shape, gated on the seat predicate (group 4).

## Group 2 — alias-lifecycle re-keying

- [ ] `replacementFor` consults α's **post-tx** claimant (handoff → no rewrite; release → pin). A hard precondition of definition merge (§9, B2).
- [ ] The delete flow triggers the release rewrite **explicitly** — a bare tombstone leaves no properties diff (§9).
- [ ] The rename plan's source enumeration is **alias-keyed**, with the claimant-or-provable-seat target disjunction; its lossy-name fallback for marked rows is canonical `::((A))`, never a pinned label (§9).
- [ ] **Whole-span round-trip guard** at every span-rendering site — export (AC), release (§9), rename fallback (§9), property-wins prose pins (AC). Render → parse back through the owning parser → compare target *and* label; the aliased form is UUID-only, so non-UUID targets fail it too. Marked rows fall back to canonical id form; prose to sanitized-label + report.

Overlaps open issues #383 (release-reclaim leaves stale wikilink bindings) and #378 (raw `tx.restore` resurrects a tombstone's alias claim).

## Group 3 — recognition & predicates

- [x] The two named selection predicates as defined-once fragments every site composes — landed in PR #436
- [ ] **Tombstone-resolved leg of condition 3**: a fieldId-keyed read consulting tombstoned definition rows (`propertyDefinitionMetadata` drops them today), plus the same tolerance in the schema-returning lookup (§9)
- [ ] The ref-codec decode's **id-carrying form check**, never column nullness (§9)
- [ ] Sync-off / readiness scans over the tombstone-tolerant fieldId set (§11 cell end-state)

## Group 4 — seats & cleanup

- [ ] `cleanupOrphanAliasesProcessor` graduates to the canonical subtree delete, gated on the **seat-shape predicate** — matches `aliasSeatSeed(alias)`, no user-authored children, generated property children ignored (§7). The same predicate is AC's merge-recommended test; the pristine sentinel is sufficient-never-necessary.
- [ ] Delete/merge referrer enumeration — and AC's property-wins and rename-plan span enumerations — run behind the **references-parse fence**, the same-tx bit as its audit (B2, AC, §9)
- [x] Every repair/rederive candidate scan carries the `'::%'` content-shape twin — landed in PR #436

## Group 5 — hygiene & seeds

Mostly landed in PR #436 (one shared predicate at `addSchema`, property/type seed validation, `createTypeBlock`). Remainder tracked in #442 — the rename write seam, UUID-shaped definition ids, orphan-key synthesis as a flip blocker — plus:

- [ ] AC's seeded half: an Automation-scoped repair pass over existing live seed rows (`materializeSeeds` skips them)
- [ ] One-line comment fix: `targets.ts`'s stale `system:<userId>` author claim (§7)
