- `repo.undoGroup<T>(description: string, fn: (grouped: Repo) => Promise<T>): Promise<T>` — mints a fresh group id, builds a facade, runs `fn(facade)`, returns its result. The caller must be able to obtain the group id (for toast matching) — e.g. expose `undoGroupId` on the facade, or return `{result, groupId}`; pick one and keep it ergonomic for the reschedule call site.
- The facade is `Repo`-shaped so existing helpers that take a `repo` parameter thread the token with zero signature changes. A prototype-chained object (`Object.create(repo)` with own `tx` override that injects `undoGroup` into opts) is the suggested mechanism.
- **Gotcha you must handle**: `repo.mutate` is a Proxy created in the Repo constructor and bound to the original repo, so a prototype-chained facade's `.mutate` (and `.run`) would bypass the facade's `tx` override. Either rebuild `mutate`/`run` on the facade so mutator dispatch opens the tx through the facade, or make the dispatch path resolve its tx-opener dynamically. **Write a test that pins this** (a `grouped.mutate.X(...)` call must join the group).
- Nested `undoGroup` on a facade that already carries a token **joins the outer group** (reuse the outer token; don't mint a new one).
- Calling `undo()`/`redo()`/queries on the facade behaves identically to the real repo (it's the same object graph underneath).
- Partial failure: if `fn` throws midway, already-committed txs remain merged in one entry covering the committed prefix (one cmd-Z reverts the partial work). Rethrow the error; don't auto-undo.

### 3. Persist `group_id` (local-only)

- Add a `group_id TEXT` column to `tx_context` and to `row_events`; the `row_events` insert triggers project it from `tx_context` the same way they read `tx_id` (NULL for sync-applied writes — mirror the existing CASE/COALESCE handling so a stale value can never leak into a sync-applied row; the engine sets it with the other fields at tx start and clears it at tx end).
- **Existing local databases must be migrated additively.** Follow the existing `PRAGMA table_info` + `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` pattern in `clientSchema.ts`. **Never drop/recreate `row_events`** — it is the user's permanent change history and preserving it is paramount in this project. Triggers can be dropped/recreated (they're stateless); tables cannot.
- No server/Postgres/PowerSync changes: `row_events` and `tx_context` are client-only.

### 4. Reschedule rollout + toast

- Wrap the body of `rescheduleBlock` (or its call site — whichever reads better) in `repo.undoGroup('Reschedule …', …)`, passing the facade to the daily-note helpers. Helpers stay untouched.
- `RescheduleToast` currently matches by `txId`. Make it group-aware: match when the top entry's `groupId` equals the reschedule's group id (keep a `txId` fallback so a groupless path still works). Same predicate at render-subscription time and click time, as today.

## Behavioral invariants (encode these as tests)

1. N txs under one group → **one** undo entry; single `repo.undo()` reverts all their writes; single `repo.redo()` restores them.
2. Fold correctness: a group touching the same block in two txs undoes to the *earliest* before and redoes to the *latest* after.
3. A group creating a block then updating it → undo removes the block (inverse-of-create path works through the merged entry).
4. Foreign ungrouped tx landing between two grouped txs → group splits into two entries; undo of the top entry does **not** revert the foreign tx.
5. Merged record clears redo; `depths()` reports 1 for a merged group.
6. `grouped.mutate.X(...)` joins the group (the facade/mutate gotcha).
7. Ungrouped txs behave byte-for-byte as before (no regression in existing undo tests).
8. Partial failure mid-group → one entry covering the committed prefix; a later undo reverts exactly that prefix.
9. Nested `undoGroup` joins the outer group.
10. `row_events` rows written under a group carry `group_id`; sync-applied writes carry NULL; a pre-existing DB without the column gets it added without losing existing rows.
11. Cross-workspace note (document, don't over-engineer): entries land in per-workspace managers; a group spanning workspaces merges per-manager. Known and accepted.

## Out of scope (do NOT build here)

- Auto-grouping at the action-dispatch boundary (`invokeAction` wildcard wrap + `repo` in action deps) — separate follow-up.
- Per-step snapshots / "step into group" undo UI.
- Events-derived persistent undo (§16.6).
- Migrating other composite actions (multi-select indent/delete, paste, merge…) — reschedule only.
- Refactoring daily-note helpers to in-tx variants.

## Process requirements

- **TDD**: write the failing test first for each unit above, then implement. Extend `src/data/internals/undoManager.test.ts` (manager-level merge semantics) and `src/data/test/repoUndo.test.ts` (repo-level integration). Follow the existing test-file conventions you'll see there: one DB per test file (`createTestDb()` once in module scope / `beforeAll`, `resetTestDb()` in `beforeEach`); never `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(...))` to wait on async outcomes — poll with `vi.waitFor`; don't write tests that merely restate constants.
- **Inner loop**: iterate against one test file with `yarn vitest run <path>` (~1s). The full gate is `yarn run check` (~64s: compile+lint+tests+config checks) — run it **before each commit**, not after every edit. (Note: a couple of bridge/server tests bind `127.0.0.1` and can fail with `listen EPERM` in restrictive sandboxes; if that happens, note it rather than "fixing" the test.)
- **Git**: work on a feature branch; commit incrementally with conventional-commit messages matching the repo's log style (e.g. `feat(data-layer): …`); open a PR early (first commit) and keep it updated. Never put user PII (workspace/page names, block ids, emails) in commits or the PR.
- **Docs**: add `docs/undo-grouping.md` recording the as-built design (a condensed version of this issue is fine). Start it with the repo's status-banner convention for markdown design docs: a `> **Status:** current — last verified against code <date>` blockquote. Update the "Reschedule (and similar actions) emit multiple `BlockDefault` txs" section of `docs/follow-ups.md` to point at the shipped mechanism, and add a short pointer under §16.4 of `docs/data-layer-redesign.md` noting the mechanism shipped as merge-at-record (don't rewrite the section).

## Post-implementation adversarial review loop (required)

After the implementation is complete and `yarn run check` is green, run an adversarial review loop before calling the work done. This mirrors a local `/areview loop` skill you don't have, so here is the protocol inline:

1. **Fan out parallel review agents** (use your subagent/Task tool if available; otherwise do sequential, genuinely independent review passes — re-read from the artifacts, not from your memory of writing them). Each agent gets a **self-contained brief**: the goal (this issue's Problem + Settled design), the full diff (committed + uncommitted), and the invariants list above. Agents are read-only; they report, they don't edit.
2. **Adversarial agents (3), one perspective each, non-overlapping**: (a) *undo-correctness / data loss* — can any sequence of group/undo/redo/interleave corrupt a block, resurrect a deleted one, or lose an edit? Trace the fold rule and replay against concrete value sequences. (b) *races & lifecycle* — concurrent txs while a group is open, workspace switch mid-group, replay failure paths, redo-stack invalidation ordering, subscriber notify ordering. (c) *contract & regression* — facade completeness (mutate/run/query paths), toast predicate at click-time vs render-time, schema migration on a populated pre-existing DB, trigger NULL-handling for sync writes. Tell each: cite `file:line`, give a concrete failure scenario + severity (blocker/major/minor/nit) + suggested fix; verify against the actual code before claiming; say plainly if the lens finds nothing.
3. **Quality agent (1, always)**: constructive axis only — duplicated logic that an existing helper already provides, needless complexity, wrong-altitude abstraction, obvious efficiency wins. It does not re-report bugs.
4. **Synthesize** into two clearly separated sections — Defects (deduped, severity-ranked) then Cleanups — in the PR description or a comment. Cross-agent agreement is a strong signal; drop findings that don't hold against the code.
5. **Fix defects worst-first** (blocker → major → minor; nits optional), then apply only the behavior-preserving cleanups you're confident in as a separate commit. Re-run `yarn run check`.
6. **Loop**: repeat steps 1–5 on the *current* state until a round surfaces no defect above nit, up to ~4 rounds. Convergence is judged on defects only. Stop early (and say why) if findings stop making progress or the check fails unresolvably.

## Definition of done

- [ ] All behavioral invariants above covered by tests, written test-first
- [ ] `UndoManager` merge-at-record + `steps` metadata
- [ ] `repo.undoGroup` + facade (incl. the `mutate` binding fix, pinned by a test)
- [ ] `group_id` persisted through `tx_context` → `row_events`, with additive migration for existing DBs
- [ ] Reschedule wrapped; toast group-aware
- [ ] `docs/undo-grouping.md` written; `docs/follow-ups.md` + redesign §16.4 cross-references updated
- [ ] Adversarial review loop run to convergence, findings + resolutions recorded on the PR
- [ ] `yarn run check` green; PR open with a summary linking back to this issue

title: Breadcrumbs render a full interactive block inside the crumb anchor (nested-<a> React error)
description:
## Symptom

Navigating to a type-definition page (or the Properties page) logs React hydration-style errors in the console:

> `<a> cannot appear as a descendant of <a>` / "cannot contain a nested anchor"

## Root cause

`BreadcrumbList` wraps each crumb's full `BlockComponent` in an `<a>` and relies on `BreadcrumbRenderer` (priority **10**, gated on `context.isBreadcrumb`) to render a compact, non-interactive preview. But renderer resolution is a priority tournament, and type-specific renderers — e.g. `BlockTypeBlockRenderer` at priority **100** — outrank it. For any crumb block whose type carries a high-priority renderer, the crumb renders the *full* interactive subtree (bullet-link anchors, inputs) inside the crumb anchor: invalid HTML, nested interactive controls, and the console error.

## Repro

1. Open any user-defined type's definition page via direct hash navigation (e.g. click a `#type` chip from PR #297, or navigate to a `block-type` block directly).
2. Watch the console — the nested-`<a>` error fires from the breadcrumbs plugin. No chips involved: reproduces on a branch without the supertags decorator (probed during PR #297's review rounds).

Affects the Types page, the Properties page, and any typed block with a custom high-priority renderer appearing in a breadcrumb trail.

## Fix direction

Either short-circuit renderer resolution when `context.isBreadcrumb` (a crumb should never resolve a type-specific renderer), or raise `BreadcrumbRenderer`'s priority above the type renderers. The first is probably safer — it makes "breadcrumbs are compact previews" an invariant instead of a priority race that every future renderer can accidentally lose.

_Surfaced during PR #297's adversarial review; the smoke tests there currently filter these two console messages — that filter can be removed once this is fixed._

title: PWA hangs on infinite "Loading…" when a stale older-version same-origin tab holds the OPFS DB
description:
## Summary

When the app is open in two places on the same origin — e.g. the installed Android PWA **plus** a browser tab still running an **older deployed version** — the newer instance can hang **indefinitely on the "Loading…" screen**. Closing the stale tab unblocks it immediately.

## Observed (real Android device)

- Installed PWA (Chrome-backed) on `stvad.github.io/knowledge-medium`.
- A separate same-origin Chrome tab was open, running an older bundle — it was showing the **"A new version is available. Reload"** prompt.
- The PWA sat on "Loading…" indefinitely. Via remote inspection: `document.readyState === "complete"` and **no JS exception was thrown** — boot was blocked, not the HTML/network load.
- **Closing the stale tab → the PWA booted immediately.**

## Likely mechanism

- DB layer: `PowerSyncDatabase` with `WASQLiteVFS.OPFSCoopSyncVFS` and `flags.enableMultiTabs: true` (`src/data/repoProvider.ts`).
- The cooperative OPFS VFS coordinates tabs via a shared worker / `navigator.locks`, which assumes open tabs run **compatible** code. With the older-version tab holding the cooperative handle, the newer instance appears to **starve at DB-open**.
- Not fully confirmed — would be nailed by reproducing two **matched**-version tabs (expected: coexist fine) vs **mismatched** (expected: wedge). On Android the installed PWA shares an OPFS partition with same-origin browser tabs, so this is easy to hit: open the app in a tab, don't reload after a deploy, then launch the PWA.

## Impact

Indefinite "Loading…" with **no feedback** — the user can't tell why the app won't start, and the natural instinct (reload the PWA) doesn't help; only closing the *other* tab does. Baffling failure mode on the user's primary device.

## Proposed fix

- **DB-open / boot timeout → actionable message.** If the connection doesn't open within N seconds, replace the infinite spinner with something like *"The app appears to be open in another tab, possibly running an older version — close or reload it,"* rather than hanging silently.
- Tie into the existing version/update flow (the "new version available" prompt) so a version-skewed tab is nudged to reload before it can wedge a sibling.
- Optional: detect the coordination stall explicitly and name which tab holds the lock.

## Notes

Discovered while debugging the mobile keyboard toolbar on a real Android device via remote CDP inspection.

title: Multi-tab (esp. Firefox): block moves & writes stall ~1s from OPFSCoopSyncVFS handle hand-off
description:
## Summary

With **2+ tabs of the app open** (most noticeably on **Firefox**), block **move up/down** — and local writes generally — become *super slow*: a single move can stall for up to ~1 second. Single-tab is unaffected. This is lock/contention-related, not a problem with the move logic itself (a move is one tiny `writeTransaction`).

## Repro

1. Open the app in two tabs (same user/workspace), Firefox.
2. In one tab, repeatedly move a block up/down (`$mod+Shift+ArrowUp/Down`).
3. Each move takes ~hundreds of ms to ~1s, vs instant with a single tab open.

## Root cause

We run PowerSync with `WASQLiteVFS.OPFSCoopSyncVFS` + `enableMultiTabs: true` ([src/data/repoProvider.ts:167](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/repoProvider.ts#L167)).

- `OPFSCoopSyncVFS` `vfsRequiresDedicatedWorkers === true`: each tab opens its **own** OPFS connection + dedicated worker. They coordinate access to the single SQLite file by **handing off one exclusive OPFS sync-access handle** via `navigator.locks` + a per-file `BroadcastChannel`.
- The hand-off is driven by a notify-and-retry loop with **`LOCK_NOTIFY_INTERVAL = 1000` ms** (`node_modules/@journeyapps/wa-sqlite/src/examples/OPFSCoopSyncVFS.js`). The requesting tab posts one immediate notify; if that races the other tab's one-shot listener registration, it then waits up to a **full second** for the next `setInterval` notify before it can acquire the handle. Each contended write transaction can eat that ~1s.
- Every move up/down is a `writeTransaction` ([src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:230](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts#L230)), so with 2 tabs it pays the hand-off stall.

### Why it's worse / unfixable-the-easy-way on Firefox

The "good" multi-tab VFS, `OPFSWriteAheadVFS` (concurrent readers + 1 writer, no hand-off), needs `createSyncAccessHandle({ mode: "readwrite-unsafe" })` to hold **multiple** handles on one file. That mode is **Chromium-only** (Chrome 121+); **Firefox and Safari don't implement it** (as of 2026-06). On Firefox there can only ever be one exclusive handle per file, so the two tabs are *forced* to pass the single handle back and forth — and `OPFSWriteAheadVFS` cannot help there.

## Already done

- Bumped PowerSync `web 1.38.1→1.38.4`, `common 1.53.1→1.55.0`, `node 0.18.4→0.19.0` (commit `55d1da48`). Picks up the 1.38.4 `watch()`/`onChange()` listener-leak fix, but **does not change the Firefox multi-tab math**.

## Candidate fixes (tradeoffs)

1. **Patch `LOCK_NOTIFY_INTERVAL` down** (1000 → ~25–50ms) via patch-package. Smallest, reversible, keeps OPFS single-tab speed; cuts the worst-case stall from ~1s to tens of ms. Cost: monkey-patches a `node_modules` wa-sqlite file (maintain a patch); doesn't remove the hand-off cost entirely, just the notify gap.
2. **IDB shared-worker VFS for multi-tab** (`IDBBatchAtomicVFS`, single shared connection — no per-tab hand-off). Robust on Firefox, no contention; cost: slower single-tab and a one-time re-sync (filename bump). We deliberately moved *to* OPFS for speed, so this regresses the common single-tab case.
3. **Conditional VFS by engine**: `OPFSWriteAheadVFS` on Chromium (genuine win) + (1) or (2) on Firefox/Safari. Best per-browser outcome, most code.

## Longer-term

Going the native-shell route (Electron + `@powersync/node`, or Capacitor/Tauri with native SQLite) replaces wa-sqlite/OPFS with real SQLite + WAL, which removes this entire class of limitation (real concurrent readers + writer, OS file locking, no hand-off). The data engine already runs on the native SDK in the test harness ([src/data/test/createTestDb.ts](https://github.com/Stvad/knowledge-medium/blob/master/src/data/test/createTestDb.ts)). Tracked separately if/when a desktop/mobile app is on the roadmap.

## Acceptance criteria

- With 2 Firefox tabs open, block move up/down feels responsive (no ~1s stalls); contended write-transaction latency is in the tens-of-ms range.
- No regression to single-tab write latency.

title: Stable /module/<blockId> URLs for user extensions (enables cross-block plugin imports)
description:
## Trigger to actually do this

**Do this only when we want cross-block (plugin→plugin) module dependencies** — i.e. one user extension block being able to `import` another. That is the *one* capability today's loader can't provide and the only thing this work uniquely unlocks. Until that's a real need, **don't build it**: the current in-thread Blob-URL path plus the now-shipped source maps cover everything else.

## Status / what's already done

- **Design:** fully specced in `docs/plugin-module-url-sw-hybrid.md` (PR #251). Went through a 2-round adversarial-review loop + several external review passes.
- **Shipped (#252, merged):** source maps + a sanitized stable `//# sourceURL` on the existing blob path — the one low-risk piece, worth having regardless of this issue. So "extensions aren't debuggable" is no longer a reason to do the SW work.
- **Not built:** the SW `/module/` route, the on-demand producer protocol, the claim handshake. Deferred behind the trigger above.

## The decision to resolve first

**Are we willing to require a controlling service worker for *user* extensions?**

This is the hinge. It's reasonable here because the `/module/` path only ever affects user-authored `type:'extension'` blocks — the built-in plugins are ordinary bundled ES modules that never touch it — and SW-unavailable environments (private mode, no-storage, policy-blocked) are already a degraded tier for this local-first app. "Custom extensions sit out when the SW is unavailable" is consistent with that tier; the app still boots on its built-ins.

- **Yes →** build the design below.
- **No →** don't; a SW route behind a *mandatory* blob fallback is pure additive cost (the rigged comparison the doc calls out). Stop at the shipped source-map change.

## Proposed design (single-path, on-demand)

Honest framing: this is a **lateral complexity trade** (removes blob-URL edge cases, adds SW-coordination ones), justified by the **capability**, not by net simplicity.

- **On-demand SW↔main proxy.** The in-thread compile core stays; the *loader* changes from "instantiate a blob, read `.default`" to "mint `${BASE_URL}module/<id>?v=<hash>` and `import()` it." On that fetch the SW `postMessage`s the requesting client (`event.clientId`) and the page produces the compiled **bytes** via a *new* approval-gated helper (NOT `loadApprovedExtension`, which instantiates) and returns them as a `Response`. No module Cache, no GC, and the pre-materialization/topological phase dissolves (production is demand-driven by the real import graph).
- **First-load control** via page-initiated, **generation-gated** `clients.claim()` (claim only when the active worker's `BUILD_ID` matches the page build — `sw.js` deliberately omits `clients.claim()` to avoid version skew), with a bounded `controllerchange` timeout whose terminal branch resolves anyway → `/module/` 404 → per-block error shells (the loader already isolates per-block failures). Gate **only** the dynamic-extension resolve, which fits the existing two-stage cold start, so app paint is unaffected. The blob fallback is dropped (scoped to "require SW for user extensions").
- **E2EE unchanged:** decryption stays in-thread (the loader reads already-plaintext `block.content`); the SW never sees keys. On-demand keeps no compiled bytes in a Cache.

## Implementation scope (from the doc's §6, in dependency order)

1. **Byte-producing helper + message handler** (`compileExtensionModule.ts` / a small `extensions/moduleHost.ts`): approval-gated "produce compiled bytes for `{id, hash}`" (reuses `transpileImpl` + the approved record; does NOT instantiate). Re-plumb the loader (`dynamicExtensions.ts`) from blob-instantiate to mint+`import()`.
2. **Transitive-import hash pinning** (producer): rewrite a dep ref → `${BASE_URL}module/<dep>?v=<depApprovedHash>` from each dep's *approved* record (cheap lookup, no compile); unapproved deps fail closed. Also defines the authoring specifier for "import another block." The fiddliest piece.
3. **`public/sw.js`:** new `/module/` branch ordered **before** `isCacheableAsset` (a module fetch has `request.destination === 'script'`), with no-client/timeout/produce-failure → `Response` mapping; add the generation-gated `CLAIM` handler; keep `@babel/standalone` in precache.
4. **Bootstrap gate** (`AppRuntimeProvider` / `registerServiceWorker`): page-initiated build-id-matched claim, then gate the dynamic resolve on `Promise.race([controllerchange, timeout])` with the terminal branch.
5. **Tests:** route ordering; SW↔main produce round-trip (incl. `event.clientId` routing, missing-client → 503, produce-throw → shell); generation-gated claim → `controllerchange` gating + the timeout terminal branch; transitive `?v=` pinning + unapproved-dep fail-closed; cycle handling.

## Open items to verify before/while building

- **`clients.claim()` on a hard reload** — empirically unverified whether it reliably takes a Shift+Reload client.
- **`event.clientId`** reliably populated for module *subresource* fetches across target engines (the proxy's linchpin).
- **Import cycles** — content-hash URLs make a cycle's URLs mutually content-dependent; needs an explicit rule (e.g. drop `?v=` inside an SCC → reload-to-apply within the cycle). The transitive-pin is itself a static specifier scan, so cycle detection rides on it.
- **Live-edit limit:** an edited block that *others import* isn't picked up live for its importers until a reload (inherent to URL-keyed module maps; new with the transitive feature, not a regression vs today).

See `docs/plugin-module-url-sw-hybrid.md` for the full analysis, grounding, and rejected alternatives (compile-in-SW; SW-reads-IDB-directly; producer-writes-Cache + mandatory fallback).

title: Wipe local data: add one-click Clear-Site-Data trigger once off GitHub Pages
description:
## Context

The `lock_and_wipe_local_data` ("Wipe all local data") panic action currently **delegates** the actual destruction to the browser/OS "clear site data" control: it drains unsynced uploads, then shows the user concise instructions for clearing the site's data. It does **not** trigger the wipe programmatically.

That's deliberate — see `docs/lock-and-wipe-coarse-recommendation.md` §0 (the analysis) and the implementation in `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts`.

## Why no programmatic trigger today

The clean one-click trigger is a dedicated origin route (e.g. `/wipe`) that responds with `Clear-Site-Data: "*"`; the app navigates there and the browser wipes the origin. But:

- The header must come from a **network response on our own origin**, and we ship on **GitHub Pages**, which can't set custom response headers.
- A service worker can **not** stand in for that. Verified by spike (`docs/clear-site-data-spike/`, Chromium 141):
  - SW that *synthesizes* the header (`new Response('', {headers})`) → **ignored, nothing cleared**.
  - SW that *passes through* a real network response carrying it → cleared, but that still needs our origin's server to emit the header.
  - Plain network response / navigation with the header → cleared.

  i.e. Chromium only honors `Clear-Site-Data` on responses that came over the network; GH Pages can't produce one.

There's also no JS API to open the browser's clear-data UI from a page, so guidance is the only option on GH Pages.

## What to do when we're on a header-capable host

When the app moves to (or sits behind) an origin that can set response headers — e.g. a small edge function / Worker, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, or a real server:

1. Add a `/wipe` route on our origin that responds with `Clear-Site-Data: "*"` (or `"cache","cookies","storage","executionContexts"`) and redirects to the logged-out app.
2. Update `lock_and_wipe_local_data` to: confirm → `flushUploadQueue` (already in `src/sync/flushUploadQueue.ts`) → navigate to `/wipe` for a true one-click wipe, **falling back** to the current guide text when the header route isn't available.
3. Re-run / extend the spike on the target host to confirm the header is honored there (and ideally check Firefox/Safari, which the spike didn't cover — only Chromium was installed).

## References
- `docs/lock-and-wipe-coarse-recommendation.md` §0.2 (trigger pattern), §0.3 (hosting reality), §0.4 (when to hand-roll)
- `docs/clear-site-data-spike/` (reproducible spike + results)
- Implementation: `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts` (`lock_and_wipe_local_data`, `WIPE_LOCAL_DATA_INSTRUCTIONS`)

title: navigation: replace the empty-string probe in resolveGlobalCommandTargetPanel with a first-class 'navigator target' query
description:
Follow-up from PR #241 (navigation intent-policy seam).

## Context
`resolveGlobalCommandTopLevelBlockId` (the daily-notes prev/next anchor) resolves *which panel a navigator global command currently targets* by routing through the intent policy verb (`navigationIntentVerb`), so a plugin that redirects where global commands land (active vs main) feeds both the navigation (write) and the anchor (read).

But the policy's contract is `gesture -> NavigateInput`, and a gesture carries a `blockId` — while the read has no destination block, it only wants the resolved `target`. So `resolveGlobalCommandTargetPanel` (`src/utils/navigation.ts`) **probes** the policy with a sentinel `NAVIGATOR_TARGET_PROBE_BLOCK_ID = ''` and reads only `input.target`.

## Why this is a (minor) smell
The probe expresses a *query* ("where would a navigator command land?") as a *fake command* (a gesture with an empty block). It works because the navigator target is block-independent in the default policy and any sane override.

It would mis-resolve only for a hypothetical future policy that legitimately branches the navigator **target** on `blockId` (e.g. "blocks of type X always open in main"): the probe passes `''`, so such a policy wouldn't see the real block and could pick the wrong target for the anchor. Failure mode is a wrong prev/next-day anchor — annoying, not data loss.

`null` is *not* a cleaner fix: it forces `NavigationGesture.blockId` to be nullable, which makes `defaultNavigationIntent` emit a block-less `NavigateInput` that `isNavigateInput` correctly rejects, tripping `onError:'fallback'` -> `ranBareDefault` -> throw in the read path.

## Proposed fix (do when a block-dependent navigator policy becomes a real use case)
Introduce a first-class, block-free "navigator target" query rather than synthesizing a fake gesture — e.g. a small `resolveNavigatorTarget(repo, viewport) -> NavigateTarget` seam the policy and the read both consume, or a typed "probe/query" mode on the gesture that policies must treat as block-independent. Until there's a concrete need, the `''` sentinel (named constant + doc comment) is the pragmatic choice.

## Pointers
- `src/utils/navigation.ts`: `NAVIGATOR_TARGET_PROBE_BLOCK_ID`, `resolveGlobalCommandTargetPanel`, `resolveGlobalCommandTopLevelBlockId`
- Design notes: `docs/navigation-redesign.md` (navigation extensibility model)

title: Backspace merge hardcodes 'concat' while the merge picker delegates strategy
description:
Surfaced by the extension-seam audit — `docs/extension-seam-gaps.md`, gap **E2**. Latent inconsistency, not introduced by recent work.

## Problem
The two block-merge paths disagree on content strategy:

- **Keyboard Backspace-at-start** (`delete_empty_block_cm`, `src/shortcuts/defaultShortcuts.ts:~849`) merges via the mutator's default `contentStrategy = 'concat'` (`src/data/mutators.ts:~769`) with no way to vary it.
- **Interactive merge picker** delegates the strategy via `pickMergeContentStrategy` (`src/plugins/merge-blocks/strategy.ts:15`) — e.g. `keepTarget` for page-typed blocks, `concat` otherwise.

So the "same" merge can produce different content depending on how it was triggered (Backspace vs picker). That's a latent correctness bug — e.g. Backspace-merging into a page-typed block concatenates, while the picker would keep the target.

## Suggested fix
Unify the keyboard Backspace path onto the same strategy resolver so both paths agree — e.g. a `mergeContentStrategyFacet` (Map/Pick keyed by the two blocks' types) that `pickMergeContentStrategy` and the Backspace handler both consume. Optionally a Chain seam for the eligibility branch (merge vs outdent vs delete) per the audit.

## Severity
Latent correctness bug (not data loss). Verify exact line numbers (the audit notes line cites may drift a few lines).

title: undo/redo: concurrent tx during _replay await can resurrect a stale redo entry (redo-clear TOCTOU)
description:
## Summary

`repo.undo()` / `repo.redo()` have a time-of-check/time-of-use gap: they pop the entry, `await this._replay(...)`, then push to the redo (or undo) stack. If another `BlockDefault` `repo.tx` for the same workspace commits **during** the replay await, its `record()` clears the redo stack — and then the in-flight `undo()`'s post-await `pushRedo` resurrects a redo entry that is now downstream of a newer committed action. Pressing redo would replay a stale `after` snapshot over rows the concurrent tx already moved past — the exact "redo after a new edit" corruption that `record()`'s redo-clear is meant to prevent.

This is **pre-existing** (the single-manager code before the per-workspace undo work had the same `await`-then-push shape) and was surfaced during the adversarial review of #186 / PR #217. It is narrow (needs a concurrent commit precisely inside the replay window) and does not corrupt cross-workspace state (the #186 invariant holds independently), but it can leave the redo branch inconsistent.

## Repro (single workspace, no switch needed)

`src/data/repo.ts` — `undo(scope)`:
```
const entry = manager.popUndo(scope)      // pop A's top off the undo stack
if (entry === null) return false
await this._replay(entry, 'before')        // async: opens its own repo.tx, hits the DB
manager.pushRedo(scope, entry)             // <-- runs AFTER the await
```
1. User presses cmd-Z. `undo()` pops the entry, then awaits `_replay`.
2. During that await, another `BlockDefault` tx for the same workspace commits (debounced autosave on blur, a second keypress, a fire-and-forget processor write). Its `record()` (`src/data/internals/undoManager.ts`) runs `getRedo(scope).length = 0` (clears redo) then `pushUndo`.
3. `_replay` resolves; `undo()` runs `manager.pushRedo(scope, entry)`, pushing the just-undone entry onto the redo stack that step 2 cleared.

Result: a redo entry exists that is downstream of a newer committed action. `redo()` then replays a stale snapshot. (`redo()` has the mirror shape with `pushUndo` after its await.)

Note: `_replay` itself does **not** record (it goes through `_runAndDispatch`, not `tx`), so the corruption requires a *separate* user/processor tx landing in the window — not the replay's own tx.

## Severity

Major in principle (redo-branch corruption), but requires a concurrent `BlockDefault` commit inside the (short) replay window, so low probability in practice. No data loss beyond an incorrect redo; the cross-workspace "don't touch unopened workspaces" invariant is unaffected.

## Proposed direction

The clean fix is mutual exclusion: serialize `undo` / `redo` / the `record` step of `tx` so a `record` can't interleave between an undo's pop and its `pushRedo`. Options:
- Run `undo`/`redo`/`tx`-record through a single async mutex (a small promise-chain lock on `Repo`).
- Lighter: capture a monotonic mutation counter (or `depths(scope)`) on the manager before the `await`, and after it only `pushRedo` if nothing recorded in between — otherwise treat the redo branch as superseded and drop the push rather than resurrecting it.

Either should be covered by a test that commits a concurrent `BlockDefault` tx during a stubbed/slow `_replay` and asserts the redo stack is not resurrected.

## Pointers
- `src/data/repo.ts` — `undo()` / `redo()` (pop → `await _replay` → push), `_replay`, `_runAndDispatch`.
- `src/data/internals/undoManager.ts` — `record()` (the `getRedo(scope).length = 0` redo-clear), `pushRedo`/`pushUndo`.

Context: found in the review of PR #217 (fix for #186).

title: Read-only flag lags active-workspace switch: transient spurious ReadOnlyError on cmd-Z right after switching into an editable workspace
description:
## Summary

`repo.isReadOnly` is a single global flag that tracks the **active** workspace's "can I write" state. `repo.activeWorkspaceId` is updated **synchronously** on a workspace switch, but `isReadOnly` is updated **asynchronously** by a React effect — so there is a window right after an in-place switch where the two disagree. A fast `cmd-Z` in that window can throw a transient, self-healing `ReadOnlyError` on a perfectly legitimate undo.

This is a **pre-existing** race (it predates the undo workspace-scoping work) surfaced during the adversarial review of #186 / PR #217. Documented there as a known limitation; this issue is the follow-up.

## Repro (B → A direction)

1. Active = read-only/viewer workspace **B** ⇒ `_activeWorkspaceId = 'B'`, `isReadOnly = true`.
2. User switches to editable workspace **A** via `WorkspaceSwitcher.navigateToWorkspace`, which calls `repo.setActiveWorkspaceId('A')` **synchronously** (`src/components/workspace/WorkspaceSwitcher.tsx:60`) and does **not** touch `isReadOnly`.
3. `isReadOnly` only flips to `false` later/asynchronously — via `resolveInitialLayout` re-running (`App.tsx:82`, behind `await resolveWorkspace` + `await getLocalMemberRole`) or the reactive role effect (`App.tsx:226-231`).
4. In that window, `cmd-Z`: `repo.undo()` is scoped to the active workspace (A), finds A's entry, and the read-only gate in `runTx` (`src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:212-214`) sees the **stale** `isReadOnly = true` ⇒ throws `ReadOnlyError` on a legitimate editable-A undo.

## Severity / impact

- Transient and self-healing: `isReadOnly` corrects within a tick or two.
- Recoverable: `undo()` pushes the entry back on failure (`src/data/repo.ts`, the `catch` in `undo`/`redo`), so a retry after the flag settles succeeds.
- User-visible symptom: a spurious error toast on a fast `cmd-Z` immediately after switching from a viewer workspace into an editable one. No data loss, no cross-workspace write (the cross-workspace invariant from #186 holds independently).

## Why the obvious fix is NOT safe

The tempting fix — resolve read-only for undo from the workspace's member role (`getLocalMemberRole`) instead of the global flag — is **unsafe**. The global `isReadOnly` flag encodes more than viewer-vs-editor role: it also encodes **e2ee lock / waiting** state (`App.tsx:98,102` force `setReadOnly(true)` for owners/editors of a *locked* workspace whose key isn't available, and for the `waiting` layout). Resolving from role alone would return "writable" for an owner of a **locked** workspace and let undo write plaintext into it — strictly worse than the transient this issue is about.

So the read-only signal for a workspace is fundamentally `role == viewer` **OR** `locked` **OR** `waiting`, and the latter two are themselves resolved asynchronously.

## Proposed direction

Make the active-workspace switch and the read-only flag update **atomic** at the App layer, so the two fields never disagree:

- In `WorkspaceSwitcher.navigateToWorkspace` (and/or the `App.tsx` switch path), set `isReadOnly` to a conservative value at the same point `setActiveWorkspaceId` is called, then settle to the resolved value once `resolveWorkspaceEntry` (role + lock + canary) completes.
- Conservative-on-switch (`setReadOnly(true)` until resolved) avoids the *spurious-error* direction here, but note it would make undo briefly *unavailable* rather than briefly *erroring* — which is the gentler failure (no toast; button just disabled). Worth confirming that's the desired trade.
- Alternatively, give `Repo` a small per-workspace "can write" resolver that consults role **and** lock/waiting state, and have the read-only gate use it for the active workspace — but this has to account for the same async lock resolution, so it does not remove the need to sequence the switch.

## Pointers

- `src/data/repo.ts` — `undo()`/`redo()`, `setReadOnly`, the `isReadOnly` field.
- `src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:212-214` — the read-only gate (`if (isReadOnly && !scopeAllowedInReadOnly(scope)) throw new ReadOnlyError(scope)`).
- `src/App.tsx:72,82,98,102,226-231` — where `setActiveWorkspaceId` / `setReadOnly` are driven (incl. locked/waiting forcing read-only).
- `src/components/workspace/WorkspaceSwitcher.tsx:49-67` — synchronous `setActiveWorkspaceId` on switch.
- `src/data/workspaces.ts:413` — `getLocalMemberRole` (role only; does **not** know about lock/waiting).

Context: surfaced in the review of PR #217 (fix for #186).

title: [meta] Correctness-audit preventive practices — tracking epic
description:
**Tracking epic** for the *preventive* practices/automations coming out of the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`). The per-finding fix issues are #182–#196 + #198; this epic is about *not reintroducing the same classes*.

## Common threads (root causes across all findings)
1. **Documented "supported-but-rare" states aren't honored by their consumers** — tied order_keys (#182), soft-deleted intermediates (#183), cross-client alias dups (#185), non-string list elements (#189), tombstoned-referenced blocks (#195).
2. **Derived data is replace-written and lost on error/absence**, instead of add-only/retain — #189, #194, #187, and the historical ~10k-backlink incident. Fixed once (reprojection); didn't propagate.
3. **Invariants live at the caller/UI, not the data-layer primitive** (no defense-in-depth) — #184, #188; the recurring "real mechanism, gated by one caller" pattern.
4. **Structured-value identity/equality done ad hoc** (`JSON.stringify` order/value-lossy) — #196; a canonical helper exists but isn't standard.
5. **Non-atomic side-effect sequencing + unisolated plugin callbacks; scoping** — #191, #182(split); cross-workspace global state #186.

## Recommendations (one issue each)
- [ ] #200 — Property-based / fuzz testing (`fast-check`) for data-layer pure functions *(threads 1, 4)*
- [ ] #201 — Shared "supported-states" fixture + kernel invariant suite *(thread 1)*
- [ ] #202 — ESLint: ban `JSON.stringify`-as-key; flag derived-column replace-writes *(threads 2, 4)*
- [ ] #203 — Codify & enforce "derived data is add-only / retain-on-source" *(thread 2)*
- [ ] #204 — Defense-in-depth: invariants at the primitive + adversarial direct-call mutator tests *(thread 3)*
- [ ] #205 — Soft-delete discipline: visibility vs structural-integrity queries *(thread 2/soft-delete)*
- [ ] #206 — Isolate plugin callbacks + throw-safe side-effect sequencing *(thread 5)*
- [ ] #207 — Audit module-global state for workspace-keying under in-place switching *(thread 5/scoping)*
- [ ] #208 — Contract-test external SDK error/response shapes *(external-shape assumptions)*

## Suggested order (highest leverage first)
1. #200 (cheapest; already found a real bug in the audit), 2. #201, 3. #202, 4. #203 (worst history), then #204/#205/#206/#207/#208.

## Process meta-point
The audit's adversarial-verify step refuted ~half the raw findings by finding the guard, and every confirmed finding was backed by a probe test. Carrying *both* habits into everyday dev — **write the bug-proving test before the fix, and try to refute your own bug first** — plus **grep the repo for sibling instances when fixing a class bug** (how #198 surfaced) is the highest-leverage change independent of any tooling.

title: [meta] Contract-test external SDK error/response shapes (PostgREST/PowerSync); stop mocking assumed shapes
description:
**Type:** test discipline · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread: assumptions about external/library shapes)

## Problem
Code that classifies/handles errors from external SDKs assumed a shape the SDK doesn't produce, and the **test mocked the wrong shape**, giving false confidence. #190: the upload-error classifier keys on `error.status`, but PostgREST errors carry no `status` field (it's a sibling of the response tuple, dropped when only `error` is destructured) — so the permanent-4xx branch is dead and the queue jams; meanwhile the existing test builds a synthetic error *with* `.status` and passes.

## Recommendation
For every boundary that switches on an external SDK's error/response shape (PostgREST, PowerSync, Supabase), derive the shape from the **actual SDK types or a recorded real payload**, not a hand-built mock. Add contract tests fed real-shaped errors. Where feasible, type the handler's input against the SDK's exported error type so a wrong assumption fails at compile time.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Upload-error classifier tested against real PostgrestError-shaped inputs (closes #190's false-confidence test).
- [ ] A documented convention: error/response-shape handlers test against SDK-derived shapes.

title: [meta] Audit module-global state for workspace-keying under in-place switching
description:
**Type:** architecture audit · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread: scoping — global state not workspace-keyed under in-place switching)

## Problem
The app is multi-workspace with **in-place** workspace switching (no reload), but some module-global / repo-level mutable state isn't keyed by workspace, so it leaks across switches. Confirmed: undo stacks (#186) — `cmd-Z` after a switch reverts/uploads an edit in the now-unopened workspace; and the single `repo.isReadOnly` flag collides with cross-workspace undo (#186 A5b). Past incidents (cross-workspace write leaks) are the same class.

## Recommendation
Inventory **all** module-global / repo-level mutable state (undo/redo stacks, `isReadOnly`, any registry or cache keyed without `workspaceId`) and apply the rule: *state that can differ per workspace must be keyed by `workspaceId` (or cleared on switch)*. Add tests that perform an in-place workspace switch and assert no cross-workspace effect (no mutation, no stale flag).

## Acceptance
- [ ] An inventory of repo/module-global mutable state with a per-item verdict (workspace-keyed / cleared-on-switch / genuinely global).
- [ ] Fixes for the identified leaks (relates to #186).
- [ ] A switch-crosstalk test pattern reusable for future state.

title: [meta] Isolate plugin callbacks + throw-safe side-effect sequencing in the sync observer
description:
**Type:** robustness pattern + tests · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread #5: non-atomic side-effect sequencing + unisolated plugin callbacks)

## Problem
Two related fragilities:
1. **Unisolated plugin callbacks.** `collectPluginInvalidationsFromSnapshots` iterates plugin `InvalidationRule`s with no try/catch (#191) — one throwing rule propagates past the watermark delete and **permanently drops that drain window's invalidation** (stale UI until reload). A buggy plugin can break a kernel invariant.
2. **Non-atomic commit→observe→cleanup ordering.** The irreversible/observable step isn't always last: #191 commits the disk write before the watermark; the split path (#182) dispatched editor text before the mutator that could throw.

## Recommendation
- Wrap **every** plugin/extension callback (invalidation rules, processors) in a `runPluginCallbackSafely` boundary so a throw is isolated (logged via `onError`) and can't break kernel flow.
- Adopt an **"observe/irreversible last"** ordering rule for commit→notify→cleanup sequences; where a fallible step must precede the watermark, make the watermark advance conditional on its success.
- Test by injecting a throwing plugin rule and asserting the kernel still completes and still invalidates the affected ids.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Plugin-callback isolation boundary used at all plugin-callback sites (closes #191's root cause).
- [ ] A test with a throwing `InvalidationRule` asserting no permanently-dropped invalidation.
- [ ] Ordering rule documented for the sync-observer side-effect sequence.

title: [meta] Soft-delete discipline: separate visibility vs structural-integrity queries; audit CTEs
description:
**Type:** architecture / SQL discipline · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread: soft-delete blindness)

## Problem
Soft-delete (`deleted=1`) is a *visibility* concept, but structural-integrity queries also filter `deleted=0`, so they miss state that is structurally present but invisible. This caused #183 (the cycle guard walks `deleted=0` and misses a cycle through a tombstoned intermediate) — and the cycle **detector** (`cycleScanSql`) shares the exact same blind spot, so nothing catches it. #184 is adjacent (reads a tombstone snapshot).

## Recommendation
Establish an explicit split with a naming convention:
- **Visibility queries** filter `deleted=0` (what the user sees / what materializes).
- **Structural-integrity queries** (ancestry, cycle detection, parent-chain, descendant walks) must **NOT** filter `deleted` — cycle-freedom and parent integrity are invariants independent of soft-delete.

One-time: audit every CTE/recursive query in `treeQueries.ts` / `clientSchema.ts` and classify it; fix the structural ones (the #183 fix is the first). Document the rule so new queries pick the right family.

## Acceptance
- [ ] `treeQueries.ts` / schema CTEs classified visibility vs structural; structural ones drop the `deleted` filter.
- [ ] The cycle detector no longer shares the blind spot.
- [ ] Convention documented.

title: [meta] Defense-in-depth: enforce invariants at the data-layer primitive + adversarial direct-call mutator tests
description:
**Type:** invariant / architecture + tests · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread #3: invariants live at the caller/UI, not the data-layer primitive)

## Problem
The audit's adversarial-verify pass refuted ~half the findings with "real corruption mechanism, but one upstream gate happens to prevent it." Correctness rests on every caller behaving — but mutators are public (agent bridge, macros, plugins). Examples: self-merge (#184 — the UI excludes self via `excludeBlockIds`, the mutator does not), merge-into-descendant (#188), and the plaintext-leak that was saved only by the entry gate.

## Recommendation
**Push invariants down to the primitive, with defense in depth:**
1. Every public mutator/tx method validates its own preconditions and fails with a **typed error or safe no-op** — never assumes the caller pre-filtered.
2. **Centralize each invariant** so a new caller can't bypass it (e.g. one `assertMergePreconditions` all merge paths funnel through), rather than scattered or UI-only checks.
3. Add a **per-mutator "adversarial direct-call" test suite**: call each public mutator *bypassing the UI* with well-typed-but-hostile args (self-merge, merge-into-descendant, move-to-descendant, delete-then-update, tied keys) and assert a typed rejection or safe no-op — never silent corruption. Treat the bridge/plugin surface as the untrusted caller it is.

Review smell to codify: "that can't happen, the UI excludes it" ⇒ the data-layer guard is missing.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Guards moved/added at the primitive for the known cases (#184, #188) with centralized precondition assertions.
- [ ] An adversarial direct-call suite over the public mutator surface.
- [ ] A note in `AGENTS.md`: data invariants must be enforced in the data layer, not only the UI.

title: [meta] ESLint guards: ban JSON.stringify-as-key; flag derived-column replace-writes
description:
**Type:** preventive automation (ESLint) · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta threads #2 and #4)

## Problem
Two recurring anti-patterns in the data layer:
1. **`JSON.stringify` as a semantic identity/equality key** — order-sensitive and value-lossy (NaN/null/undefined collide). This is exactly #196. A correct canonical helper already exists (`stableJsonValue` / `jsonValuesEqual` in `txEngine`) but isn't the enforced standard.
2. **Whole-object replace-writes of derived columns** (`references_json`, `properties_json`) where add-only/retain semantics are required — the strip class (#189) and the historical backlink incident.

There's precedent for ESLint guards here (the `no-restricted-syntax` ban on `window.CustomEvent`, audit B3).

## Recommendation
Add `no-restricted-syntax` rules scoped to `src/data/**`:
- Ban bare `JSON.stringify(x)` used as a `Set`/`Map` key or in an equality comparison → require `stableJsonValue`. Opt-out per-site with a justified `eslint-disable`.
- Flag direct replace-writes of `references_json` outside the sanctioned add-only projection path (point reviewers at the add-only contract — see the derived-data issue).

## Acceptance
- [ ] Rule 1 added + violations fixed/justified.
- [ ] Rule 2 added (or a documented lint-comment convention if a clean AST match isn't feasible).

title: [meta] Build a shared "supported-states" fixture + kernel invariant suite
description:
**Type:** preventive practice / test infrastructure · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread #1: documented "supported state" invariants not honored by consumers)

## Problem
The data model explicitly allows several unusual-but-supported on-disk states, but the code operating on them assumes the clean shape, and the invariant is asserted in only one place (often a header comment or a non-unique index). Confirmed bugs of this class: tied `order_key`s (#182), a soft-deleted node still on a parent chain (#183), cross-client alias dups (#185), a non-string element in a typed list (#189), a tombstoned-but-referenced block (#195). Notably the **read** side tests tied keys (`treeQueries.test.ts:89`) while the **write** side did not — that asymmetry *is* #182.

## Recommendation
Build a shared **"supported-states" fixture module** that seeds each documented unusual state (tied keys; soft-deleted intermediate; cross-client alias dup; multi-workspace; non-string list element; tombstoned-referenced block), and a kernel suite that drives the core mutators/queries over each fixture asserting "no throw / no silent corruption / well-formed result." This converts prose invariants into executed assertions and gives future code a ready harness.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A reusable fixture builder for each supported state.
- [ ] A suite exercising create/move/split/outdent/merge/delete/restore + the main queries against each, asserting safety.
- [ ] New mutators are expected to extend this suite (note it in `AGENTS.md`).

title: [meta] Adopt property-based / fuzz testing (fast-check) for data-layer pure functions
description:
**Type:** preventive practice / tooling · **From:** the 2026-06-18 correctness audit (`docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md`) (meta thread: "supported-but-rare states unhandled" + "ad-hoc structured-value identity")

## Problem
Several confirmed bugs were in pure/data-layer functions whose example-based unit tests used "nice" inputs and missed degenerate shapes. The one-off fuzz pass in the audit found a real bug (#196, `mergeProperties` dedup) that the existing unit test missed because it used identical object key order on both sides. No property-based testing exists today (only `vitest`).

## Recommendation
Add **`fast-check`** and a standing set of property tests for the data-layer pure functions, asserting invariants rather than examples:
- `src/data/orderKey.ts` — `keyBetween`/`keysBetween`/the new tie-safe helpers: results strictly ordered; never throw on supported inputs incl. ties; monotone (relates to #182/#198).
- `src/data/api/codecs.ts` — `decode(encode(x)) ≈ x` for every supported value shape; malformed/oversized input → typed error, never an unhandled throw or half-parsed object.
- `src/data/mergeProperties.ts` / `blockMerge.ts` — never mutates inputs; dedup is canonical (key-order- and value-insensitive); scalar collisions deterministic (#196).
- reference normalization (`blockData.ts`) — never collapses two genuinely-distinct refs.

## Acceptance
- [ ] `fast-check` in devDependencies; property tests for the four targets above, runnable in CI via `yarn run check`.
- [ ] Each property documents the invariant it pins.

title: Tie-unsafe order_key in paste.ts and panelLayoutProjection.ts (same class as #182)
description:
**Severity:** Medium · **Area:** data kernel (order-keys) · **Status:** confirmed (same root cause as #182) · **Surfaced by:** the #182 fix work

## Summary
The tie-safe `order_key` fix in #182 (commit `bc714a01`) centralized the equal-bounds problem in `src/data/orderKey.ts` and routed the *tree mutators* through new tie-safe helpers. Two more call sites compute `order_key`s between neighbors **without** going through those helpers, so they still throw `"<key> >= <key>"` (and roll back) when the bounding siblings/panels share an `order_key`:

- **`src/utils/paste.ts:281` and `:350`** — `keysBetween(insertion.lower, insertion.upper, blocks.length)`. If the insertion neighbors tie, the whole paste throws and rolls back → **lost pasted content** (a multi-block paste silently fails).
- **`src/utils/panelLayoutProjection.ts:266`** — `keyBetween(previous?.orderKey ?? null, next?.orderKey ?? null)`. Two panels with tied `order_key`s make a panel insert throw. (The other sites at `:289,:344,:434` use `null` bounds and are safe.)

## Proposed fix
Reuse the centralized tie-safe helpers added in #182 (`keysAfterIndex`/`keysBeforeIndex`/`keyAfterIndex`/`keyBeforeIndex` in `src/data/orderKey.ts`). Both sites need the ascending sibling key list + an anchor index rather than precomputed `lower`/`upper`; adapt the call sites to pass those (or add a small tie-tolerant `keyBetween` variant that widens an equal bound to the nearest distinct key).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a multi-block paste whose insertion neighbors share an `order_key` succeeds (no lost content).
- [ ] Test: panel insert between two tied panels succeeds.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

_Related: #182 (tree-mutator fix + the reusable helpers)._

title: mergeProperties array dedup is key-order-sensitive and value-lossy (fuzz-confirmed)
description:
**Severity:** Medium (reachability-gated) · **Area:** data kernel (property merge) · **Status:** confirmed by fuzzing · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (F1)

## Summary
`mergeProperties` dedups list items by `JSON.stringify(item)`, which is key-order-sensitive and value-lossy. A randomized property-merge fuzz run surfaced two concrete failures. Only bites `unsafeIdentity` object-lists with divergent key order (SRS snapshots, user "Options" lists); the built-in ref/refList/list(string) codecs are string-valued and immune.

## Where
- `src/data/mergeProperties.ts:42-57` (`unionArrays`)

## Concrete failures (minimized reproducers)
```ts
// BUG A: key-order-sensitive dedup leaves a duplicate of an equal object
mergeProperties({refs: [{id:'x', alias:'A'}]}, {refs: [{alias:'A', id:'x'}]}).refs
// => length 2 (should be 1)

// BUG C: top-level NaN and null collide on the dedup key, dropping a distinct value
mergeProperties({xs: [NaN]}, {xs: [null]}).xs   // JSON.stringify(NaN) === "null" === JSON.stringify(null)
// => length 1 (should be 2)

// BUG C2: nested undefined and null collide
mergeProperties({xs: [[undefined]]}, {xs: [[null]]}).xs   // both stringify to "[null]"
// => length 1 (should be 2)
```

## Proposed fix
Canonicalize the dedup key with sorted object keys and a value-distinguishing encoding (NaN/null/undefined must be distinct). `stableJsonValue` already exists in `txEngine` (used by `jsonValuesEqual`) and can back the key.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The three reproducers above behave correctly (dedupe the equal-but-reordered objects; keep NaN vs null vs undefined distinct).
- [ ] `mergeProperties` never mutates its inputs (already holds; keep covered).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Roam import: placeholder restore blanks a tombstoned real content block to an empty root stub
description:
**Severity:** Medium · **Area:** plugin (Roam import) · **Status:** confirmed (data-loss, 2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (C2)

## Summary
Placeholder restore blanks a tombstoned **real** content block to an empty workspace-root stub, destroying its prior content/properties/backlinks. Narrow ordering dependency, but conflicts with "preserving live user data including history is paramount".

## Where
- `src/plugins/roam-import/import.ts:1106-1135` (`ensurePlaceholderRow`; `tx.restore(id, {content:'', references:[], properties:{}})` + move-to-root)

## Scenario
A real imported block at `id = roamBlockId(ws, uid)` was user-deleted (tombstoned with content/properties/backlinks). A later export references that uid only as `((uid))` and does NOT include the real block, so `collectPlaceholderUids` registers it as a placeholder (`!knownUids.has(uid)`). `ensurePlaceholderRow`'s `createOrGet` throws `DeletedConflictError`, and the catch branch resurrects the deleted data-bearing block as a blank stub at root. If the real-block export never re-runs (or runs in the other order), the data-bearing block stays a blank stub.

## Proposed fix
Don't blank-restore a tombstone that holds real content — create a distinct placeholder id, or skip restore when the existing (deleted) row has non-empty content/properties.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: import a real block with content+properties under uid U, delete it, then import an export that references `((U))` but doesn't include U — assert the row at `roamBlockId(ws,U)` is NOT silently resurrected as an empty stub.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Throw after committed sync write but before watermark delete permanently drops that window's invalidation
description:
**Severity:** Medium · **Area:** sync observer (invalidation) · **Status:** confirmed (2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (B3)

## Summary
A throw after the committed Phase-2 sync write but before the watermark delete permanently drops that drain window's cache/handle invalidation. `collectPluginInvalidationsFromSnapshots` iterates plugin `InvalidationRule`s (a live extension point) with no try/catch; a throwing rule skips the watermark `DELETE`, and on retry the disk gate skip-stales the now-equal stamp so `handleStore.invalidate` never re-fires. UI stays stale until an unrelated change or a reload. Disk is correct; only the notification is lost.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/syncObserver/observer.ts:178-215` (commit → applyOutcome → watermark DELETE)
- `src/data/internals/syncObserver/invalidate.ts:80-87` (cache write, then `snapshotsToChangeNotification`, then `handleStore.invalidate`)
- `src/data/invalidation.ts:67` (plugin-rule loop, no try/catch)
- `src/data/internals/syncObserver/reconcile.ts:88-108` (skip-stale on equal stamp)

## Proposed fix
Wrap the plugin-rule loop in try/catch (isolate per rule), or advance the `blocks_synced_changes` watermark only after invalidation succeeds.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: a plugin `InvalidationRule` that throws once for a given id still results in that id's handle being invalidated (no permanently-stale handle).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Merge-into-descendant throws CycleError → alias-collision Merge button gets permanently stuck
description:
**Severity:** Medium · **Area:** data kernel (merge) / alias UX · **Status:** confirmed (2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A7)

## Summary
Merging a block into one of its own descendants throws `CycleError` mid-fold (clean rollback, no corruption) but the merge can never succeed — and the alias-collision "Merge into…" button drives exactly this direction automatically, so for a nested-aliased-page rename it gets **permanently stuck** (every retry fails identically with a raw error).

## Where
- `src/data/blockMerge.ts:51-56` (re-homes `from`'s children under `into` via `tx.move`)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:411-415` (cycle guard throws)
- `src/plugins/alias/AliasCollisionToast.tsx:68` (`intoId=conflictingBlockId, fromId=attemptedOn`)

## Scenario
`merge({intoId: descendant, fromId: ancestor})`: one of `from`'s children is on `into`'s ancestor path, so `tx.move` trips `IS_DESCENDANT_OF_SQL` → `CycleError`. Reachable via the natural rename flow: rename an aliased ancestor page to a descendant aliased page's alias → collision toast offers "Merge into…" with the descendant as target → merge throws → the catch surfaces the raw message and re-enables the button → stuck.

## Proposed fix
Pre-check ancestry in the merge mutators / alias path and emit a typed, user-actionable precondition error (or swap merge direction) instead of a raw `CycleError`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: merge where `into` is a descendant of `from` yields a typed precondition error (not a raw `CycleError` surfaced as "Merge failed").
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Same-tx processors re-run during undo/redo replay (no replay-skip gate)
description:
**Severity:** Medium (latent) · **Area:** data kernel (commit pipeline / undo replay) · **Status:** confirmed (probe) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A6)

## Summary
`applyRaw` is documented to drive a row to *exactly* the restored state during undo/redo replay, but the post-function same-tx processor pass runs on the replay tx too and re-derives — overriding the restore. No current production processor derives non-idempotently, so no live data loss, but the replay contract has a hole any future value-deriving same-tx processor falls into.

## Where
- `src/data/internals/commitPipeline.ts:277-300` (same-tx pass runs on ANY tx, including replay)
- `src/data/repo.ts` `_replay` → `_runAndDispatch` → `runTx` (same `sameTxProcessors` registry)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:603-622` (`applyRaw` doc: "drive the row to exactly target")

## Scenario (probe-proven)
Register a same-tx processor on `content` that appends `'!'`. Seed `content='orig'`; update → `'changed'` → processor → `'changed!'`. Undo: `_replay applyRaw` writes `content='orig'`, which is a content change in the replay tx → the same-tx pass fires again → `'orig!'`, NOT the intended `'orig'`. Production processors (`normalizeReferences`, alias-sync) are idempotent so no live corruption today.

## Proposed fix
Skip the same-tx processor pass on `_replay` (or run `applyRaw` outside it), and pin the invariant with a test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: undo/redo replay does not re-run a value-deriving same-tx processor (restore = exact).
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Cross-workspace undo: cmd-Z reverts/uploads an edit in an unopened workspace
description:
**Severity:** Medium · **Area:** data kernel (undo) · **Status:** confirmed (2 verifiers) · **Audit:** `docs/correctness-audit-2026-06-18.md` (A5)

## Summary
Undo stacks are keyed only by `ChangeScope`, not by workspace, and a workspace switch is in-place (no reload, no stack clear). So `cmd-Z` after switching workspaces reverts — and uploads — an edit in a workspace you are no longer looking at. Violates the project rule "don't touch unopened workspaces".

## Where
- `src/data/internals/undoManager.ts:52` (`undoStacks` keyed by scope; `UndoEntry` has no `workspaceId`)
- `src/data/repo.ts:971,988` (`undo()`/`redo()` take no workspace arg)
- `src/components/workspace/WorkspaceSwitcher.tsx:60-66` (in-place switch, no `undoManager.clear()`)
- `src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:649,669,703` (`applyRaw` pins the write to the snapshot row's workspace)

## Scenario
Edit block in workspace A (entry pushed to the global `BlockDefault` stack) → switch to workspace B → `cmd-Z` (global action, `defaultShortcuts.ts:345`) pops the A entry and `_replay` drives the A row to `before`, pinned to A's workspace. You see nothing change in B; an edit in an unopened workspace was reverted and uploaded.

### A5b (same root cause)
If B is a viewer-role workspace, `repo.setReadOnly(true)` makes that same `cmd-Z` spuriously `ReadOnlyError` on your editable-A entry — so you **cannot** undo legitimate A edits while viewing B. Either branch is wrong.

## Proposed fix
Add `workspaceId` to `UndoEntry` and scope `undo()`/`redo()` to the active workspace (skip/ignore entries from other workspaces), or clear the stacks on workspace switch. Resolve read-only against the entry's workspace, not the active one.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test: edit in ws-A, `setActiveWorkspaceId('ws-B')`, `undo()` → the ws-A block is NOT mutated.
- [ ] Test: undo of an editable-A entry is not blocked by viewing a read-only B.
- [ ] `yarn run check` green.

title: Perf audit 2026-06: heavy renderer libs (react-player, react-google-maps) in the eager boot graph - add first React.lazy boundary
description:
## Locations
- `src/extensions/staticAppExtensions.ts:28-51` (eager plugin graph)
- `src/plugins/video-player/VideoPlayerRenderer.tsx:1` — `import ReactPlayer from 'react-player'`
- `src/plugins/geo/.../MapView.tsx:26` — `@vis.gl/react-google-maps`, via `geoContentDecorator.tsx:24`

## Problem
The build uses `preserveModules:true` (`vite.config.ts:138`), emitting standalone modules with no app-level bundling. The boot path eagerly evaluates the full plugin import graph (`AppRuntimeProvider.tsx:57` and `workspaceBootstrap.ts:59` both call `staticAppExtensions({repo})`). Two plugins pull large libs into the eager graph via direct static imports. The `systemToggle` only gates **activation** of facet contributions, not whether the module code loads. The app uses zero `React.lazy` and only 2 real dynamic `import()` calls anywhere.

## Why it matters
`dist/index.html` modulepreloads both libs, so they are fetched/parsed/evaluated on every cold start even with geo/video disabled and even when the graph has no Place/Map/video blocks (the common case).

Severity: verified, adjusted high → **medium**, with corrected size claims: `@vis.gl/react-google-maps/dist/index.modern.js` is ~91 KB raw / ~22 KB gz (NOT "1.2 MB" — that was source-on-disk incl. all formats + sourcemaps). react-player v3.4.0 is ~21.6 KB raw / ~5 KB gz across 8 modules; its heavy media deps (hls.js/dashjs) are already lazily imported and NOT in the startup preload graph. Combined on-the-wire cost ~27 KB gz — real, but an order of magnitude smaller than originally claimed.

## Fix (small–medium)
Wrap `VideoPlayerRenderer` and `MapView` in `React.lazy(() => import(...))` behind a `Suspense` boundary (none exists in these files today). The facet contribution (`blockRenderersFacet` / `blockContentDecoratorsFacet`) stores a component reference and only instantiates on matching render, so a lazy wrapper is a valid contribution; plugin entry + facet registration stay eager and cheap. Establishes the codebase's first lazy-boundary pattern.

## Effort
Small–medium.

## Note
The dominant cold-start cost is the unbundled `minify:false` build shipping ~11.7 MB raw / ~2.4 MB gz across 1,152 preloaded modules; `@babel/standalone` is the single biggest offender (separate issue), and `minify:false` itself is tracked in the bundle/build grab-bag.

title: Perf audit 2026-06: ~65-75 sequential single-statement DB worker round-trips block first paint on cold start
description:
## Location
`src/data/repoProvider.ts:251-340`

## Problem
`initializePowerSyncDb` runs all client DDL as individually-awaited `execute()` calls: 2 PRAGMAs (`:280-281`), blocks/blocks_synced tables + indexes (`:284-292`), `ensureBlockUserUpdatedAtColumn` (`:297`, itself 2 PRAGMA round-trips every boot), workspaces/members + `ensureWorkspaceE2eeColumns` (`:300-306`), then `for (const stmt of CLIENT_SCHEMA_STATEMENTS) await powerSyncDb.execute(stmt)` (`:314-316`). `CLIENT_SCHEMA_STATEMENTS` has ~44 source entries; `withTriggerRecreate` (`clientSchema.ts:1156-1160`) expands each of ~21 triggers into DROP + CREATE, yielding ~65 statements in the loop alone, ~75 total round-trips. The PowerSync DB runs in a Web Worker accessed via a Comlink proxy and `execute()` runs exactly one statement per call; `RepoProvider` suspends on `initRepo` (`repo.tsx:61`) which awaits the entire init before first paint. Idempotent `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` statements still execute and round-trip on warm starts.

## Why it matters
Runs on every cold start / hard reload for every user. With a small fleet reloading continuously across deploys, the serialized message latency is paid repeatedly before React can resolve the first suspended render.

Severity: verified, adjusted high → **medium** — the cited ~65–200 ms rests on a 1–3 ms/round-trip estimate that is **unverified** for in-process Web Worker `postMessage` (often sub-ms, though structured-clone + OPFS I/O contention can push it higher). A fixed serialized tax worth removing, magnitude unmeasured.

## Fix (medium)
Join the parameterless DDL/PRAGMA/trigger statements into one (or a few) `;`-separated SQL strings and run each in a single `execute()`.
**Verified safe:** `WASQLiteDB.executeRaw` iterates `api.statements(db, sql)` and steps through ALL statements when no bindings are passed (`if (bindings) break`), so a multi-statement parameterless string runs fully in one round-trip; all `CLIENT_SCHEMA_STATEMENTS` are literal SQL with zero bind params. Collapses ~65 → ~3–4 round-trips. Keep the param'd/probe calls (`getOptional` backfill markers, deferred ANALYZE) separate, and preserve the DROP-then-CREATE ordering `withTriggerRecreate` already produces.

## Effort
Medium.

## Related
- #91 (parallel reads for cold-start contention — different mechanism, same boot path)
- #150 (cold-start query re-resolve storm)
- Companion candidate: bootstrap get-or-create page writes run strictly sequentially (`workspaceBootstrap.ts:154-167`) — see the low-priority misc grab-bag.

title: Perf audit 2026-06: tx.update always rewrites properties_json/references_json, firing alias/type triggers on content-only edits
description:
## Location
`src/data/internals/txEngine.ts:375` (also `restore()` at `:345`)

## Problem
`update()` builds a fixed wide SET clause regardless of which patch fields changed:
```sql
UPDATE blocks SET content=?, references_json=?, properties_json=?, updated_at=?, user_updated_at=?, updated_by=?
```
SQLite's `AFTER UPDATE OF properties_json` triggers fire whenever the column appears in the SET list, **even when the assigned value is byte-identical** (verified via a `node:sqlite` probe: a wide UPDATE re-assigning the same value fires; a narrow content-only UPDATE does not). So every content edit needlessly fires `blocks_alias_update` (`clientSchema.ts:762`: DELETE + `json_each(properties_json,'$.alias')`) and `blocks_type_update` (`clientSchema.ts:863`), plus re-serializes both JSON blobs.

## Why it matters
Runs on the hottest write path — `core.setContent` (`mutators.ts:138-146`) calls `tx.update(id, {content})` with no properties/references — i.e. every debounced keystroke commit, plus paste, find-replace, block-tagging, geo. The same wide-SET upsert on sync-apply (`syncObserver/materialize.ts:61`) amplifies it across initial-sync / bulk-import of tens of thousands of rows.

Severity: verified, adjusted high → **medium** (per-edit waste is one PK-keyed DELETE + a single-row `json_each` scan + two JSON serializations — cheap per keystroke, but compounds on every commit and amplifies during bulk sync/import).

⚠️ The test claiming this is safe (`clientSchema.test.ts:840`) passes for the wrong reason: the harness `updateBlock` (`:192`) emits a narrow `UPDATE blocks SET content=?`, not the engine's wide SQL — false confidence.

## Fix (small)
Build the SET clause dynamically — include `content=?` only when `patch.content!==undefined`, `properties_json=?` only when `patch.properties!==undefined`, `references_json=?` only when `patch.references!==undefined` (always include metadata stamps). `updatePatchChangesBlock` (`txEngine.ts:98-113`) already inspects each field.

**Verified safe:** the upload trigger (`clientSchema.ts:578-595`) diffs values via `OLD.x IS NOT NEW.x`, not the SET list, so the upload envelope is byte-identical before/after; FTS gates on `content` (an inverse improvement for property-only edits); history/`recordWrite` takes JS before/after objects independent of the SET clause. Add a test that drives the change through the **real engine SQL** (not the narrow harness) and asserts `block_aliases` is untouched on a content-only edit.

## Effort
Small.

## Related
- Narrowing the SET clause also shrinks the per-write `row_events` snapshot (#132) and reduces the redundant work compounded by `normalizeReferences`.
- Adjacent: #73 (properties_json/references_json → JSONB).

title: Perf audit 2026-06: lodash monolithic barrel (~91 KB gz) preloaded for only 4 functions
description:
## Summary
The `lodash` main entry is a non-tree-shakable CommonJS module; the unbundled build emits and modulepreloads the whole thing (~91 KB gz) on every cold start, though only 4 functions are used.

## Locations
7 source files import from `'lodash'`:
- `src/context/repo.tsx:9`
- `src/plugins/left-sidebar/shortcuts.ts:1`
- `src/data/stateBlocks.ts:14`
- `src/plugins/command-palette/CommandPalette.tsx:15`
- `src/components/BlockEditor.tsx:11`
- `src/hooks/block.ts:28`
- `src/data/internals/handleStore.ts:27`

## Problem
Collectively only `debounce`, `groupBy`, `isEqual`, and `memoize` are used. `lodash` main is a single monolithic CJS module that is not tree-shakable, so the unbundled build emits the whole `node_modules/lodash/lodash.js` (489,957 bytes raw / ~91 KB gz) and modulepreloads it (`dist/index.html:163`). `isEqual` is the default structural-diff equality in `handleStore` (`handleStore.ts:508`) and the block-hook deep equality (`hooks/block.ts:66`) — both core query-dedup paths — so it loads on every startup.

## Fix (small)
Switch imports to `lodash-es` (drop-in; named-import syntax unchanged) or per-method default imports (`import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'`). `lodash-es` is the lowest-churn option.

## Realistic saving (corrected)
Not "a few KB" — the dependency closure of these 4 functions is ~99,597 bytes raw / ~20 KB gz. Realized saving is ~390 KB raw / ~71 KB gz — still large.

## Effort
Small.
