title: Perf audit 2026-06: @babel/standalone (~0.8 MB gz) eagerly preloaded into the startup critical path
description:
## Summary
`@babel/standalone` is statically imported at module top-level and ends up modulepreloaded on every cold start for every user. Lazy-importing it is necessary but **not sufficient** — see the complication below: the current fleet recompiles its custom extensions on every startup, so Babel must also be backed by a **persistent compile cache** before its cost actually leaves the common path.

## Location
`src/extensions/compileExtensionModule.ts:1` — `import * as Babel from '@babel/standalone'`

## Problem
Line 1 is a static `import * as Babel`. It is reachable from the boot graph: `main.tsx:6` → `App.tsx:11` (`AppRuntimeProvider`) → `AppRuntimeProvider.tsx:3` (dynamicExtensions) → `dynamicExtensions.ts:2` (`compileExtensionModule`). `Babel.transform` is only ever called inside the async `defaultCompileViaBabelBlob` (`compileExtensionModule.ts:76`), which runs when a block extension is compiled.

## Why it matters (verified against the prod build)
`dist/index.html` contains `<link rel="modulepreload" crossorigin href="/node_modules/@babel/standalone/babel.js">`. `babel.js` is 4,795,957 bytes raw / 846,710 bytes gz — ~39% of the ~11.7 MB raw startup JS payload — fetched, parsed, and evaluated on every cold load. The build uses `preserveModules:true` + `minify:false` (`vite.config.ts`), so there is no tree-shaking escape hatch; the static edge puts `babel.js` directly into the eager preload set.

## ⚠️ Complication — the current fleet recompiles every startup (rescoped after review)
The naive fix (move the import to a dynamic `await import(...)`) only helps users who have **no enabled custom extensions**. That is **not** the current fleet:

- The compile cache in `compileExtensionModule.ts:40-43` is a process-wide **in-memory singleton** ("bounded only by ... this session") — it is **empty on every cold start / reload**.
- `dynamicExtensionsExtension` (`dynamicExtensions.ts`) walks every `type: 'extension'` block and compiles each **enabled** one via Babel at workspace load.
- There is **no persistent (cross-reload) cache** today.

So every user with ≥1 enabled custom extension — currently the entire ~2-user fleet — recompiles via Babel on **every** startup. For them, lazy-importing Babel alone does not remove the cost: Babel still loads (just later in boot), and a post-boot dynamic import may even *delay* extension readiness versus today's preload.

## Proper fix (two parts; the cache is the load-bearing one)
1. **Persistent compile cache (required).** Persist the transpiled output (the `transpiled` JS string produced at `compileExtensionModule.ts:76-79`) keyed by `contentHash` — already computed by `hashContent` and salted by `COMPILER_VERSION` (`:67-73`), so a transform-config bump auto-invalidates. Store in IndexedDB (preferred over localStorage for code blobs / size). On boot, a cache hit builds the module from the cached JS via the existing blob-URL path **without loading Babel**. Only a miss (first-ever compile, or the extension's source changed) loads Babel. Needs bounding / eviction (the in-memory cache already flags eviction as a follow-up).
2. **Lazy-load Babel.** `const Babel = await import('@babel/standalone')` inside `defaultCompileViaBabelBlob`, so Babel is fetched/evaluated only on a cache miss.

With both, `babel.js` leaves the eager preload set **and** is invoked only when an extension's source actually changes (rare) — so even users with custom extensions stop paying it every startup.

## Effort
Medium. (The lazy import is a one-liner; the persistent, bounded, hash-keyed cache is the real work.)

## Related
- #67 — extension trust / content-hash re-approval on source change. A persistent cache keyed on the exact source hash recompiles whenever the source changes, so it is compatible with that trust model — but the cache must not become a path that serves output for unapproved source. Coordinate with #67.
- The existing in-memory cache (`compileExtensionModule.ts`) is the natural place to add the L3 persistent layer.

---
_From the 2026-06 performance audit (`docs/perf-audit/performance-audit-report.md`, finding 1, verified). Rescoped after review: lazy-load must be paired with a persistent compile cache._

title: Class B: per-column patch can desync derived refs from source content (sync gate) — detect first, structural fix if it recurs
description:
## Summary

Track the potential structural fix for **class B** (per-column patches desyncing derived data from its source) in the sync reconcile gate. **Decision for now: start with detection (L3 + L5) and only build a gate change if detection shows this recurs.** Captured from the data-integrity design (`docs/data-integrity-defense.html`, decision D1).

## The gap

The reconcile gate is whole-row LWW on `updated_at` (`src/data/internals/syncObserver/reconcile.ts:88`). It has no notion that a given `references_json` was *derived from a specific content version*. So a **references-only patch** from a sync-lagged (or parallel) client can win the `references_json` column carrying refs computed from **stale content**, independently of the content no-clobber — the "matrix `[[…]]` resurrection" incident shape (class B).

## Options (if/when we act)

- **(a) Tie derived columns to a content version** — stamp `references_json` writes with the `updated_at` of the content they were derived from; reject a references apply whose basis is older than the local content. Strongest, but adds a column/semantic to the gate.
- **(b) Re-derive on apply** — when applying a references-only staging row, re-run the projection locally instead of trusting incoming refs. Moves derivation to the consumer; cost on the sync path.
- **(c) Accept + detect (current decision)** — leave the gate; rely on the L3 client consistency eval and the L5 server anomaly detector to surface a desync after the fact, and the L6 re-pointer/recovery harness to fix it.

## Trigger to revisit

Promote to (a) or (b) if the L3/L5 detectors show class-B desync **recurring** (not a one-off). Until then this is a design record, not active work.

## References

- Design doc: `docs/data-integrity-defense.html` (decision D1; failure class B; invariants R1/R3).
- Gate: `src/data/internals/syncObserver/reconcile.ts`.
- Derivation: `src/plugins/references/referencesProcessor.ts`.

title: Dangling wikilink refs on page delete: inline (Roam) vs re-point-on-rebind vs leave-lazy
description:
## Summary

Decide how dangling **wikilink** (`[[page]]`) references should behave when their target page is deleted (and later re-created or the alias re-assigned). Three candidate models: **inline-to-text (Roam-style)**, **re-point-on-rebind**, or **leave-lazy + recovery tool** (current behavior). Captured from a data-integrity design discussion; relates to invariant **R7** in `docs/data-integrity-defense.html`.

## Current behavior

A wikilink ref stores the target id the alias resolved to **at parse time**, and nothing re-resolves it when the target later changes. The references processor only re-parses a block when *that block's own* `content`/`properties` change; there is no "target X deleted/renamed → re-parse its referrers" path. `block_aliases` (what `aliasLookup` reads) excludes `deleted=1` rows (`src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:139`).

Trace — page `P` (alias `"page"`, id `oldId`), referenced via `[[page]]` in blocks `B1…Bn`:

1. **Delete `P`** → soft-deleted, its `block_aliases` row dropped. The inline-deleted-block-refs processor does **not** touch `B1…Bn` (those are wikilinks, `alias ≠ id`, not `((id))` block-refs). `B1…Bn` keep pointing at `oldId` → **n dangling wikilink refs at once**.
2. **Re-create / re-assign the alias**:
   - If `P` was a **real page** (had content/children/props), its tombstone fails the restorable-stub predicate (`src/data/targets.ts:294`), so the deterministic seat is **not** reused — the new "page" gets a **different id**. `B1…Bn` still store `oldId`, stay dangling, and do **not** become backlinks of the new page. They re-point only **lazily, per-block**, when each `Bi` is next edited (re-parse → `aliasLookup` → new id).
   - If `P` was a **pristine stub** (auto-created by `[[page]]`, never edited), the seat **is** reused on restore (`newId == oldId`), so the refs heal automatically.

So for a real, heavily-linked page, **delete → recreate / reassign does not transfer backlinks**; the old refs go dangling and migrate one block at a time as referrers are edited.

## Renderer bug (orthogonal, fix regardless)

A dangling wikilink today renders as a **normal clickable link pointing at the deleted id** — there is no "broken / create-page" state (`src/plugins/references/markdown/wikilinks/Wikilink.tsx:42-49`). A live-looking link to a tombstone is the worst of the options and should change independent of the decision below.

## Options

**A — Inline-to-text on delete (Roam-style).** Replace `[[page]]` with the display text in every referrer, atomically with the delete (analogous to the existing block-ref inline, `src/plugins/references/inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor.ts`).
- ✅ Clean index (R7 baseline ≈ 0, no "deleted a popular page → dangling spike"); one uniform "a deleted mark inlines to its displayed text" rule.
- ❌ **Lossy and not symmetric with the block-ref case.** A block-ref target is a *specific instance*, gone and unrecoverable on delete → inlining *preserves* otherwise-lost content. An alias is a *rebindable name* whose relationship is *recoverable* (recreate the page / reassign the alias) → inlining *destroys* a recoverable relationship; re-create "page" later and the inlined blocks never re-link.
- ❌ Fights **undelete**: rewriting n referrers to plain text means a later undelete of the page does not restore the links.
- ❌ **Blast radius**: aliases are far more numerous than block-refs; deleting a popular page rewrites hundreds of referrers — heavy same-tx delete, or a sync-queue flood if done post-commit.

**B — Re-point on rebind (preferred).** When a live block claims an alias (create page / assign alias), eagerly re-point the dangling wikilink refs whose alias text matches. The inverse of inlining: reconnect links when a target reappears instead of killing them when it dies.
- ✅ Same "no lingering dangling" outcome as A, but **no data loss**; fixes "backlinks don't transfer on delete+recreate"; dangling becomes truly transient.
- ✅ Structurally the merge-survivor re-pointer in `scripts/dangling-refs/`, promoted from a recovery script to an event-driven pass.
- ❌ A re-bind write pass over referrers (amplification on rebind rather than on delete); needs an alias-claim event/trigger that doesn't exist today.

**C — Leave lazy + recovery tool (current).** Keep refs dangling, re-point lazily per-block on next edit; provide the `scripts/dangling-refs/` re-pointer for bulk cleanup.
- ✅ Cheapest; lowest instantaneous write amplification; preserves links.
- ❌ Backlinks don't transfer until each referrer is edited; dangling persists; needs the renderer fix to not look broken.

## Recommendation (for discussion)

Lean **B (re-point on rebind)** + the renderer fix, with **C** as the no-effort interim (current behavior + the existing re-pointer script). Avoid **A**: for aliases it's the most lossy option and conflicts with soft-delete/undelete and the "preserve the link graph" principle. This is partly a product-taste call — if the desired model is "delete is final, Roam-style," A is internally consistent.

## References

- Design doc: `docs/data-integrity-defense.html` (invariant R7 — dangling refs).
- Alias seat resolution / restorable-stub reuse: `src/data/targets.ts:294-342`.
- Block-ref inline precedent: `src/plugins/references/inlineDeletedBlockRefsProcessor.ts`.
- Renderer: `src/plugins/references/markdown/wikilinks/Wikilink.tsx`.
- Recovery re-pointer shape: `scripts/dangling-refs/`.

title: Native declarative leader key support in km keyboard bindings
description:
Claude:

  What works today, and how

  Keyboard dispatch lives in src/shortcuts/HotkeyReconciler.tsx +
  src/shortcuts/resolve.ts:

  - Each installable binding gets its own tinykeys matcher (makeMatcher, line ~729),
  created with createKeybindingsHandler(bindingMap, { ignore: () => false }). The
  matcher's callback does not run the handler — it just records the action into 
  completedRef when its chord completes on the current event.
  - A single keydown/keyup coordinator (dispatchPhase, ~line 365) feeds the event to
  every matcher, then reads back the completed list — "the bindings whose chord
  completed on this event" — and calls resolve(...) to order them and dispatch a
  single winner.
  - resolve → compareContexts (resolve.ts:103) orders candidates by exactly three
  keys: tier (modal > global > scoped) → priority ('low' | 'default' | 'high') →
  activation recency (order.indexOf into the active-contexts map).

  The gap

  compareContexts has no notion of chord length / specificity, and the per-binding 
  matcher split defeats tinykeys' own longest-match. Because d and g d are separate
  tinykeys instances, tinykeys never sees them as competing chords in one keymap — so
  when you press g then d, both the d matcher and the g d matcher complete on the d
  keydown and both land in completed. The coordinator then picks between them using
  only context tier/priority/recency. A longer, more specific chord that completed on
  the same event has no inherent advantage over a single key.

  Consequence: to make g d (goto) beat bare d (e.g. an editor/agenda "set deadline"),
  there is no declarative lever. The author must:
  1. put the sequence in a higher-tier or higher-priority context than the single
  key, and
  2. when those are equal (both 'high', since priority caps at three levels), fall
  back to activation/registration order as the only remaining tiebreaker.
  
  That order-dependence is the hacky part — correctness hinges on which
  shortcutSurfaceActivation was registered last, which is invisible at the call site
  and silently breaks if contributions are reordered.

  Concrete issues the absence introduces

  1. Leader sequences silently lose to their own second key. g d ties with bare d
  and, absent context gymnastics, the single key wins — the leader appears "dead."
  Observed directly.
  2. No way to declare a leader at all. There's no leader/prefix concept; authors
  reverse-engineer the precedence comparator and lean on recency. Fragile and
  non-obvious.
  3. First-key collisions need the same hack. Any X + X y pair (e.g. Space = preview
  vs Space s = schedule) has the same shape and the same order-dependent workaround.
  4. Double-dispatch risk. Since both chords complete, anything that reads completed
  (telemetry, future "did any binding fire?" gates) sees two winners for one
  keystroke.
  5. Related: GLOBAL bare/sequence bindings fire while typing. shouldHandleEvent
  (HotkeyReconciler) returns true if any active context's eventFilter matches, and
  EDIT_MODE_CM's filter (defaultContexts.ts:55) returns true whenever focus is in a
  .cm-editor. That short-circuits the default skip-while-typing filter for all active
  contexts, so a GLOBAL g a / Space c matches a literal "ga" / " c" typed into a
  block. The only workarounds are moving the binding to NORMAL_MODE (breaks if its
  second key is a vim command, per #1) or a handler-level document.activeElement
  guard.

  What to implement

  Pick any of these, roughly increasing in scope:

  - (Minimal) Chord-specificity tiebreaker. Before/within compareContexts, when
  multiple candidates completed on the same event, prefer the longest chord (most
  keys), then fall back to the existing tier/priority/recency. This alone makes g d
  beat d with zero context tricks — purely declarative defaultBinding: { keys: 'g d' 
  }.
  - (Better) Sequence-aware coordinator with prefix suppression. Track, across all
  installed bindings, whether the current key is a live prefix of any longer
  installed chord. If so, defer/suppress the shorter completion until the sequence
  either completes or aborts (timeout / non-matching next key → "exit leader,"
  cleanly, dispatching nothing). This restores real leader semantics and removes the
  double-complete. Could be a single shared tinykeys keymap, or a small prefix-trie
  the coordinator consults.
  - (Declarative sugar) A leader concept. e.g. register leader: 'g' (or infer leaders
  from the installed chord set) so authors just declare g a, g d and get proper
  "press g → only g-prefixed bindings live; any non-match exits" behavior for free.
  - (Orthogonal fix) Scope eventFilter to its own context. shouldHandleEvent should
  let a context's eventFilter govern only that context's candidates, not bless every
  active context's candidates. Then EDIT_MODE_CM matching the target wouldn't let
  GLOBAL bindings fire while typing — removing the need for per-action editor guards
  (issue #5).

Appendix: our current workaround (a concrete example of the hack)
  
  We have three global-ish bindings that hit every gap above: g a (open agenda), g d
  (open daily note), Space c (quick-capture). Here's the contortion they forced, in a
  runtime extension (agent-extensions/agenda/):

  1. Space c → moved from GLOBAL to NORMAL_MODE. Originally GLOBAL so it works from
  any pane. But GLOBAL + the EDIT_MODE_CM eventFilter short-circuit (issue #5) meant
  typing " can…" into a block fired capture. Moving it to NORMAL_MODE fixed the
  typing-fire only because Space isn't a vim command — nothing binds bare Space in
  NORMAL_MODE to tie with, so the Space c sequence wins uncontested.
  2. g a / g d could not use the same move. In NORMAL_MODE the second keys a and d
  are vim append / delete. Per issue #1, g a ties with bare a and the single key wins
  — so g a just did vim-append, g d just deleted. So we couldn't put them in
  NORMAL_MODE at all.
  3. We hand-rolled a priority: 'high' "leader" context (AGENDA_LEADER_CONTEXT) plus
  a shortcutSurfaceActivation that activates it on any focused block outside edit 
  mode. 'high' outranks NORMAL_MODE's 'default', so g a/g d beat bare vim a/d; gating
  activation on !inEditMode keeps them from firing while typing. This is essentially
  re-deriving "normal-mode but wins ties," by hand, per extension.
  4. For g d inside our own agenda we hit the priority ceiling. Our agenda surface
  also binds bare d (set deadline) at priority: 'high' — so g d (leader, high) and d
  (agenda, high) tie at the top priority level. Priority maxes at three values, so
  there was no level left to outrank it. The only remaining tiebreaker is activation 
  recency — so we deliberately register the leader activation after the agenda 
  activation in the extension's contribution array, relying on compareContexts's
  order.indexOf to make the leader "more recent" and win. Correctness now depends on
  the ordering of two shortcutSurfaceActivationsFacet.of(...) lines, documented only
  by a comment that says "keep this order." That's the line that should never have to
  exist.

  Net: ~40 lines across a custom context, a custom activation, a priority hack, and
  an order-of-registration dependency — to express what should be defaultBinding: { 
  keys: 'g d' } winning over d because it's the longer chord. The minimal-fix
  (chord-specificity tiebreaker) would collapse all of #2–#4 to nothing, and scoping
  eventFilter (issue #5) would remove #1.

title: Cold-start query re-resolve storm for users with a disabled data-extension plugin
description:
## Summary
After the query-registry-epoch rework (#147), cold start re-resolves the entire visible block tree's kernel queries (`subtree`/`children`/`childIds`/…) **once** for any user who has **disabled a data-extension plugin**. Users with all data-ext plugins enabled are unaffected (their cold-start swap is purely additive → no epoch bump).

## Root cause
A query handle is keyed by a global `queryEpoch` (`src/data/repo.ts`). `swapQueries` bumps the epoch on a REPLACE or REMOVE, but **not** on a purely-additive swap. Cold start runs two registry swaps while the block tree is mounted:

1. **bootstrap** — `initRepo` in `src/context/repo.tsx` calls `resolveFacetRuntimeSync(staticDataExtensions, …)`, which is **toggle-blind** (`src/facets/facet.ts`): it registers *every* data-extension plugin's queries, ignoring per-workspace enable/disable overrides (it runs with `workspaceId: null`).
2. **base** — `src/extensions/AppRuntimeProvider.tsx` calls `resolveAppRuntimeSync(staticAppExtensions, {overrides, …})`, which is **toggle-aware**: it prunes disabled non-essential plugins.

For a user who disabled e.g. `todo` or `grouped-backlinks`, that plugin's query is present after the bootstrap swap and **absent** after the base swap → a REMOVE → epoch bump. Blocks resolve their kernel-query handles at the bootstrap epoch (child effects run before the provider's base effect), so the bump re-keys them and the next render (the async dynamic-plugin swap, which changes the runtime context) re-resolves the whole visible tree.

This is also a regression vs the pre-epoch per-name scheme, which only bumped the removed query's own generation and left unrelated kernel handles intact.

## Why it wasn't fixed in #147
The clean fix is to make bootstrap registration toggle-aware so bootstrap and base agree (no REMOVE). But bootstrap runs before the workspace/overrides are known (toggles are per-workspace), so it can't evaluate them. This is an init-sequencing change, separate from the query-epoch mechanism (which is correct). It is documented as a known limitation in the `swapQueries` / `queryEpoch` doc comments in `src/data/repo.ts`.

## Options
- **Gate first block-resolve on the toggle-aware base runtime being applied to the repo** — so blocks first resolve at the base epoch and the bootstrap→base REMOVE happens before any handle exists (harmless). Costs ~a frame of first-paint delay.
- **Make the bootstrap data-layer registration toggle-aware** once the workspace/overrides are resolvable (may require deferring/restructuring the bootstrap swap).
- **Accept it** as a one-time cold-start cost for the subset of users who disable a plugin (current state, documented).

## Impact
- One-time, cold-start only.
- Only affects users who've disabled ≥1 data-extension plugin.
- Magnitude: re-resolve the visible tree's kernel queries once (+ SQLite-connection contention with cold-start reprojection).

title: Agent cli loses connection to live tab
description:
Claude that is driving extension development through yarn agent bridge periodically loses the connection to the live tab (clients: []) and gets stuck until I refresh the tab manually

Claude's summary:

When driving the app via the agent CLI (yarn agent 
  <eval|run-action|install-extension|reload|…>, and kmcli), the CLI intermittently
  starts failing with:

  Agent token is not registered with the local bridge. Open or focus the app tab for
  the
  same workspace, then retry; if needed, run `yarn agent connect` to pair a fresh
  token.
  Common causes: the bridge restarted, the app tab disconnected or idled out, the
  token was
  revoked, or the CLI is using a token/profile from another workspace or browser
  profile.
  
  Once this state is hit, every subsequent CLI command fails the same way until the
  app tab is manually refocused (or yarn agent connect is re-run). The bridge does
  not re-pair on its own, even though the app tab is still open and the same
  workspace is loaded.

  Observed triggers (in rough order of reliability)

  1. Full-page reload of the app — calling window.location.reload() (e.g. via yarn 
  agent eval 'window.location.reload()', which I use to force a fresh
  extension/stylesheet load) reliably drops the token, and it does not come back
  without manual refocus. This is the most reproducible trigger.
  2. App tab losing focus / idling — after the tab has been backgrounded for a while,
  the token appears to expire ("idled out"), and the next CLI command fails.
  3. Occasionally mid-session with no obvious cause (possibly a bridge restart).

  Expected behavior   

  - The CLI ↔ bridge pairing should survive a normal app reload, OR the CLI should
  transparently re-pair (retry/reconnect) instead of hard-failing.
  - If the token genuinely expires on idle, the CLI should attempt an automatic
  re-pair before erroring, rather than requiring the human to physically focus the
  browser/app tab.

  Impact

  This is painful for headless / agent-driven workflows (and for Claude Code /
  scripted automation specifically): a single reload or a stretch of the tab being
  unfocused breaks the whole session, and recovery requires a human to focus the app
  tab — which defeats unattended/automated use. During extension development it's
  especially disruptive because forcing a clean stylesheet/contribution reload
  (window.location.reload()) is exactly the operation that kills the connection.

  Environment

  - Bridge: the agent-runtime plugin (the agent-runtime.bridge app-effect).
  - CLI: packages/agent-cli (yarn agent …).
  - App running in a browser tab (token tied to the focused/active app tab +
  workspace).
  - macOS.

  Notes / questions for triage

  - Is the token bound to the tab's visibility/focus state or a heartbeat that pauses
  when the tab is backgrounded? If so, a keepalive that survives visibilitychange
  would help.
  - Could the CLI auto-run the equivalent of yarn agent connect (re-pair) on a token 
  not registered error and retry once, instead of failing?
  - Could the token survive window.location.reload() (e.g. persisted in storage and
  re-claimed on app boot)?

title: Audit D2: move App.tsx's five-layer module-level bootstrap out of the render path
description:
## Problem

430 of `App.tsx`'s 594 lines are a module-level bootstrap pipeline spanning five layers, executed from the render path:

- six-way workspace resolution incl. a Supabase RLS probe (lines 102-180);
- E2EE entry-gate orchestration — the *read-inputs* half lives here while the *decide* half lives in `sync/keys/workspaceAccess.ts`, one concern split across layers (lines 263-295);
- bootstrap writes (lines 327-344);
- the landing-runtime cache (lines 197-231 — carries the toggle-blind walker bug fixed in #134);
- URL→layout application;
- an LRU promise cache + `navigationVersion` bust protocol that exists only because all of the above is one promise consumed via React `use()`.

## Proposal

Split at the three comment-fenced phase boundaries:

1. `bootstrap/resolveWorkspace.ts` — pure async; already has the right signature.
2. `resolveWorkspaceEntry()` moved next to `decideWorkspaceEntry` in `sync/keys` — reunites the E2EE gate's read and decide halves.
3. `bootstrap/workspaceBootstrap.ts` for the write phase — testable without rendering.

Keep the phase **ordering** in one composing function: the gate-before-writes and seedTutorial-before-parseReferences constraints are currently encoded only in comments.

## Payoff

Bootstrap becomes testable without rendering; the LRU/`navigationVersion` machinery can shrink once the pipeline isn't one opaque promise.

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding D2 (god-objects lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit D1: Repo bundles four separable engines — split idle jobs, type-tagger, facet bridge, RAISE protocol
description:
## Problem

`Repo` bundles four separable engines (2,446 lines, 118 referencing files), each already communicating with the rest through a narrow surface:

1. **Facet-registry bridge** (~400 lines): rebuild steps, bucket mirror, 5 listener channels.
2. **Idle maintenance jobs** — reprojection, workspace backfills, reconcile rescans — with the identical requestIdleCallback-with-2s-timeout scheduler hand-rolled **three times** (byte-identical `globalThis` casts at lines 1811/1877/1969), plus three pending sets, three drain loops, and 21 marker-SQL references. The duplication is undersold: `src/utils/scheduleIdle.ts` already exists with a near-verbatim docstring and 5 users — repo.ts just doesn't use it.
3. **Type-tagging API** (4 variants, lines ~2000-2185).
4. **SQLite RAISE-protocol parsing** (hex codec, lines 428-494) whose format contract spans two files (`repo.ts` + `clientSchema.ts`) with no shared constant.

## Proposal — dependency order

- **(a)** `internals/idleMarkerJobs.ts` — a `OneShotWorkspaceJob` owning scheduler (reusing `utils/scheduleIdle`) + pending-set drain + marker persistence. The next one-time migration becomes a job registration — they keep arriving (the reconcile rescan is from commit bbc7bffa).
- **(b)** `data/typeTagger.ts`, with Repo keeping spec-pinned delegating methods.
- **(c)** Extract the facet bridge — pairs with the runtime-swap compensation removal in #136.
- **(d)** One owner module for the RAISE protocol, shared with `clientSchema.ts`.

Preserve `setFacetRuntime` ordering (replay → rebuild → listeners) exactly.

## Payoff

repo.ts roughly halves; each engine becomes unit-testable without a full Repo (idle jobs currently need `__reset*ForTesting` hooks).

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding D1 (god-objects lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit C1: @/data/internals is a paper boundary — promote the proven surface to @/data/api, then lint
description:
## Problem

`@/data/internals` is a paper boundary: **23 production files outside `src/data` import it**, and `eslint.config.js` has no `no-restricted-imports` rule at all. Highlights:

- `aliasesProp` alone has 9 external importers (its own file header says facet registration was deferred);
- geo embeds raw kernel SQL constants;
- plugins import kernel invalidation channel ids, `runAnalyzeIfStale`/`runAnalyzeNow`, `blockMerge`, `revealChildren` (a plain helper at `kernelMutators.ts:130`).

## Proposal — order matters

1. **First promote** the proven contract surface to `@/data/api`: `aliasesProp`, `revealChildren`, the invalidation channel ids, a maintenance entrypoint; give geo a registered query instead of raw SQL constants.
2. **Then** add the eslint `no-restricted-imports` rule with an allowlist for what remains.

Lint-first would just force 23 files into worse workarounds.

## Payoff

The internals boundary becomes real and enforced; future "should this be public API?" questions get answered at promotion time instead of by drift.

## Sequencing

Last of the three boundary moves: #137 (facet-kernel extraction) → #138 (sync-observer move) → **this**. Doing it last means the lint rule lands on the final directory layout.

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding C1 (layering lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit C3: data and sync are one subsystem in two directories — move the observer into the data engine
description:
## Problem

`data` and `sync` are one subsystem wearing two directories. Runtime imports are mutual: `repo.ts:90-93` imports the blocks-synced observer; `observer/*` imports `BlockCache`, `handleStore`, `treeQueries`, and the block schema. Tarjan over production imports puts repo + 14 internals + all three observer files + `src/types.ts` in one **35-file strongly-connected component**. All 11 sync→data import statements are in `observer/*`; `sync/keys`, `sync/crypto`, and `transform` are data-free.

## Proposal

Move `src/sync/observer/*` into the data engine (`src/data/internals/syncObserver/`) — it is the download half of the engine `repo.ts` already owns via `startSyncObserver`. `src/sync` then becomes a genuinely lower layer (keys/crypto/transform).

Build the sync resolver once in `repoProvider` and pass it through the existing `syncObserverDeps` parameter instead of re-deriving it in `context/repo.tsx`.

## Payoff

Breaks the 35-file SCC along the real seam; the directory structure stops lying about the dependency direction.

## Sequencing

Second of the three boundary moves: #137 (facet-kernel extraction) → **this** → C1 (internals promote-then-lint).

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding C3 (layering lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit C2: extract the zero-import facet kernel from src/extensions into a bottom layer
description:
## Problem

`src/extensions` fuses two layers. `facet.ts` has **zero imports** — the purest module in the codebase — yet sits beside `staticAppExtensions.ts` (39 plugin imports) and `AppRuntimeProvider.tsx` (imports shortcuts). Meanwhile `src/data` imports `@/extensions` from 6 files, making data↔extensions bidirectional.

## Proposal

Extract the leaf facet kernel into its own bottom layer (e.g. `src/facets/`):

- `facet.ts`, `variantFacet.ts`, the tree walkers (natural home for the unified walker from the B2 issue), `runtimeEvents.ts`;
- `togglable.ts`, with its `aliasesProp` label-decode **inverted** — the caller passes the label — so the kernel stays data-free.

`src/data` then imports only the kernel; the rest of `src/extensions` is declared app-layer.

**Compat constraint:** the `@/extensions/api.js` barrel must keep re-exporting from the new path — user extensions import it via the importmap, and module identity matters.

## Payoff

The declared layering becomes true in imports; gives the C3 observer move and C1 promote-then-lint stable ground.

## Sequencing

First of the three boundary moves: **C2 → C3 → C1** (this issue → sync-observer move → internals promote-then-lint).

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding C2 (layering lens, also flagged by mechanisms + god-objects lenses; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit B1: setFacetRuntime's wholesale-REPLACE spawns four compensation mechanisms
description:
## Problem

Each facet-runtime swap REPLACES every registry, so four manual compensation mechanisms exist:

- **(a)** kernel mutators/queries/processors are registered **twice** — constructor flags in `src/data/repo.ts:836-850` AND `kernelDataExtension.ts` facets; the file header documents the silent breakage if either path is forgotten;
- **(b)** `Repo` mirrors the runtime's contribution buckets purely to replay them onto each fresh runtime (`src/data/repo.ts:1486-1547`);
- **(c)** data extensions are listed in `src/extensions/staticDataExtensions.ts` AND must be re-bundled per plugin — the `daily-notes/index.ts:176` comment exists because this already bit someone; srs-review re-bundles four sibling plugins' dataExtensions;
- **(d)** every swap tears down and restarts ALL app effects, even for a single-extension toggle.

## Proposal

Keep the decided atomic-rebuild semantics; remove the compensations:

1. Construct `Repo` empty + immediately install a kernel-only runtime — deletes the dual registration path and five flags.
2. Make replay the runtime's job: `FacetRuntime.withContributionsFrom(prev)`.
3. Derive both the data runtime and the app manifest from one per-plugin record `{appExtension, dataExtension}`.
4. Diff `appEffectsFacet` contributions by effect id; restart only changed effects.

Preserve the existing swap ordering (replay → rebuild → listeners) exactly.

## Payoff

Deletes the three comment-enforced contracts most likely to bite a plugin author, ~150 LOC of mirror/flag machinery, and stops toggle-one-extension from restarting every plugin's subscriptions.

## Sequencing

Pairs with the facet-bridge extraction in audit D1(c) — do them together or back-to-back.

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding B1 (mechanisms lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit B3: untyped window.CustomEvent bus runs parallel to typed mechanisms — and extensionLint canonizes it
description:
## Problem

29 `window.dispatchEvent` sites across 18 plugin files vs exactly **2** plugin consumers of the typed `openDialog` channel. Three verified antipatterns:

1. Action handlers whose only body is dispatching an event.
2. Cross-plugin coupling over stringly event names (`app-intents` imports and fires quick-find's event).
3. Synchronous request/response RPC over the broadcast bus — `src/plugins/video-player/events.ts` passes `respond()` callbacks inside event detail.

Worse, `src/plugins/agent-runtime/extensionLint.ts` flags `useSyncExternalStore` as an anti-pattern while the typed `DialogHost` itself uses it — the authoring lint actively penalizes the better mechanism.

Files: 8 plugin `events.ts` files; `src/utils/dialogs.ts`, `src/extensions/dialogAppMount.tsx`, `src/plugins/video-player/events.ts`, `src/plugins/agent-runtime/extensionLint.ts`.

## Proposal

Bless one typed channel per shape:

- **Dialogs/pickers** → the existing promise-returning `openDialog` queue.
- **Toggle/open intents** → actions via `runActionById`.
- **Genuine broadcast** → CustomEvents stay, but only for that.

Update `extensionLint` + the authoring catalog in the same change. Keep old listeners as a deprecation shim — user extensions in the wild depend on current event names.

## Related

#92 (explicit typed events for state changes) is the adjacent data-layer discipline; this issue is about the UI/plugin event bus.

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding B3 (mechanisms lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit B2: unify the seven AppExtension tree-walkers — bare walkers are toggle-blind (live bug: disabled daily-notes steers landing)
description:
## Problem

Seven recursive walkers over the AppExtension grammar with three divergent semantics; `isFacetContribution` copy-pasted verbatim ×3; `pushValidatedContribution` duplicated with a stale "mirrors" comment. The bare collectors (no toggle boundaries, no `enables` recursion) are used in production at three sites: `src/App.tsx:201`, `src/context/repo.tsx:40`, `src/data/localSchema.ts:12`.

**Live bug (verifier-confirmed):** `App.tsx`'s landing resolution uses the bare walker, and `system:daily-notes` — a non-essential, user-disableable plugin — is the sole `workspaceLandingFacet` contributor. A user who disables daily-notes still gets it steering first paint.

Files: `src/extensions/facet.ts`, `resolveAppRuntime.ts`, `discoverToggleTree.ts`, `dynamicExtensions.ts`, plus the three call sites above.

## Proposal

1. One parameterized walker in `facet.ts` with `{boundaries, functions, dedup, visitor}` options encoding today's deliberate differences explicitly; the other walkers become thin configurations of it.
2. Switch App.tsx's landing resolution to `resolveAppRuntimeSync` with the current overrides map — this is the bug fix.

## Payoff

Grammar changes become single-point edits (the `enables` recursion was already missed once — see `dynamicExtensions.ts:194-201`); fixes the disabled-plugin-steers-first-paint bug; ~150 LOC deleted.

## Sequencing

Quick win — good first item. If/when the facet kernel is extracted (audit C2), the unified walker moves with `facet.ts`; doing this first is fine.

---
*Source: `docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md` — finding B2 (mechanisms lens; adversarially verified 2026-06-11/12).*

title: Audit A2 (rescoped): UI-state sync is deliberate — fix stale docs now; icebox upload/history policy for shared workspaces
description:
## Status (rescoped 2026-06-12)

Owner correction: syncing UI state through ordinary block rows is a **deliberate, affirmed decision** — device-local ephemeral state was removed on purpose, and the uniform substrate (one storage model, cross-device focus/scroll restore) has been worth it. The audit's mechanics were accurate but its "three docs say otherwise" framing was backwards: the docs are stale, not the behavior wrong.

## Do now

Fix the stale docs the audit caught, so the next reader doesn't re-derive the wrong conclusion:

- `globalState.ts:152-155` claims the plugin ui-state block "never enters the upload queue" — it does;
- `docs/navigation-redesign.md` describes UiState panel rows as "(not synced)" — they are.

Both should state the actual, deliberate behavior.

## Icebox — revisit when the triggers fire

Two costs only materialize under conditions that don't currently hold; recording them with their triggers:

1. **Privacy** — workspace peers receive each member's focus/selection/scroll trail. *Trigger: the first workspace genuinely shared with another person.*
2. **Server history growth** — every selection change (150 ms debounce) and scroll settle adds a `blocks_history` row, so the append-only server table grows with interaction rather than content, and interaction churn has ~no recovery value. *Trigger: blocks_history size alerts.*

If a trigger fires, the mechanism menu (no commitment implied): per-`PropertySchema` upload opt-out; a DeviceLocal change-scope; or a server-side filter excluding UiState-scope writes from `blocks_history` only — that last one keeps sync and cross-device restore fully intact, but is an explicit "interaction churn is not history" decision for the owner, never a silent default.

## Evidence (verified by the audit)

`src/data/api/changeScope.ts:46-50`, `src/data/internals/clientSchema.ts:444-450`, `src/data/properties.ts:346-374`, `src/components/BlockEditor.tsx:104-118`, `src/components/renderer/PanelRenderer.tsx:87-88`, migration `20260522062437_add_blocks_history.sql`.

---
*Source: audit finding A2 (`docs/architecture-audit-2026-06.md`), rescoped per owner correction 2026-06-12.*

title: Integrate pointer dispatch into the context lifecycle (retire the pointer modal-shadowing bypass)
description:
## Background

PR #123 (input unification, Phase 3) routes pointer gestures through the same `resolve` + coordinator + run-until-handled path as keyboard. To get there, the pointer trigger arm in `resolve()` deliberately **skips** the active-context + modal-shadowing filter:

```ts
// src/shortcuts/resolve.ts — resolve(), {kind:'pointer'} arm
case 'pointer':
  // Candidates are pre-filtered by binding match and dispatched with supplied
  // deps, so the context need NOT be active — the click provides the context.
  // FIXME(phase3): blanket bypass is only sound for spatially-targeted gestures.
  return true
```

Combined with `resolveDeps(..., supplied)` (deps handed in from the clicked block rather than read from the active map), this makes pointer a **parallel path** that doesn't participate in the context lifecycle at all — no activation/deactivation, no precedence, no modal shadowing.

This is correct for the one pointer action that exists today (shift-click spatial selection): a click is *spatially targeted*, so firing it regardless of which mode owns the keyboard matches prior behavior and is what the user wants. But it's a flagged assumption, not a principled design.

## The problem

Keyboard events are **ambient** — no inherent target — so "which action?" must be answered by external state (the active-contexts map + modal shadowing). Pointer events are **located** — the target element names the region. Today we model that difference by giving pointer its own bypass path.

The deeper cause is that `ActiveContextsMap` is **singleton-per-type** (`Map<ContextType, deps>`): there is exactly one `normal-mode`, belonging to the *focused* block. A click on a different block can't be expressed as "normal-mode, but for block B," so we sidestep the map entirely.

The bypass breaks down the moment a pointer action is **not** purely spatially-targeted — e.g. a gesture that should be *suppressed* while a modal overlay (command palette) is up, or any click that shouldn't "click through" a mode that owns input. There's currently no mechanism to say "shadow this pointer action while a modal is active"; it would fire anyway. The next pointer migration (`blockClickHandlersFacet` click-to-edit is the likely first) will inherit this silently.

## Proposal: one region tree, two entry points

Stop treating contexts as a flat global singleton map and model them as **provided by nodes in a region/focus tree**. Panels, block surfaces, and modal layers are nodes; each provides a context with its deps. Then resolution is the same operation from two entry points:

- **Keyboard** enters the tree at the **focused** node and walks to the root, gathering provided contexts.
- **Pointer** enters at the **clicked (hit)** node and walks to the root, gathering the same way.

Same tree, same `resolve`/`compareContexts`, same gather — the only difference is the entry point. The `supplied` deps seam added in #123 is the embryonic form of "the node provides its deps" (caller hand-supply → region node provides).

The key payoff: **modal shadowing becomes a tree property instead of a special case.** A modal layer is a node flagged "shadow everything not contained under me." Then:

- Click *inside* a modal layer (palette body) → it's on the walk → it wins / others shadow. ✅
- Click on a block while *multi-select* is active → multi-select is scoped to the panel/selection and the block is *under* it → the walk sees it, so shift-click extends. ✅ (the case the current blanket bypass only gets right by accident)
- Click on a region *not* under an overlay modal → modal isn't on that node's walk → shadowed/declined (or simply unreachable because the overlay ate the click). ✅

i.e. shadowing becomes "whatever the click's containment says" — the same rule keyboard already obeys, sourced from spatial containment rather than focus state.

This is the plan's deferred **focus-tree / capability-provider** track (see `docs/action-system-implementation-plan.html` "focus-tree model" + critique weakness 6 "derive from tree"), not a retrofit into #123.

## Incremental path (doesn't require the full tree)

The minimal honest step that retires the blanket bypass without building the whole focus-tree:

1. The shell already tags the DOM with what's needed: `data-block-nav-item`, `data-panel-id`, `data-render-scope-id`. Add one marker for shadowing layers (e.g. `data-shortcut-modal`) on overlays/modes that should own input.
2. On a pointer event, walk from `event.target` to the root, collecting `(contextType, deps, isModal)` from the tagged region nodes. That list **is** an `ActiveContextsMap` for this click — the located analogue of the focus-derived one.
3. Generalize `computeInstallableContexts` to operate on "the contexts in scope for *this trigger*" rather than always the global focus map. Then `resolve({kind:'pointer'})` runs **unchanged** — shadowing/tiers/recency all apply.

Today's behavior is the degenerate case (per-click active set = `{clicked block's context}`, no shadow layer → everything fires), so this is a strict generalization, not a rewrite.

## The one semantic decision to make

Does a modal that's active but **doesn't visually cover** the click (multi-select; a non-overlay palette) suppress a pointer action outside its region?

- **(a)** Containment + hit-testing decide — a modal only shadows clicks under it; a mode that wants to block out-of-region clicks must render a blocking overlay (then it's on the walk anyway).
- **(b)** A context may declare "captures pointer globally" — folds the global active modal into every click's shadow decision regardless of containment.

**Recommendation: (a) as the default, (b) as an explicit per-context opt-in.** "You can act on what you can reach, scoped by the region you reached it through" is the most defensible rule, makes the common cases fall out from containment, and reserves global suppression for the rare mode that genuinely needs it — rather than baking it into the one comparator everything routes through.

## Acceptance / done-when

- `resolve()`'s `{kind:'pointer'}` arm no longer hardcodes `return true`; it resolves against a per-trigger context set derived from the hit node's containment.
- Modal shadowing for pointer is decided by the tree, not bypassed; the `FIXME(phase3)` in `resolve.ts` is removed.
- A non-spatially-targeted pointer action can be correctly suppressed under a modal without a bespoke per-action hack.
- Regression coverage: shift-click extend still fires under multi-select; a click outside an overlay modal is suppressed; a click inside it resolves to the modal's context.

## References

- PR #123 (the bypass + `supplied` deps seam)
- `src/shortcuts/resolve.ts` (`resolve` pointer arm, `computeInstallableContexts`, `resolveDeps`)
- `src/shortcuts/ActiveContexts.tsx` (the singleton-per-type active map)
- `docs/action-system-implementation-plan.html` (Phase 3, focus-tree track) and `docs/action-system-critique.html` (weakness 6)

title: Remove the E2EE rollout pin-seed after the rollout window (close server-trust downgrade residual)
description:
## Context

PR #105 (E2EE Phase D+E) added a one-time **rollout pin-seed** (`src/sync/keys/rolloutSeed.ts` / `seedModePinsOnce`) that pins pre-existing workspaces from the server's `encryption_mode` on the first pin-aware boot, so existing plaintext workspaces don't hit the §6 first-encounter quarantine gate. It deliberately trusts the server flag **once**, which is safe under the §6 assumption that no E2EE workspace exists during the coordinated rollout.

## The residual (Codex P1, consciously accepted for the rollout window)

The seed has an irreducible downgrade residual under a narrow failure: a **fresh device** whose empty first-boot "seeded" marker write fails (localStorage blocked/quota) and then **recovers on a later boot** with post-rollout data already synced — at which point it could pin a hostile/stale `none`-flagged E2EE workspace as `plaintext`, bypassing the gate (silent downgrade).

It can't be closed with localStorage-only sealing: a genuine rollout-cohort device and a fresh-device-with-failed-seal are indistinguishable without an external signal (the pre-pin app recorded no version; a DB marker is unsafe because Lock & wipe clears it and would re-arm the seed when E2EE workspaces *do* exist).

We accept it during the rollout window because the exposure is extraordinarily narrow and no E2EE workspace exists during the coordinated rollout.

## Action — do after ~1 week of the rollout release running

Once all rollout-cohort devices have seeded, **remove the server-trusting seed**:
- [ ] Delete `src/sync/keys/rolloutSeed.ts` + `rolloutSeed.test.ts`, and the call in `ensurePowerSyncReady` (`src/data/repoProvider.ts`).
- [ ] Drop now-unused `seedModePinsOnce` / `markPinsSeeded` / `arePinsSeeded` (+ their tests) from `src/sync/keys/modePin.ts` if nothing else uses them. Keep `canPersistPins` / `confirmPlaintextForSession` / the session-plaintext fallback.
- [ ] Confirm: after removal, fresh devices gate every unpinned workspace (quarantine for server-`none`, key-required for server-`e2ee`).

This permanently closes the downgrade residual — it's the "trust the server flag only during the coordinated bootstrap, then never again" approach.

Refs: PR #105; Codex review thread on `src/sync/keys/rolloutSeed.ts` (P1, comment 3359485241).

### Fixed
- [x] **userSchemasService subscription-rebuild flake** — the CI flake behind PR #115 (failed at L238 / L226 / L179 across attempts). Two parts:
  - *Production:* the service rebuilt its reverse-map through `repo.block(id)` facades that lag the typed-blocks query's `BlockCache`; now it builds from the authoritative `BlockData` the subscription delivers (`peekRowProperty`) — removes the facade-hydration race (`842e0e6`).
  - *Tests:* the subscription is still **multi-tick** under load — `waitForPropertySchemasChange` resolves on the first change event, which can precede the rebuild that registers the schema — so the subscription-path + valuePresets-path reads must `vi.waitFor` (`9e2db90`, `42f8c66`). The synchronous `addSchema` path stays synchronous. *(A mid-sweep attempt to make these fully synchronous after the production fix flaked under full-suite load; reverted to polling.)*
- [x] **roam-import import-log `todayIso()` midnight race** — froze `Date` only (timers/async stay real) in `beforeEach` so production and assertions read the same day (`91e1b09`).
- [x] **"No-fire" fixed sleeps** (`kernelQueries` L715/796/816, `grouped-backlinks/query.test.ts`) — replaced `sleep + assert nothing fired` with a deterministic **control-write fence**: after the unrelated write, a write that *does* change the handle's value, `vi.waitFor` that single emission, assert the exact sequence. Robust against the loader's structural-diff dedup + mid-load coalescing; no fixed wait (`ceffab5`).
- [x] **`dueCards.integration.test.ts` → `command_events.tx_id` UNIQUE-constraint flake** (newly surfaced under full-suite load; ~50%). Suite shares one PowerSync DB; an awaited write's `command_events` insert can land just after the next test's `resetTestDb` (PS write-behind), and `tx_id` came from a `newId` counter reset to `gen-1` each test → the late id collided with the next test's own ids. - [x] **theme-toggle `dispose()` in `it()` bodies** — `afterEach` already resets the only global state; `dispose()`'s extra cleanup is on a per-test, GC'd runtime.

title: Conflict detection: flag a single-key binding that strictly prefixes a co-active sequence chord
description:
The single-winner keyboard coordinator (`HotkeyReconciler`) gives each candidate its own tinykeys matcher, then orders the set that completed *this* event via `resolve(...)` by context tier → priority → recency. Chord **length** is not a factor.

So if a single-key binding is a strict prefix of a sequence in a co-active context — e.g. a plugin binds `g` while vim normal mode keeps `g g` — both matchers complete on the second `g`, and the prefix can out-rank the sequence by context, so `g g` never fires.

### Why not a resolver/comparator change
- A "prefer the longer completed chord" tiebreak can't live cleanly in the shared comparator: it would have to rank **below** the modal/global tiers (a modal that binds `g` must still beat a background `g g`, since modal "owns all chords"). Baking length into the one comparator everything routes through is the wrong layer.
- The single-key prefix completes and dispatches on the **first** press regardless (its matcher fires immediately), so even a perfect press-2 tiebreak can't undo the press-1 dispatch.

It's fundamentally a **misconfiguration** — a key racing a sequence it prefixes — which the conflict detector is the right place to catch.

### Fix shape
Extend `src/shortcuts/keybindingConflicts.ts` (which already buckets chords via the Phase-0 canonical key and warns on collisions) to also flag "binding X is a strict prefix of sequence Y in an overlapping context" as an intentional-shadow-style warning, surfaced in shortcut settings. Use the sequence-aware `parseChord` (landed in Phase 0) to compare press lists, not just the atomic key.

### Not reachable today
The repo has exactly one sequence binding (`g g`, vim normal mode) and no single-key `g` binding in any context, so no prefix/sequence collision currently exists. Build this when a real collision appears, or alongside the conflict-UI work in the action-system plan's "Opportunistic" section.

title: Explore: focus-tree-derived activation model for the action system
description:
## Summary

Documented-for-later exploration spun out of the action-system design discussion (PR #57 docs). **Not scheduled** — tracking so it isn't lost. The phased implementation plan explicitly does **not** depend on this; it runs as a separate prototype track gated on its own evidence.

## The idea

Replace the flat, runtime-maintained `ActiveContextsMap` with an active set **derived from the focus/DOM tree**, and split the single `activate` verb into two declarations:

- **establish scope** — containment, structural (innermost wins), derivable from the tree
- **override** — precedence claim (priority/modal), explicitly declared

Today's model flattens a tree into an unordered map and then uses *activation timing* (insertion order) as a precedence proxy. That timing-as-precedence is the root cause of the "new display surface activates early, normal-mode activates late, so the generic layer wrongly wins" bug class (critique weakness #4). Deriving the active set from structure kills that bug class at the root because there's no separate registry that can desync from reality.

## Why it's attractive

- Retires the timing-as-precedence bug **class**, not just an instance.
- Eliminates activation churn + the staleness window (and much of `HotkeyReconciler`'s `activeRef`/`useLayoutEffect` machinery): scopes activate once, dep values read fresh at dispatch.
- It's the same shape as the provider/capability dependency model (scopes provide typed tokens, actions declare needs) — the focus-tree version is just "the provider chain *is* the React component tree."

## Why it is NOT urgent / not a dependency

- **It does not fix the surface bug.** The surface wants to override *against* containment depth (it's the ancestor; the focused block is deeper), which needs an explicit priority/override signal in *any* architecture. Structural depth alone gives the same wrong answer as last-wins.
- **It composes with the resolver spine rather than competing.** `resolve(activeSet, trigger)` consumes an active set; this only changes what *produces* it. So the planned phases (resolver core + `priority`) already patch the bug symptom without it.
- It is the **heaviest** change discussed: ~27 activation call sites, typed-deps threading, plus non-focus-shaped scopes (e.g. `multi-select-mode` concerns blocks scattered across the tree, not a single focus path) that would stay explicitly declared.

## Suggested first step

Throwaway-branch **prototype** to validate the two genuinely-uncertain parts before it's a real proposal:
1. typed-dependency threading through tree nodes / focus handles (replacing the type-keyed active map);
2. non-focus-shaped scopes (multi-select) — how they coexist with a tree-derived model.

## References

- `docs/action-system-critique.html` — weakness #4 (lifecycle-order-as-precedence) and #6 (scope/deps conflation + the provider/capability model).
- `docs/action-system-implementation-plan.html` — "The separate bet — do NOT gate anything on it."
- `docs/shortcut-context-precedence.html` — the originating surface-vs-normal-mode inversion.

title: Mark transient alias-seat cleanup tombstones explicitly
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. The current shape-matching predicate works; this is an alternative worth picking up only under the conditions below.

## Idea

Today the probe in `src/data/targets.ts` decides whether to restore a tombstoned alias seat by comparing its `(content, properties)` against `aliasSeatSeed(alias)` and rejecting any row with live children (`isRestorableTransientTombstone`). Shared `aliasSeatSeed` + a drift-detection test keep writer and matcher in lockstep, but the predicate still **infers intent from row shape after the fact**.

The alternative: have `cleanupOrphanAliasesProcessor` stamp an explicit synced marker (e.g. `system:transient-seat: true`) on the seat *before* soft-deleting. The probe predicate then collapses to "tombstoned + marker present"; `ensureAliasTarget`'s restore path strips the marker so a touched-then-tombstoned seat never carries it. Drift between writer shape and the restorability predicate becomes irrelevant — cleanup's positive intent is the contract.

## Tradeoffs

Adds one synced property + a codec entry; one `row_events` / `ps_crud` write per cleanup tombstone (cheap, non-zero); requires backfilling existing tombstones if we want them restored too (the seed-shape predicate covers them today — all ~435 in the audited DB match it).

## Trigger to build

(a) The shape predicate starts producing **false negatives** in practice (e.g. `PAGE_TYPE`'s default props grow and the seed gets harder to keep in sync), or (b) a second seat-with-cleanup domain shows up and we'd rather not generalize the seed pattern across both.

Related: the "Legacy alias-seat cleanup tombstones" audit — if this Option B lands, that cleanup becomes "purge where marker present" instead of shape-matching.

title: Generic "move type" / "move property" primitive
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. Earns its keep only once a second caller wants it.

## Idea

SRS has a dedicated cut/paste swipe action (`src/plugins/srs-rescheduling/moveSrsState.ts` + `srsClipboard.ts`, wired through `srs.cut` / `srs.paste`). The shape generalizes: every `TypeContribution` declares its field list via `properties` (`src/data/api/blockType.ts`), so a kernel-or-shared-util "move type with fields" operation could subsume the SRS case once a second caller appears.

```ts
// The only piece that needs the type registry is enumerating TypeContribution.properties.
moveTypeInTx(tx, { typeId, sourceId, targetId, mode: 'move' | 'copy' })
```

Semantics (from the SRS implementation):

- Enumerate the type's declared property schemas; copy each encoded value present on source into target.
- Add the type to target if absent. Clear any target field the type declares but source didn't set, so target ends with exactly source's state (move-not-merge).
- On `mode: 'move'`, remove the type from source and delete each declared property — **but only if no other type still on source declares that property** (the collision rule SRS gets for free; the generic version doesn't).
- Don't run `TypeContribution.setup` on target — values transplanted verbatim.
- Skip if `sourceId === targetId` or source lacks the type.

## Why deferred

Likely callers after SRS: `todo` (move done/snoozed state), any future structured-data type. A generic primitive only earns its keep once one actually wants it — the SRS-only path was deliberately picked to validate the cut/paste UX before paying the generic-API tax. Bigger open question: is "move type" even the right framing for the second caller, or do they want "swap state between these two blocks"?

A **"move property"** primitive (one field, no type) is intentionally **not** part of this — a property usually exists because some type put it there; moving it without the type leaves an orphan field nothing renders. Hold off until a real free-floating-annotation case shows up.

## Where it lives (decide at build time)

`mutatorsFacet` is preferred over a `Repo` method if it can read the type registry from extension context (keeps it plugin-contributable). Current `repo.addTypeInTx` / `repo.removeTypeInTx` are kernel methods only because of privileged registry access; a `moveType` mutator could compose them.

**UX:** the SRS cut/paste swipe pattern (per-type `<type>.cut` / `<type>.paste` actions filtered by `QuickActionItem.canRun`) is the working model. Don't build a generic "which type to cut?" submenu — let `canRun` sort visibility.

title: Explicit typed events for state changes (event-sourcing discipline)
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. A refactoring direction, not a feature — mostly invisible from outside the data layer.

## Idea

Today every state change goes through `repo.tx` → kernel mutators → row writes on `blocks`. `command_events.mutator_calls` records mutator-name + args per tx — morally close to an event log but **not enforced**: a mutator body can read state and call `tx.update(...)` based on what it sees, so the recorded `mutator_calls` row is not guaranteed to be a *replayable* description of the change. The row write is the truth; the call record is a hint.

**Discipline shift:** treat every state change as a named, typed event. The mutator becomes a pure `(event-args, current-state) → row writes` materializer. The recorded `mutator_calls` row is then a complete, replayable description.

## Why flag it now

- **PITR / time-travel:** row-state history reconstructs *what* a block looked like at T but not *what operation* produced it. Typed events give the operation back ("I see a deletion at 3pm — what command issued it?" becomes a lookup, not a diff inference).
- **Cross-device history (sidecar `block_events`):** clients push `command_events` upstream for a uniform global event stream without full LiveStore-style event-sourced sync. Richness is bounded by mutator discipline — diffuse mutators don't compress to useful events.
- **Future optionality:** if event-sourced sync ever becomes right (per-edit cross-device history, deterministic conflict resolution), migration cost scales with how close mutators already are to materializers. Tightening now lowers that cost for free.
- **Testability / clarity:** `(args, state) → writes` is far easier to test/audit than an opaque mutator body.

## Why deferred

No current feature *requires* this; the existing mutator surface works.

## Trigger to build

(a) PITR UI lands and people ask "what command did this?" not just "what state was this?"; (b) a serious sidecar event-stream feature is on the table; (c) the mutator surface is being reworked for another reason and the marginal cost is low; or (d) we're seriously evaluating an event-sourced sync engine.

**Adjacent direction:** make `mutator_calls` the audit primary key instead of `row_events` — `row_events` becomes a derived index for fast row-state reconstruction; `command_events` carries the user-meaningful operation log; pruning policies become independent.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (Architectural ideas)._

title: Parallel reads for cold-start contention (PowerSync read pool)
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. Estimated 1–2 weeks for path 2; only worth it if path 1 doesn't materialize and the contention returns as the dominant cold-start cost.

## Problem

Every SQL call (read or write) goes through `@powersync/web`'s single `DatabaseClient` — "a single-connection ConnectionPool based on a worker connection." `readLock` / `writeLock` exist but serialize through one Comlink remote. As of `@powersync/web@1.37.2` there's no read-pool flag in `WebSQLOpenFactoryOptions`; multi-reader is on PowerSync's roadmap but unshipped.

Cold-start traces: when the page mounts dozens of concurrent reads (one `core.childIds` per visible BlockComponent, one `core.ancestors` per backlink breadcrumb absent batching) plus bootstrap writes, per-read SQL is fast (~1.5 ms) but the queue wall-clock at the tail is ~140 ms across ~100 reads, and writes block reads behind them. Mostly amortized today by deferring writes to idle and batching reads, but the constraint remains.

## Two paths to add parallelism

1. **Wait for upstream PowerSync multi-reader.** Opt in via `WASQLiteOpenFactoryOptions` when it ships. Zero engineering, no parallel-adapter maintenance. Watch the changelog at major bumps.
2. **Open a parallel WA-SQLite read-only connection** alongside PowerSync's worker. `OPFSCoopSyncVFS` (already used) supports multiple cooperative connections via Web Locks; WAL mode lets readers see committed state mid-writer-tx. Trigger-maintained side tables (`block_aliases`, `block_types`, `block_references`, `row_events`) are written by the writer and visible to the reader.

**Why we don't need PowerSync for the read path:** its value is the Rust sync engine + `db.watch` reactivity. We don't use the reactivity (we rolled our own via `row_events` triggers + tail processor), so the connection-owning worker exists for sync, not reads.

## Hard parts of path 2

- Schema bootstrap timing (wait for `ensurePowerSyncReady` before opening the reader).
- WAL checkpoint coordination (readers briefly blocked during checkpoint).
- Worker isolation — a main-thread reader re-introduces contention with React render; the reader probably wants its own worker (two worker setups to maintain).
- Maintenance burden on PowerSync upgrades (verify the parallel adapter still matches WAL/schema-migration assumptions).
- Test surface — `createTestDb()` would have to spin up the parallel reader too.

## Trigger to build

`db.getAll.maxMs` consistently above ~200 ms with correlated `writeTransaction` activity, **and** batching/deferral can't eliminate contention at the call site, **and** path 1 hasn't materialized. Until then: keep cutting reads at the call site and writes off the critical path; re-check PowerSync's changelog at each major bump.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (Architectural ideas)._

title: Data-defined contributions over facets — projector-shim pattern
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. Don't extract before the third instance lands.

## Idea

If the data-defined `type-definition` block (see companion issue) lands, it sits inside a broader pattern: a **meta-typed block + a resolver that watches matching blocks and contributes into a facet**, with `refreshAppRuntime()` triggering rebuilds.

Strong follow-up candidates for the same projector-shim shape:

- **commands / actions** (`actionsFacet` + `actionContextsFacet`) — declarative `command-definition` blocks for keybinding-bound macros, generalizing what `agent-runtime` already does for AI-callable commands.
- **saved queries / live searches** — a `query-definition` block riding the typed-query primitive (§8 of the type-system doc); substrate for agendas, todo inboxes, dashboards.
- **type templates** — a subtree to materialize on instance creation, declared *on* the type contribution.
- **view templates** — kanban / calendar / table configs binding type fields to view axes.
- **property-schema definitions** — users mint typed properties via a `schema-definition` block, replacing v1's name-only references.

**Code-only stays code-only** for things with real logic: mutators, kernel queries, post-commit processors, codecs, layout/decorator/click facets, markdown extensions, property *editors* (React components don't compress to declarative blocks), header items, app mounts.

## Direction

Once two or three projectors exist, look for the abstraction — a `definitionBlockProjectorFacet` carrying `{metaType, project, targetFacet}` driven by one shared effect — but **don't extract before the third instance lands**; cheaper to pull from real cases than design upfront.

## Sequencing

Commands and queries are the highest-leverage next two after the type-system phases — together they unblock most "Tana-feeling" workflows on top of the type substrate.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (Architectural ideas)._

title: Data-defined type-definition blocks (deferred from type-system v1)
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. Design sketch survives in §9 of `docs/type-system.md`.

## Idea

Type-system v1 (`docs/type-system.md`) ships types as **facet contributions only** — an end user who wants a new type writes a small `extension` block that calls `typesFacet.of({...})`. The dedicated declarative `type-definition` block + property-panel UI for non-coding authors is deferred until there's user demand to remove the "write a tiny extension" friction.

Design sketch: a kernel query `findTypeDefinitionBlocksQuery` mirroring `findExtensionBlocksQuery`, a resolver `userDefinedTypesExtension` symmetric to `dynamicExtensionsExtension`, and a small `appEffect` watching `block_types WHERE type='type-definition'` that calls `refreshAppRuntime()` on change.

Explicitly **not** a mutable `FacetRuntime` contribution sink — the immutable-then-rebuild shape is load-bearing (atomic switchover for mutators+processors+schemas, upfront validation, deterministic `combine`, order-independent visibility).

## Trigger to build

Real users hit the "to add a new type I have to author code" wall and ask for a UI. Until then, code-extension types are sufficient.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (Architectural ideas)._

title: Plugin payload side-table (plugin_block_data) — deferred bandwidth escape hatch
description:
> **Status:** Architectural idea, **no current trigger**. Captured so the analysis isn't re-derived later. Do not build until the trigger below fires.

## Idea

The plugin-extensibility plan has plugins write into namespaced subtrees of `properties_json` (scalars) or `edges_json` (relationships), with local-only derived tables maintained by Shape-A triggers (JSON is source of truth, local rep derived from a `LocalSchemaContribution`). This works at typical sizes but **pools all plugins' bandwidth into one of the two JSON columns**: a plugin that frequently mutates a large opaque payload re-syncs the whole blob on every edit, sharing wire bytes with everything else on that block.

**Escape hatch:** one core-provided `plugin_block_data(block_id, plugin_id, payload TEXT)` table, one row per (block, plugin). Bandwidth-isolated per plugin; lifecycle (insert/delete cascade, workspace_id propagation) via shared core triggers; sync via plugin-aware PowerSync rules. Plugins still derive their query/index tables via Shape-A triggers, sourced from `plugin_block_data` rows filtered by `plugin_id` instead of a JSON namespace. Plugin-skew passthrough carries over (rows for not-installed plugins ride round-trip intact).

## Why deferred

No current plugin needs it. Backlinks fits `edges_json`; scalar-prop plugins fit `properties_json` namespaces; both fine at alpha scale. Pre-user, building later ≈ building now — the only thing that makes "later" expensive is plugins building workarounds (shoving large payloads into `properties_json`) before the proper surface exists.

## Trigger to build

A plugin shows up with a **non-relational, large-or-high-churn** payload that doesn't fit `edges_json` and would meaningfully hurt other plugins' write bandwidth in `properties_json`. Examples: rich annotations, embedded media metadata, per-block AI summaries — payload routinely exceeds a few KB and updates independently of block content.

## Migration path (for an existing plugin to graduate)

Backfill rows from the plugin's `properties_json` namespace → switch triggers to source from `plugin_block_data` filtered by `plugin_id` → drop the namespace. Same per-plugin state-marker pattern as `block_references_backfill_v1`. Local derived tables don't change shape; only their source-of-truth does. Bounded, reversible.

## Open decisions (at build time)

- Bucket strategy: per-`(workspace_id, plugin_id)` (clean install/uninstall, requires `powersync deploy` per new plugin id) vs. per-`workspace_id` only (simpler ops, clients pull payloads for uninstalled plugins).
- Core generic write API (`tx.setPluginData(blockId, pluginId, payload)`) vs. each plugin owns its write path.
- `payload` opaque `TEXT` vs. `JSON` (defaults toward `TEXT` since plugins maintain their own indexed local tables).

**Considered and rejected:** generic `block_props(block_id, key, value)` normalization — read regression on the hot path (aggregating N rows per block load vs. one blob parse) outweighs the bandwidth win; the 1:1 (block, plugin) shape is strictly better.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (Architectural ideas)._

title: Semantic action groups for decorator targets
description:
## Problem

SRS (and a future Readwise plugin) want to intercept the same user intent — "mark this block as complete/reviewed" — across three concrete actions: `todo.cycle`, `edit.cm.todo.cycle`, and `block.swipe-right`. Today each plugin contributes three decorators. That's locally simple and matches the current `actionDecoratorsFacet` contract, but it leaks the physical action list into every plugin that wants to specialize the semantic behavior.

Important distinction: the todo actions already delegate to one implementation (`cycleTodoState`), but decorators don't wrap implementation calls — they wrap registered `ActionConfig` records by exact `action.id` (+ optional context). So "decorate only todo cycle" would miss edit-mode and swipe-right unless those stopped being distinct action records.

## Current state (verified)

- `ActionDecorator` (`src/shortcuts/types.ts`) has `{ actionId, context?, decorate }` — no `groupId` / `groups` / `aliases`.
- `matchesAction` (`src/shortcuts/effectiveActions.ts`) matches by exact `actionId` or wildcard — no group matching.
- SRS registers one decorator per concrete action id (`srs-rescheduling/rescheduleDecorator.ts`, `swipeRightDecorator.ts`, todo-cycle decorators). No Readwise plugin exists yet.

## Direction

Explore semantic grouping metadata on actions (e.g. `groups: ['block.primary-complete']`) and let decorators target a group as well as an id. Todo marks all three concrete actions with the group; SRS/Readwise contribute one group decorator that checks block type and either consumes or falls through. Keep group membership as metadata during `getEffectiveActions` expansion — **not** a dispatch alias — so `block.swipe-right` stays gesture-owned.

Questions to answer first: does `ActionDecorator` grow `groupId?`, or do actions expose `aliases?` and decorators keep single `actionId`? Ordering when both id- and group-targeted decorators match? Should group decorators constrain context? How does the palette/shortcut UI display grouped semantics without hiding the concrete id the user binds?

Acceptance: a small design note or spike with tests around `getEffectiveActions`, compared against a helper-only option (`decorateActions([ids...], factory)`), before migrating SRS/Readwise. Avoid making `block.swipe-right` delegate to `todo.cycle`.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P2)._

title: Route swipe-quick-action invocation through the dispatcher
description:
## Problem

`SwipeActionMenu.handleRun` → `runBlockAction` invokes `action.handler(deps, trigger)` **directly**, bypassing `useRunAction` / `runActionById`. The rationale is mobile-pragmatic: the swipe gesture targets a block regardless of which one is focused, so requiring the action's declared context to be active upfront would mean the menu couldn't expose NORMAL_MODE actions on a non-focused block.

The cost surfaces when a handler opens UI that itself reads `useActiveContextsState`. The command palette is the canary: its action list is filtered by the currently-active context map, not by the deps handed to a handler. So `commandPaletteForBlockAction.handler` has to first `await focusBlock(uiStateBlock, block.id, ...)` before dispatching the toggle, or the palette won't list block-context actions. Every future "quick action that opens a context-aware UI" needs an analogous dance, and forgetting it produces a degraded-but-not-broken palette that's easy to miss in review.

## Current state (verified)

- `src/plugins/swipe-quick-actions/SwipeActionMenu.tsx`: `handleRun` → `runBlockAction` calls `action.handler` directly.
- `src/plugins/command-palette/index.ts`: `commandPaletteForBlockAction.handler` still does the inline `focusBlock` dance.

## Fix shape

Have `handleRun` route through the dispatcher for actions whose `context` is not `GLOBAL`: "before invoking the handler, make this block the active one for `action.context`" — for NORMAL_MODE that's `focusBlock(uiStateBlock, block.id)` (or a broader `activateBlockNormalMode`), then `runActionById(actionId, trigger)`. GLOBAL actions pass through unchanged.

Trade-off: every NORMAL_MODE action invoked from the swipe menu now flips global focus to its target block as a side effect — desirable for the palette case, possibly surprising for "Copy". Likely acceptable (swipe UX already implies "operate on this block") but worth a UX pass.

Lower-effort variant: keep the direct-call pattern but lift the focus dance into a named helper (`runWithBlockContext(deps, action)`) that authors opt into — flags the requirement without centralizing the invariant.

_Triaged from `docs/follow-ups.md` (P2). Originally surfaced on PR #21._

title: Strict-mode-with-checked-overrides for name-keyed facets
description:
## Problem

Every name-keyed facet (`propertySchemasFacet`, `propertyEditorOverridesFacet`, `postCommitProcessorsFacet`, `sameTxProcessorsFacet`, `queriesFacet`, `mutatorsFacet`, `typesFacet`, `valuePresetsFacet`, …) follows the same convention: warn on duplicate name, last-wins.
